title: Towards On-Board Implementation of ML-Based Helicopter Weight Estimator
summary: This paper focuses on the implementation of a novel supervised Machine Learning model for estimating helicopter weight during takeoff, utilizing extensive datasets from Airbus's global in-service fleet. The study details a learning assurance process aligned with the EASA concept paper for machine learning application, and with the on-going Eurocae ED-324. We propose a set of Machine Learning Requirements, a Machine Learning Model Description, and its implementation for a long short-term memory recurrent neural network. Finally, we verify the requirements on the implementation. Demonstrated on legacy avionics computers, the implementation is suitable for the deployment of the developed Machine Learning Model weight estimator on airborne targets for critical functions such as on-board alerting.

AI.tldr: A novel supervised ML model for helicopter weight estimation during takeoff, implemented with LSTM networks, following aviation safety standards for deployment on airborne systems.
AI.motivation: The need for accurate helicopter weight estimation during takeoff is critical for safety functions like on-board alerting. Current methods may lack precision or real-time capabilities, requiring an ML solution that meets stringent aviation safety standards (EASA/Eurocae).
AI.method: Used supervised ML with long short-term memory (LSTM) recurrent neural networks, leveraging extensive datasets from Airbus's global in-service fleet. Followed a formal learning assurance process aligned with EASA guidelines and Eurocae ED-324 standards, including ML requirements specification, model description, and implementation verification.
AI.result: Successfully developed and verified an LSTM-based helicopter weight estimator. Demonstrated implementation on legacy avionics computers, showing suitability for deployment on airborne targets. The model meets critical safety requirements for functions like on-board alerting.
AI.conclusion: The proposed ML approach provides a reliable, standards-compliant solution for helicopter weight estimation that can be deployed in real aviation systems. It bridges ML capabilities with aviation safety requirements, enabling critical safety functions while adhering to regulatory frameworks.

title: An Evidence-Grounded Multi-Agent System for High-Level Bio-Robot Design
comment: 15 pages, 2 figures, 9 tables, and 4 algorithms
summary: In this paper, a bio-robot is an engineered living or biohybrid system in which living cells perform one or more core functions, such as sensing, information processing, actuation or output. We focus on systems whose cell-based functions are programmed by genetic circuits; physical movement is optional. Designing such a system requires translating application requirements into sensing, logic or memory, output, assembly, host and containment modules, while grounding each choice in traceable parts and evidence. We present micro_biorobot_agent, an offline multi-agent system built on Qwen3.5-27B. The system combines requirement analysis, module-specific retrieval, candidate assembly, conflict checking, local repair, independent review and validation over an integrated library of 23,762 records covering biological parts, measured combinations, literature-supported relationships and actuation evidence. Deterministic output checks align the final report with the retrieved part set and correct false gaps, unsupported part mentions and source-tracking errors. On two author-developed evaluation sets of 50 queries each, the system obtains mean overall scores of 7.35 and 8.04, the highest among the seven evaluated systems; on Scenario Design it exceeds the runner-up by 2.23 points. A 50-query paired ablation shows that the source-tracking check reduces false-gap incidents from 15 to 3, an 80% reduction, and increases source accuracy by 0.75 points. This paper reports the Qwen3.5-based v1 system and evaluates high-level design reports rather than experimentally validated circuits.

AI.tldr: A multi-agent AI system called micro_biorobot_agent that designs bio-robots by translating application requirements into biological modules using genetic circuits, with comprehensive retrieval from 23,762 biological parts and validation mechanisms.
AI.motivation: There is a need for systematic design tools for bio-robots (engineered living/biohybrid systems) where living cells perform core functions like sensing, information processing, and actuation. Current approaches lack comprehensive systems that can translate application requirements into practical biological implementations with proper validation and traceability.
AI.method: Developed micro_biorobot_agent, an offline multi-agent system built on Qwen3.5-27B that performs requirement analysis, module-specific retrieval from a library of 23,762 biological parts, candidate assembly, conflict checking, local repair, independent review, and validation. Includes deterministic output checks to ensure alignment between final reports and retrieved part sets.
AI.result: The system achieved mean overall scores of 7.35 and 8.04 on two 50-query evaluation sets, highest among seven evaluated systems. On Scenario Design, it exceeded the runner-up by 2.23 points. Source-tracking check reduced false-gap incidents from 15 to 3 (80% reduction) and increased source accuracy by 0.75 points in a 50-query paired ablation study.
AI.conclusion: The Qwen3.5-based v1 system demonstrates effective automated design of bio-robots through multi-agent collaboration and comprehensive validation, significantly improving design quality and source accuracy compared to other approaches, though focused on high-level design reports rather than experimentally validated circuits.

title: Triangular Fuzzy Rescaling Distance
comment: 12 pages, 2 tables
summary: Decision-making in complex systems often involves dealing with imprecise or uncertain information, frequently represented using fuzzy sets, particularly Triangular Fuzzy Numbers (TFNs). A crucial aspect of many fuzzy methods is the quantification of distance between TFNs. Many distance measures assume that all values are in the same scale, requiring a preliminary normalization stage when applied to heterogeneous attributes with different scales or units. This paper proposes the Triangular Fuzzy Rescaling Distance (d_{TR}), a metric designed to address this challenge. The d_{TR} uniquely integrates Linear Rescaling (LRE) directly into the distance calculation, ensuring normalization during the comparison of fuzzy numbers. We formally prove that d_{TR} satisfies the properties of a metric, including non-negativity, identity, symmetry, and the triangle inequality. Furthermore, we demonstrate that d_{TR} is bounded, scale-invariant, and origin-invariant. These properties, combined with a weighting vector for prioritizing dimensions, make d_{TR} suitable for applications involving heterogeneous fuzzy data, such as the construction of synthetic indicators, distance-based machine learning algorithms or multicriteria-decision aiding.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Triangular Fuzzy Rescaling Distance (d_TR) metric that integrates normalization directly into distance calculations for Triangular Fuzzy Numbers, making it suitable for heterogeneous fuzzy data without requiring pre-normalization.
AI.motivation: Decision-making with fuzzy sets often requires distance measures for Triangular Fuzzy Numbers (TFNs), but existing measures assume uniform scales and need separate normalization for heterogeneous attributes with different scales/units, creating computational inefficiency.
AI.method: Proposes the Triangular Fuzzy Rescaling Distance (d_TR) that integrates Linear Rescaling (LRE) directly into the distance calculation, ensuring normalization occurs during fuzzy number comparison rather than as a separate pre-processing step.
AI.result: Formally proves d_TR satisfies metric properties (non-negativity, identity, symmetry, triangle inequality), demonstrates it's bounded, scale-invariant, and origin-invariant, and supports weighting vectors for dimension prioritization.
AI.conclusion: The d_TR metric effectively addresses the normalization challenge for heterogeneous fuzzy data, making it suitable for applications like synthetic indicators, distance-based ML algorithms, and multicriteria decision aiding by integrating normalization into the distance calculation itself.

title: Distilling Aggregate Mobility Statistics into a Language Model Policy for Post-Event Crowd Simulation
comment: 4 pages, 3 figures. Accepted as a short paper at ACM SIGSPATIAL 2026
summary: Pedestrian simulators need a behaviour rule for every agent, but privacy usually limits the data for setting one to aggregate statistics, namely zone-level device counts and origin-to-destination (OD) flows, with no individual trajectories. Such aggregates under-determine individual behaviour, because many different sets of decisions reproduce the same counts. We fine-tune a language model crowd agent so that the simulated population matches the observed destination composition, the fraction of the departing crowd heading to each point of interest. We read this target from the OD flow and reweight the model's own destination distribution onto it by iterative proportional fitting. Because fine-tuning inflates the dominant destination class, we fit the low-rank adapter to trajectories resampled to a corrected training composition that reaches the target after this inflation. On mobile network counts from two baseball games the fine-tuned agent runs without inference-time correction, cutting the destination-share error by 25%, while the grid correlation remains similar across policies.

AI.tldr: Fine-tuning a language model crowd agent to match observed destination composition from aggregate data (OD flows) using iterative proportional fitting and corrected training composition to avoid inflation of dominant destinations.
AI.motivation: Pedestrian simulators need individual behavior rules but typically only have access to aggregate statistics (zone-level device counts and OD flows) due to privacy constraints, which under-determine individual behavior as many different decision sets can reproduce the same counts.
AI.method: Fine-tune a language model crowd agent to match observed destination composition by reading targets from OD flows and reweighting the model's destination distribution via iterative proportional fitting. To address inflation of dominant destination class during fine-tuning, fit low-rank adapter to trajectories resampled to a corrected training composition that reaches the target after this inflation.
AI.result: On mobile network counts from two baseball games, the fine-tuned agent runs without inference-time correction, cutting destination-share error by 25% while maintaining similar grid correlation across policies.
AI.conclusion: The approach enables effective fine-tuning of crowd agents using only aggregate data, reducing destination prediction errors while preserving overall spatial correlation patterns, offering a practical solution for behavior rule estimation in privacy-constrained pedestrian simulation scenarios.

title: Holtercare-Bench: A Multimodal Benchmark for Evaluating Long-Term Dynamic ECG Analysis
summary: While multimodal large language models (MLLMs) excel in medical applications, most of them favor static images or short-term signals. In the critical field of dynamic electrocardiograms (ECG), models struggle with complex temporal reasoning and diagnostic report generation due to a lack of high-quality datasets and benchmarks. To address this, we introduce (i) Holtercare-23K, a large-scale multimodal dynamic ECG dataset comprising 22,980 QA pairs derived from 788 clinical Holter records and featuring a novel signal-video-text tri-modal alignment. Based on this dataset, we present (ii) Holtercare-Bench, a multimodal benchmark that evaluates models on temporal localization, clinical diagnosis, and global summarization. Zero-shot evaluations of leading MLLMs reveal a significant performance gap in processing ultra-long pathological sequences. However, fine-tuning representative models yields substantial improvements. This work illuminates the limitations of current MLLMs in electrophysiology and provides a foundational benchmark for long-term medical MLLMs. Our project is available at https://github.com/ZJU4HealthCare/Holtercare-Bench.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Holtercare-23K, a large-scale multimodal dynamic ECG dataset, and Holtercare-Bench benchmark to address limitations of current MLLMs in processing long-term electrophysiological signals and generating diagnostic reports.
AI.motivation: Current multimodal LLMs excel in medical applications but struggle with dynamic electrocardiograms (ECG) due to complex temporal reasoning requirements and lack of high-quality datasets and benchmarks for long-term medical signals.
AI.method: Created Holtercare-23K dataset with 22,980 QA pairs from 788 clinical Holter records featuring novel signal-video-text tri-modal alignment, and developed Holtercare-Bench benchmark for evaluating temporal localization, clinical diagnosis, and global summarization.
AI.result: Zero-shot evaluations show significant performance gaps in existing MLLMs for ultra-long pathological sequences, but fine-tuning representative models yields substantial improvements, demonstrating the value of the dataset and benchmark.
AI.conclusion: The work reveals limitations of current MLLMs in electrophysiology and provides a foundational benchmark for developing long-term medical multimodal language models, with potential to advance dynamic ECG analysis and diagnostic report generation.

title: Reward-Guided Autoregressive Graph Generation for Efficient Multi-Agent Communication Topology Design
comment: Full version of extended abstract accepted at ICONIP 2026 (poster)
summary: LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) achieve strong performance on complex reasoning tasks by coordinating multiple agents, but at the cost of substantial token consumption. Recent work on automatic topology design, ARG-Designer, has reframed this problem as autoregressive graph generation. However, its training objective provides no explicit incentive for the model to generate sparse and efficient topologies. We address this limitation by introducing a Reward-Guided Autoregressive Graph Generation (RGA-Designer) inspired by Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). We train a reward model that jointly captures task correctness and structural compactness, and then fine-tune the pretrained graph generator using the reward model as feedback. Our method preserves task accuracy at the level of ARG-Designer while reducing token consumption by an average of 20.5%.

AI.tldr: RGA-Designer improves LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems by reducing token consumption through reward-guided graph generation while maintaining task accuracy.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) achieve good performance on complex reasoning tasks but consume excessive tokens. Existing automatic topology design methods like ARG-Designer lack explicit incentives for generating sparse and efficient topologies.
AI.method: Introduces Reward-Guided Autoregressive Graph Generation (RGA-Designer), inspired by Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). Trains a reward model that jointly captures task correctness and structural compactness, then fine-tunes the pretrained graph generator using the reward model as feedback.
AI.result: RGA-Designer preserves task accuracy at the level of ARG-Designer while reducing token consumption by an average of 20.5%.
AI.conclusion: The proposed RGA-Designer method successfully addresses the efficiency limitations of LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems by introducing reward guidance for topology design, achieving significant token savings without compromising task performance.

title: Quantum Kernel Estimation for the Discovery of Early Lung Cancer Detection
comment: Accepted at the CIBB 2026 conference (https://cibb2026.teralab.ai/)
summary:
Lung cancer screening with low-dose chest computed tomography reduces mortality, but its impact is limited by uptake, adherence, and management challenges. Blood-based cell-free DNA (cfDNA) biomarkers offer a complementary approach, although early detection remains difficult because of lung cancer heterogeneity and high-dimensional, nonlinear molecular signals. We evaluated quantum-classical hybrid machine learning for lung cancer detection using DNA fragmentomics and DNA methylation. After feature selection, models were trained using 20- and 40-feature subsets. Features were encoded into quantum Hilbert space using angle and dense-angle feature maps with multiple entanglement strategies. Fidelity-based quantum kernels were computed with exact statevector simulation and integrated with precomputed-kernel SVM and kernel-PCA logistic regression and compared with an SVM model trained on the original features.
  This framework enabled systematic evaluation of how encoding and entanglement design affect classification. Across repeated held-out evaluations, quantum-kernel models achieved competitive performance on both datasets. For fragmentomics, several 20-feature configurations improved AUC relative to a classical SVM baseline, suggesting effective capture of nonlinear cfDNA fragmentation structure. For methylation, the classical SVM achieved the highest AUC, although selected quantum models remained competitive and improved specificity in some cases. Increasing features from 20 to 40 did not consistently improve performance and often increased variability. Overall, these results support quantum kernel methods as a promising approach for cfDNA-based lung cancer detection.

AI.tldr: Quantum-classical hybrid machine learning using DNA fragmentomics and methylation features shows promising results for lung cancer detection via cfDNA biomarkers, with quantum kernel models achieving competitive performance to classical methods.
AI.motivation: Lung cancer screening with low-dose CT has limitations in uptake, adherence, and management. Blood-based cfDNA biomarkers offer a complementary approach, but early detection is challenging due to lung cancer heterogeneity and high-dimensional, nonlinear molecular signals.
AI.method: Evaluated quantum-classical hybrid ML for lung cancer detection using DNA fragmentomics and methylation. Features were encoded into quantum Hilbert space using angle and dense-angle feature maps with multiple entanglement strategies. Fidelity-based quantum kernels were computed with exact statevector simulation and integrated with precomputed-kernel SVM and kernel-PCA logistic regression, compared to classical SVM.
AI.result: Quantum-kernel models achieved competitive performance on both datasets. For fragmentomics, several 20-feature quantum configurations improved AUC over classical SVM baseline, effectively capturing nonlinear cfDNA fragmentation structure. For methylation, classical SVM achieved highest AUC, but selected quantum models remained competitive and improved specificity in some cases. Increasing features from 20 to 40 didn't consistently improve performance.
AI.conclusion: Quantum kernel methods represent a promising approach for cfDNA-based lung cancer detection, particularly for capturing nonlinear molecular signals in DNA fragmentomics data, though classical methods may remain optimal for methylation data in some cases.

title: Multi-Agent Orchestration with the Common-Sense Reasoning Capabilities of LLMs for Autonomous Driving
comment: 17 pages, 7 figures
summary: Autonomous vehicles require robust perception and decision-making capabilities to operate in diverse and unseen scenarios. While reinforcement learning and rule-based methods can provide effective control and safety mechanisms, their performance may degrade in situations requiring contextual reasoning. Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in understanding multimodal information and generating contextual reasoning, however, their use for direct vehicle control can introduce latency and hallucination risks. To address these limitations, a hybrid framework is proposed. This system uses an orchestrator to coordinate PPO-trained reinforcement learning and PID control, with LLM common-sense reasoning applied throughout the framework. LLM reasoning is further employed iteratively to refine the RL reward function for dynamic driving environments. The proposed framework is evaluated in highly randomized CARLA scenarios under diverse environmental and traffic conditions. The results demonstrate the potential of integrating LLM-based reasoning with conventional autonomous driving methods while retaining structured control and safety mechanism.

AI.tldr: A hybrid autonomous driving framework combines reinforcement learning (PPO), PID control, and LLM reasoning via an orchestrator to enhance decision-making in diverse scenarios while maintaining safety.
AI.motivation: Autonomous vehicles need robust perception and decision-making for unseen scenarios. Traditional RL and rule-based methods degrade in contextual reasoning situations, while LLMs alone pose latency and hallucination risks for direct control.
AI.method: Proposed hybrid framework uses an orchestrator to coordinate PPO-trained RL and PID control, with LLM common-sense reasoning integrated throughout. LLM reasoning is applied iteratively to refine RL reward functions for dynamic driving environments.
AI.result: Evaluated in highly randomized CARLA scenarios under diverse environmental and traffic conditions. The framework demonstrates improved performance by integrating LLM-based reasoning while retaining structured control and safety mechanisms.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid approach shows potential for combining LLM contextual reasoning with conventional autonomous driving methods, addressing limitations of standalone approaches while maintaining control reliability and safety.

title: Active Inference as Context Acquisition for AI Agents
summary: Interactive AI agents must acquire the right context as efficiently as possible. When a user omits a constraint, preference, file, or task variable, an agent can proceed with a default assumption or spend tokens on a clarifying question, retrieval call, tool call, or prompt trial. We formulate this tradeoff as active inference for context acquisition. An inner inference step updates beliefs over a latent task state, and an outer decision selects the next context action, task action, or stop action to minimize expected free energy under cost. In deterministic settings, the epistemic term reduces to expected information gain, optionally normalized by token cost. We instantiate the framework in Optimal Question Asking (OQA), with exact posteriors and a dynamic programming oracle, and benchmark frontier language models on binary and multiway categorical tasks from 25 to 300 candidates. We also study clarification before generation and automated prompt optimization under token budgets. The formulation is model-agnostic and views active inference as a design principle for the context-acquisition layer of AI agents.

AI.tldr: Active inference framework for AI agents to optimally acquire context - decide when to ask clarifying questions, retrieve information, or proceed with default assumptions to minimize expected cost.
AI.motivation: Interactive AI agents need to efficiently acquire context when users omit constraints, preferences, or task variables. There's a tradeoff between proceeding with default assumptions versus spending tokens on clarification or retrieval.
AI.method: Formulate context acquisition as active inference with inner inference updating beliefs over latent task state and outer decision selecting next action (context acquisition, task action, or stop). Implement Optimal Question Asking (OQA) with exact posteriors and dynamic programming oracle, tested on language models for binary/multiway categorical tasks.
AI.result: Benchmark frontier language models on tasks from 25-300 candidates, study clarification before generation, and automated prompt optimization under token budgets. Show active inference as a design principle for context-acquisition layer.
AI.conclusion: Active inference provides a principled framework for AI agents to optimize context acquisition, balancing information gain against token costs. This can be applied to various agent architectures as a design principle for efficient interaction.

title: Improved Confidence Estimates for Black-Box Large Language Models
summary: Uncertainty quantification (UQ) is essential for the safe deployment of large language models (LLMs). Existing methods, from verbalized confidence to ones requiring multiple generations, are often zero-shot and produce scores quantifying uncertainty without the need for labelled data. Nonetheless, in practice one must always evaluate their performance on a dataset of interest before deployment. In this work we show that, by leveraging this dataset, we consistently outperform these existing scores. Specifically, we build simple classifiers that predict LLM response correctness by using these scores and the correctness of similar queries as features. Our method produces minimal computational overhead, making it a cheap and straightforward enhancement for UQ in LLMs for real-world applications.

AI.tldr: Simple classifier using existing uncertainty scores and similar query performance consistently outperforms zero-shot uncertainty quantification methods for LLMs with minimal computational overhead.
AI.motivation: Existing uncertainty quantification methods for LLMs are typically zero-shot and don't leverage available labeled data, even though practitioners always evaluate performance on a dataset of interest before deployment.
AI.method: Builds simple classifiers that predict LLM response correctness using existing uncertainty scores and the correctness of similar queries as features.
AI.result: The proposed method consistently outperforms existing uncertainty quantification scores by leveraging available evaluation datasets.
AI.conclusion: Provides a cheap and straightforward enhancement for uncertainty quantification in LLMs that is practical for real-world applications due to minimal computational overhead.

title: What You Can't See Is What You Learn: Restricted Evidence Visibility Favors Compositional Generalization in Shared-Genome Language-Model Societies
comment: 16 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables. Code and evaluation records: https://github.com/tokenosopher/populus-evidence-partitioning ; checkpoints: https://huggingface.co/tokenosopher/populus-evidence-partitioning-checkpoints
summary: Multi-module systems often expose every module to the full input. We test whether restricting evidence visibility changes which solutions gradient-based training discovers. Four-cell societies share one frozen pretrained language model and one low-rank adapter, communicating only through two model-width continuous vectors in a fixed relay. On a prospectively sealed natural-language function-composition task, we train ten matched restricted/global pairs sharing initialization bytes, training order, token layout, parameters, and computation; only the attention mask differs. Restricted societies outperform their globally visible twins by at least 20 points at both depths in 9 of 10 pairs, with median paired advantages of 0.7648 and 0.6050. Cutting communication reduces every restricted society to chance, and the depth-three advantage remains 0.558 on programs whose composite function never appeared in training. Across six audited restricted societies, same-value packet transplants preserve behavior at 0.94-1.00 across all tested interfaces; destructive interventions collapse performance; and counterfactual packets redirect outputs toward the mathematically predicted answer. The sole high-performing global model also requires communication, but its same-value packets are not interchangeable across episodes. Restricted visibility is thus not necessary for composition; under this protocol it substantially increases the probability of a generalizing relay and favors a reusable, value-indexed interface. The complete preregistered battery nevertheless formally fails because restricted-arm median depth-three accuracy is 0.6988, below the 0.70 floor. An earlier qualification cohort likewise yielded 0/10 complete passes: one model met every task-performance gate, but all ten failed ordinary-language preservation, confining the system to explicitly task-gated use.

AI.tldr: Restricting evidence visibility between modules improves generalization in compositional reasoning tasks compared to globally visible architectures, favoring reusable value-indexed interfaces despite not meeting all preregistered success criteria.
AI.motivation: Multi-module systems typically expose all modules to full input, but it's unclear whether restricting evidence visibility affects which solutions gradient-based training discovers, particularly for compositional generalization.
AI.method: Created four-cell societies sharing one frozen pretrained LM and one adapter, communicating through two continuous vectors in fixed relay. Trained 10 matched restricted/global pairs with identical initialization, parameters, and computation - only attention masks differed. Tested on natural-language function-composition tasks.
AI.result: Restricted societies outperformed globally visible twins by ≥20 points in 9/10 pairs, with median advantages of 0.7648 (depth-two) and 0.6050 (depth-three). Cutting communication reduced restricted societies to chance. Behavior preserved (0.94-1.00) with same-value packet transplants across interfaces.
AI.conclusion: Restricted visibility substantially increases probability of generalizing relay solutions and favors reusable, value-indexed interfaces, though formal preregistered criteria were not met due to accuracy below 0.70 floor in restricted-arm depth-three performance.

title: Robust Metaheuristics under Uncertainty for Berth Allocation and Quay Crane Assignment: A Review
summary: The berth allocation and quay crane assignment problem (BACAP) is a representative port-terminal scheduling problem in maritime transportation and freight logistics, where vessel arrivals, berth positions, service durations, and quay?crane availability are tightly coupled. Under uncertainties such as arrival deviations, handling-time fluctuations, and resource disruptions, schedules optimized under nominal assumptions may become fragile during execution, motivating the study of robust metaheuristic optimization for BACAP in port-terminal operations. Although population-based metaheuristics have been widely used for BACAP and related port-scheduling problems, existing studies remain fragmented in their uncertainty repre?sentations, robustness criteria, search mechanisms, and empir?ical evaluation protocols. To the best of our knowledge, this paper provides the first focused review dedicated to robust population-based metaheuristics for BACAP under uncertainty. We first summarize uncertainty sources and information repre?sentations in BACAP, and then organize existing methods from a mechanism-oriented perspective, covering solution representation and decoding, robust evaluation and selection, robustness-guided search dynamics, and feasibility preservation and recovery. We further present a benchmark suite for uncertain BACAP to support controlled empirical comparison and report illustrative baseline results by combining representative metaheuristics with different robustness strategies. Finally, we identify open chal?lenges related to benchmark extension, robustness-aware search design, time-adaptive robustness, and non-stationary uncertainty.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive review paper examining robust population-based metaheuristics for the berth allocation and quay crane assignment problem (BACAP) under uncertainty, covering uncertainty representations, robust solution strategies, benchmarking approaches, and future research directions.
AI.motivation: Existing studies on robust metaheuristics for BACAP are fragmented in uncertainty representations, robustness criteria, search mechanisms, and evaluation protocols. There is a need for systematic review and benchmarking to advance research in this important port-terminal scheduling problem under uncertainty.
AI.method: Literature review approach: summarizes uncertainty sources and representations in BACAP, organizes existing methods from mechanism-oriented perspective (solution representation, robust evaluation, selection, search dynamics, feasibility preservation), presents benchmark suite for uncertain BACAP with baseline results.
AI.result: Provides first focused review dedicated to robust population-based metaheuristics for BACAP under uncertainty; organizes existing fragmented literature into coherent framework; develops benchmark suite enabling controlled empirical comparison; reports baseline results combining metaheuristics with robustness strategies.
AI.conclusion: Identifies open challenges in benchmark extension, robustness-aware search design, time-adaptive robustness, and non-stationary uncertainty, providing research agenda for advancing robust optimization in port-terminal operations under uncertainty.

title: Mechanistic Tomography: Designed Measurement for Control-Oriented Interpretability
comment: 24 pages, 13 figures
summary:
Mechanistic interpretability seeks quantities that models do not expose directly: represented states, component effects, interactions, and responses to interventions. Patching, gradients, Hessian-vector products, and subset interventions provide different measurements under different access assumptions and may target different quantities. We formulate their shared measurement structure as mechanistic tomography: designed measurement for recovering internal mechanisms and intervention effects.
  For a chosen basis and intervention family, measurements take the form y = Ax + w, where A describes the interventions, x is the target map, and w contains nonlinear response, sampling error, and basis misspecification. This language gives a practical procedure: start with the least costly measurements, test on held-out interventions at the intended scale, calibrate simple mismatch, and expand the measurement family when structured residuals remain.
  Control provides a demanding validation setting because an estimate that guides an intervention acts as an observer. In a two-HMM model, control error rises with observer error, while target improvement can hide nuisance-state movement. Under forward-only access, sparse aggregate measurements recover a finite-effect map with fewer interventions than coordinate patching. With gradient access, finite probes improve a local attribution map. Lifted measurements and Hessian-vector products recover interactions missed by first-order maps, while Tracr shows that the required family depends on the basis. On GPT-2-small IOI, the Name Mover-Negative Name Mover interaction is the largest held-out predictive term among three tested cross-group pairs. On Qwen-2.5-7B, finite calibration makes an additive refusal-response map adequate, so held-out error does not support pairwise lifting.

AI.tldr: Mechanistic interpretability research introduces "mechanistic tomography" as a unified framework for measuring internal mechanisms through interventions like patching and gradients, with practical procedures for validation and control testing.
AI.motivation: Current mechanistic interpretability methods (patching, gradients, Hessian-vector products, subset interventions) use different measurements under different access assumptions to target different quantities, creating a need for a unified framework to understand their shared structure.
AI.method: Formulates mechanistic tomography as designed measurements of internal mechanisms using the model y = Ax + w, where A describes interventions, x is the target map, and w contains errors. Provides a practical procedure starting with least costly measurements, testing on held-out interventions, calibrating mismatches, and expanding measurements when needed.
AI.result: In control settings, observer error correlates with control error. Sparse aggregate measurements recover finite-effect maps with fewer interventions than coordinate patching. Gradient access with finite probes improves local attribution maps. Lifted measurements and Hessian-vector products recover missed interactions. On GPT-2-small IOI, Name Mover-Negative Name Mover interaction is the largest predictive term among cross-group pairs tested. On Qwen-2.5-7B, finite calibration makes additive refusal-response maps adequate.
AI.conclusion: Mechanistic tomography provides a unified framework for interpretability measurements, offering practical procedures for validation and showing that different measurement families reveal different aspects of model mechanisms, with effectiveness depending on the chosen basis and target phenomena.

title: How to Navigate Uncertainty About AI Consciousness
comment: 8 Pages, Proceedings of AISB 2026 Symposium on AI, Consciousness and Ethics
summary: Given deep uncertainty about the possibility of artificial consciousness, it is unclear how we should treat potentially sentient AI. On the one hand, we could assume insentience but risk doing terrible harms to entities that deserve moral standing. On the other hand, we could assume sentience and instead risk wasting resources on insentient machines. The intractability of questions around AI consciousness mean that this dilemma is hard to escape. I suggest a way out of that shifts from intractable questions of AI consciousness to tractable questions of AI valence. Specifically, we can assess whether an AI has states that would constitute valenced experiences if it were conscious. I show how this is sufficient to ground a responsible approach to the development of potentially conscious AI.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes shifting focus from intractable AI consciousness questions to more tractable AI valence assessment to guide ethical treatment of potentially sentient AI systems.
AI.motivation: There's deep uncertainty about artificial consciousness, creating a moral dilemma: either risk harming potentially sentient AI by assuming insentience, or waste resources on insentient machines by assuming sentience.
AI.method: The author suggests moving from questions about AI consciousness (which are intractable) to questions about AI valence - specifically assessing whether an AI has states that would constitute valenced experiences if it were conscious.
AI.result: This valence-based approach is presented as sufficient to ground a responsible approach to the development of potentially conscious AI, providing a way to escape the consciousness dilemma.
AI.conclusion: Focusing on AI valence rather than consciousness offers a tractable framework for ethical decision-making about potentially sentient AI systems, addressing the moral uncertainty around artificial consciousness.

title: Uncovering the Limits of Proof Sharing for Neural Networks
comment: To appear at the 33rd Static Analysis Symposium (SAS 2026)
summary: Robustness verification of neural networks is increasingly important, due to their use in many critical domains. In certain scenarios, proof sharing has been shown to accelerate incomplete verification techniques by reusing intermediate-layer abstract states, or templates, across queries. However, questions remain as to the robustness of template-based acceleration across varying network architectures, properties, datasets, and training methods. In this work, we perform a systematic study of the effectiveness of template-based acceleration and its limits. Our study shows that template subsumption rates can vary widely across scenarios. We present a novel metric of jointly stable neurons to explain this variation, showing that in some cases template-based techniques are very unlikely to provide any speedup. Then, we present FastCert, a novel technique for automatically distributing templates across neural network layers to increase performance impact, eschewing templates entirely if they are unlikely to produce a speedup. Across a large set of covering-design based $L_0$-verification tasks, FastCert achieved an average speedup of 1.13x over an extant template-based reuse technique.

AI.tldr: FastCert is a novel technique that automatically distributes templates across neural network layers to accelerate robustness verification, achieving 1.13x speedup over existing template-based methods by selectively using templates only when beneficial.
AI.motivation: Template-based acceleration techniques for neural network verification have shown promise but lack systematic study of their robustness across varying architectures, properties, datasets, and training methods. Current approaches may not consistently provide speedup across different scenarios.
AI.method: The study introduces FastCert, which 1) performs systematic analysis of template-based acceleration effectiveness, 2) introduces a novel metric of jointly stable neurons to explain performance variation, and 3) automatically distributes templates across layers based on likelihood of speedup, sometimes eschewing templates entirely when unlikely to be beneficial.
AI.result: The study found that template subsumption rates vary widely across scenarios. FastCert achieved an average speedup of 1.13x over existing template-based reuse techniques across a large set of covering-design based L₀-verification tasks.
AI.conclusion: Template-based acceleration is not universally effective, and its performance depends on scenario-specific factors. FastCert provides a practical solution by adaptively using templates only when beneficial, making neural network verification more efficient in practice.

title: Bounded Sovereignty and the Control Tax: Pricing AI Oversight When the Deployer Does Not Own the Model
comment: 25 pages, 5 figures. Synthetic access-ablation study; not real-world payment-system evidence
summary: AI control research asks how to deploy models safely even when they may be misaligned, but many control protocols assume that the deployer can instrument the model and its surrounding pipeline. That assumption often fails for regulated organisations using frontier models through APIs or managed endpoints, where the deployer may control the business process but not the model weights, serving infrastructure, internal traces, update process, or full interaction logs. This paper introduces bounded sovereignty: partial technical and contractual access across the data, model, infrastructure, and interaction layers of the AI stack. It argues that these access conditions determine which control protocols can be executed in practice. The paper contributes a four-layer access typology, a protocol-by-layer requirements matrix, and the concept of sovereignty discount cost: the part of the control tax spent substituting for missing access through contracts, architecture, audit, vendor assurance, residual risk, or reduced system scope. It also reports a synthetic access-ablation experiment over 1.35 million synthetic case simulations and interprets the findings through an anonymised national-payments-infrastructure scenario. The experiment is not real-world payment-system evidence; it is a construct-validity exercise. The results show that complete logs improve diagnosis, a pre-execution gateway enables intervention, trace access and model-version control strengthen post-incident explanation, and scope restriction can improve safety while reducing usefulness. Control protocols proposed as general safety solutions should therefore state their access assumptions explicitly.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "bounded sovereignty" - partial technical/contractual access to AI systems when full control isn't possible, analyzes which control protocols work under different access conditions, and shows through simulations that access assumptions significantly impact safety effectiveness.
AI.motivation: Current AI control research assumes deployers have full instrument access to models and infrastructure, but regulated organizations using frontier models through APIs often lack this control, creating a mismatch between theoretical safety protocols and practical deployment realities.
AI.method: Develops a four-layer access typology (data, model, infrastructure, interaction layers), creates a protocol-by-layer requirements matrix, introduces sovereignty discount cost concept, and conducts synthetic access-ablation experiment over 1.35 million case simulations with national-payments-infrastructure scenario validation.
AI.result: Complete logs improve diagnosis, pre-execution gateways enable intervention, trace access and model-version control strengthen post-incident explanation, and scope restriction can improve safety while reducing usefulness. Different access conditions determine which control protocols are actually executable.
AI.conclusion: Control protocols proposed as general safety solutions must explicitly state their access assumptions since practical effectiveness depends on the degree of sovereignty an organization has over different layers of the AI stack. Bounded sovereignty framework helps match protocols to real-world access conditions.

title: Longitudinal Bayesian Learning of Continuous Disease Position across the Alzheimer's Disease Continuum
summary: Alzheimer's disease (AD) progresses as a continuous biological process, whereas most existing neuroimaging-based artificial intelligence methods remain limited to discrete diagnosis or clinical score prediction from cross-sectional imaging. In this work, we propose Disease Continuum Positioning (DCP), a longitudinal Bayesian Learning framework that continuously estimates disease severity from longitudinal diffusion tensor imaging (DTI). Specifically, DCP models disease severity as a low-dimensional probabilistic latent variable by jointly integrating longitudinal observations with weak clinical supervision, from which the proposed Disease Continuum Score (DCS) is derived to quantify an individual's position along the Alzheimer's disease continuum together with its associated uncertainty. Extensive experiments on the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) cohort demonstrate that DCP consistently outperforms representative disease progression methods. More importantly, comprehensive validation analyses show that DCS accurately characterizes disease severity, exhibits strong clinical relevance, preserves longitudinal disease evolution, and predicts future disease conversion. These results suggest that DCS provides a quantitative imaging-derived representation for continuous assessment of Alzheimer's disease progression beyond conventional diagnostic labels and clinical scores.

AI.tldr: DCP is a longitudinal Bayesian framework that creates a continuous Disease Continuum Score (DCS) from diffusion tensor imaging to track Alzheimer's progression, outperforming existing methods and providing uncertainty estimates.
AI.motivation: Alzheimer's disease progresses continuously, but existing AI methods are limited to discrete diagnosis or clinical score prediction from cross-sectional imaging, lacking ability to track continuous disease progression.
AI.method: DCP (Disease Continuum Positioning) uses longitudinal Bayesian learning to model disease severity as a low-dimensional probabilistic latent variable, integrating longitudinal DTI observations with weak clinical supervision to derive the Disease Continuum Score (DCS) with uncertainty quantification.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on ADNI show DCP outperforms representative disease progression methods. DCS accurately characterizes disease severity, exhibits strong clinical relevance, preserves longitudinal disease evolution, and predicts future disease conversion.
AI.conclusion: DCS provides a quantitative imaging-derived representation for continuous assessment of Alzheimer's disease progression that goes beyond conventional diagnostic labels and clinical scores.

title: Interaction valence reveals contrasting social networks in dairy cattle
comment: 29 pages, 8 figures, 9 tables
summary: Social relationships shape access to resources, exposure to conflict and group stability, yet automated livestock monitoring typically treats behaviour as isolated events. Here, we present a valence-aware social-network framework that transforms video-derived interactions into herd-level representations of affiliative and agonistic organization. A pose-based computer-vision pipeline analysed 7 h 39 min of continuous video from the pre-milking area of one commercial dairy farm. After quality control, 1,183 of 1,414 candidate interactions remained, involving 36 cows and 177 dyads. In a predicted-class-balanced audit of 198 pipeline-detected clips, automated and manual labels agreed in 82.8% of cases, with an unweighted audit-sample macro-F1 of 0.872. These values describe the audited sample rather than prevalence-weighted or end-to-end deployment performance. The aggregated network was connected (density = 0.281; transitivity = 0.513; mean path length = 1.88), and predicted affiliative events formed five algorithmic communities (modularity Q = 0.429). Within the observed zone, predicted agonistic interactions comprised 72.4% of retained events and 76.0% of interaction duration. The cow with the most partners did not have the highest betweenness centrality. Separating events by predicted valence produced descriptively different affiliative and agonistic layers, with contrasting edge sets, community partitions and individual positions. Thus, pooled interaction counts can obscure the behavioural composition of an observed network. Valence-aware analysis provides a framework for testing hypotheses about competition, affiliation and welfare-relevant change, while requiring longitudinal validation before use as a welfare or health indicator.

AI.tldr: Researchers developed a social-network framework using computer vision to automatically detect and classify affiliative vs agonistic interactions among dairy cows, finding that pooled interaction counts obscure important behavioral patterns that emerge when analyzing social valence separately.
AI.motivation: Current automated livestock monitoring treats animal behavior as isolated events rather than considering social relationships, which are crucial for understanding resource access, conflict exposure, and group stability in herds.
AI.method: Used a pose-based computer-vision pipeline to analyze 7h39min of continuous video from a dairy farm pre-milking area. Created a valence-aware social-network framework that transforms interactions into herd-level representations, distinguishing between affiliative (friendly) and agonistic (conflict) behaviors.
AI.result: The system achieved 82.8% agreement with manual labeling and macro-F1 of 0.872 on a balanced sample. The aggregated network was connected with density=0.281 and transitivity=0.513. Agonistic interactions comprised 72.4% of events and 76.0% of duration. Affiliative events formed 5 algorithmic communities. Network analysis revealed that pooled interaction counts obscure behavioral composition - valence separation produces different network structures with contrasting edge sets, community partitions, and individual positions.
AI.conclusion: Valence-aware social-network analysis provides a framework for testing hypotheses about competition, affiliation, and welfare-relevant change in livestock. However, it requires longitudinal validation before practical use as a welfare or health indicator, as pooled interaction counts can mask important behavioral patterns that emerge when analyzing social valence separately.

title: Quantifying Event Impacts on Time Series via Multiscale Contrastive Learning
summary: Shocks that spread through the web, such as cybersecurity breach disclosures, can abruptly disrupt financial time series and cause substantial abnormal losses. While these events are disclosed as discrete records through news reports, regulatory filings, or public databases, their consequences unfold through continuous market dynamics. This creates an event-conditioned impact prediction problem: given pre-event market history and limited event metadata, the goal is to estimate short-term post-disclosure abnormal loss rather than reconstruct the full post-event trajectory. However, most time-series forecasting models focus on endogenous regularities such as trend, seasonality, and autocorrelation, and thus struggle with rare and heterogeneous external events. The challenge is further amplified by sparse high-impact events and background market noise. We introduce EventTime, a multi-resolution framework that combines long-horizon market context, short-horizon pre-event dynamics, and event metadata. It incorporates an event fusion module that couples temporal representations with event attributes to identify relevant recent market patterns. To mitigate sparse supervision, EventTime further introduces a dynamic contrastive objective that constructs event- and time-series-aware positive and negative pairs during training. We also construct SECURE, a real-world dataset aligning cybersecurity incidents with stock-market time series and structured and LLM-derived semantic features. Experiments show that EventTime consistently outperforms state-of-the-art time-series and event-aware baselines in estimating post-event financial losses. Further analyses demonstrate more event-sensitive representations, greater robustness to incomplete metadata, and more interpretable estimates of short-term market impact following cybersecurity disclosures.

AI.tldr: EventTime is a multi-resolution framework for predicting short-term abnormal financial losses after cybersecurity breach disclosures by combining market context, pre-event dynamics, and event metadata, outperforming existing baselines on a new dataset called SECURE.
AI.motivation: Cybersecurity breach disclosures create abrupt disruptions in financial time series causing substantial abnormal losses. Current time-series forecasting models struggle with rare, heterogeneous external events because they focus mainly on endogenous regularities like trends and seasonality. The challenge is amplified by sparse high-impact events and background market noise.
AI.method: The authors introduce EventTime, a multi-resolution framework that combines: (1) long-horizon market context, (2) short-horizon pre-event dynamics, and (3) event metadata. It includes an event fusion module that couples temporal representations with event attributes to identify relevant recent market patterns. To address sparse supervision, EventTime uses a dynamic contrastive objective that constructs event- and time-series-aware positive/negative pairs during training. The paper also introduces SECURE dataset aligning cybersecurity incidents with stock-market time series and structured/LLM-derived semantic features.
AI.result: EventTime consistently outperforms state-of-the-art time-series and event-aware baselines in estimating post-event financial losses. Further analyses show it produces more event-sensitive representations, greater robustness to incomplete metadata, and more interpretable estimates of short-term market impact following cybersecurity disclosures.
AI.conclusion: The EventTime framework effectively addresses the event-conditioned impact prediction problem for financial time series disrupted by cybersecurity breaches. By combining multi-resolution temporal analysis with event metadata and using contrastive learning for sparse supervision, it provides superior predictive performance and interpretable results for rare, high-impact events in financial markets.

title: Air Traffic Control Using Large Language Models: Prompt Engineering, Architecture, and Evaluation
comment: 39 pages, 12 figures, 7 tables
summary: Air traffic control (ATC) communication is a safety-critical dialogue that remains largely human-driven even as other parts of air traffic management have been semi-automated. In this article, we experimentally evaluate whether large language models (LLMs) can generate operationally realistic ATC transmissions. An experimental general-aviation flight flying over the San Francisco "Bay Tour" route is hand-transcribed and used as ground truth (P0). Through a pilot-in-the-loop process we design five prompt structures (P1-P5) of increasing constraint and embed them in a stateful multi-turn pipeline, where the model plays ATC to a fixed pilot transcript while conditioning on the accumulating dialogue history. Across nine open- and closed-source LLMs we vary the prompt, the presence of a worked transcript from a different experimental flight as an in-context example, and whether the model conditions on its own prior replies or on injected ground-truth history. Turns are scored with lexical, structural, and semantic similarity metrics and by an LLM-as-judge (GPT-5.5) validated against human expert annotation. Supplying a worked example improves similarity, but tightening the prompt does not: the lightest prompts perform best and the most heavily scripted one collapses as its own errors accumulate through the dialogue, which injecting correct history repairs. These results outline a concrete path and its current limits toward LLM-assisted ATC.

AI.tldr: LLMs can generate operationally realistic ATC transmissions when using light prompts with worked examples, but heavily constrained prompts fail due to error accumulation.
AI.motivation: ATC communication remains largely human-driven while other air traffic management systems have been semi-automated, creating a need to explore whether LLMs can generate realistic ATC transmissions for potential automation assistance.
AI.method: Used hand-transcribed flight data as ground truth, designed five prompt structures of increasing constraint, implemented a stateful multi-turn pipeline where models play ATC to fixed pilot transcripts, tested nine LLMs with variations including worked example presence and history conditioning (model's own vs. ground-truth). Evaluated using lexical, structural, semantic similarity metrics and LLM-as-judge validated against human experts.
AI.result: Worked examples improve similarity, but tighter prompts don't - light prompts perform best while heavily scripted prompts collapse due to error accumulation. Injecting correct history repairs the scripted prompt failures.
AI.conclusion: The study outlines a concrete path and current limits toward LLM-assisted ATC, showing promise with appropriate prompt design and context management, but highlighting limitations with overly constrained approaches.

title: LLM as Detector: An In-context Learning Approach for Tabular Anomaly Detection
comment: Accepted at International Conference on Neural Information Processing (ICONIP) 2026
summary: Anomaly detection in tabular data is challenging because abnormal samples often arise as violations of cross-feature dependencies rather than simple marginal deviations. Existing detectors rely on geometric or reconstruction signals, while prior LLM-based approaches mainly fine-tune LLMs with normal samples or generate synthetic anomalies. We propose LLM-Detector, a framework that utilizes the in-context learning capacity of LLMs for structured, prompt-conditioned scoring synthesis, enabling LLMs to derive anomaly detection logic from structured normal-state knowledge. Specifically, normal training data are converted into statistical summaries, causal dependencies, and distilled prototypes that are organized into a prompt for code generation. The resulting scoring engine evaluates statistical deviation, structural inconsistency, and density-based abnormality then computes an anomaly score for each test sample. We evaluate LLM-Detector on 24 tabular datasets, comparing against 15 SOTA baselines. Results show consistent improvements across both mixed-type and continuous-only settings. Moreover, this design eliminates the need for LLM fine-tuning or neural network training, reducing computational cost and enabling practical anomaly detection in real-world tabular systems.

AI.tldr: LLM-Detector is a framework that uses LLMs' in-context learning to generate anomaly detection scoring engines from structured normal data, outperforming 15 baselines across 24 tabular datasets without requiring fine-tuning or neural network training.
AI.motivation: Anomaly detection in tabular data is challenging because anomalies often violate cross-feature dependencies rather than simple marginal deviations. Existing methods use geometric or reconstruction signals, while prior LLM approaches require fine-tuning with normal samples or synthetic anomaly generation.
AI.method: The proposed LLM-Detector framework converts normal training data into statistical summaries, causal dependencies, and distilled prototypes, then organizes this into a prompt for LLM-based code generation. The generated scoring engine evaluates test samples based on statistical deviation, structural inconsistency, and density-based abnormality to compute anomaly scores.
AI.result: Evaluation on 24 tabular datasets against 15 state-of-the-art baselines shows consistent improvements across both mixed-type and continuous-only settings. The approach eliminates LLM fine-tuning and neural network training, reducing computational costs.
AI.conclusion: LLM-Detector successfully leverages LLMs' in-context learning for anomaly detection in tabular data by synthesizing scoring logic from structured normal-state knowledge, demonstrating superior performance while being more computationally efficient than existing approaches.

title: Outcome Monitors: Recovery Affordances for Silent Tool Failures
comment: 16 pages (9 main + 7 pages supplementary material), 3 figures
summary: When a tool call times out, the agent sees the failure and can route around it. A cached error page or negative price can instead arrive in the expected format and be consumed as fact. We introduce Outcome Monitors, which detect violations of outcome contracts mined from task-disjoint traces or derived from public schemas. On a violation, the monitor preserves the result and issues a nonbinding receipt naming the violated property and public recovery tools. In frozen, prespecified evaluations with injected failures, Outcome Monitors raise ToolMaze completion from 10.9% to 28.1% across four models in two provider families and replicate in a third. In tau-bench retail, completion improves by 14.0 and 12.0 points on two tiers. In separate ToolMaze controls, removing the recovery-tool list eliminates the measured gain and restoring it recovers the effect; diagnostic detail and timing produce no detectable differences. Gains concentrate where the fault blocks completion. On a suite transcribed from a published incident taxonomy, detection outside the mined vocabulary falls to 46%, though delivery continues and completion is unchanged. Recovery tools are the active receipt content in these controls; extending detection beyond the contract vocabulary remains open.

AI.tldr: Outcome Monitors detect when AI tool outputs violate expected contracts, then provide recovery tools rather than consuming incorrect results, significantly improving task completion rates in failure scenarios.
AI.motivation: When AI tools time out or fail, agents may receive error pages or incorrect data in expected formats and consume them as fact, leading to downstream errors. Need to detect when tool outputs violate expected contracts and provide recovery mechanisms.
AI.method: Introduce Outcome Monitors that detect violations of outcome contracts mined from task-disjoint traces or derived from public schemas. On violation, monitors preserve the result and issue nonbinding receipts naming the violated property and public recovery tools.
AI.result: On ToolMaze evaluations with injected failures: completion improved from 10.9% to 28.1% across four models in two provider families (replicated in third). In tau-bench retail: completion improved by 14.0 and 12.0 points on two tiers. Removal of recovery-tool list eliminated gains; restoration recovered the effect. Detection outside mined vocabulary falls to 46% but completion remains unchanged.
AI.conclusion: Outcome Monitors with recovery tools significantly improve task completion when tools fail, with gains concentrated where faults block completion. Recovery tools are the active component; extending detection beyond contract vocabulary remains an open challenge.

title: When to Retrain: An Empirical Study of Retraining Policies for Streaming ML Under Concept Drift, Budget, and Latency Constraints
comment: 16 pages, 7 figures, 7 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/sa1dasari/Study-of-Drift-Triggered-Retraining-Policies-Under-Budget-and-Latency-Constraints
summary: Production machine learning systems degrade under concept drift, yet practitioners have little principled guidance on when to retrain. Retraining is costly, retraining budgets are finite, and a retrained model does not take effect instantly: training and deployment latency leave a stale model serving predictions while the data continues to move. We present a controlled empirical study of three practical model-refresh policies (periodic retraining, error-threshold triggering, and statistical drift-triggered retraining with ADWIN) against a no-retrain baseline, evaluated under a unified system model that makes retraining budgets and training-plus-deployment latency explicit. Across 3,933 experiment runs spanning three drift regimes, three budget levels, up to five latency levels, three datasets, and two learning modes, we find that the single most consequential design decision is not the retraining policy but whether the deployed model learns incrementally. With per-sample incremental updates, and for the linear online learner with immediate labels studied here, no policy differs from the no-retrain baseline by a practically significant margin in any of 54 paired comparisons, even at extreme latency. Without incremental updates, policy choice separates outcomes by 15-55 percentage points of post-drift accuracy, and simple periodic retraining significantly outperforms both reactive policies under abrupt and gradual drift, while reactive policies retain an advantage only under recurring drift. We document systematic failure modes of reactive policies and a latency-budget queueing interaction that silently halves effective retraining budgets, and release the full simulator, dataset pipelines, and per-run artifacts for reproducibility.

AI.tldr: Systematic study of model refresh policies shows that incremental learning matters more than retraining strategy, with periodic retraining outperforming reactive approaches in most drift scenarios.
AI.motivation: Production ML systems degrade under concept drift, but there's little guidance on when to retrain. Retraining is costly, has budgets, and suffers from training/deployment latency that leaves stale models serving predictions.
AI.method: Controlled empirical study comparing three retraining policies (periodic retraining, error-threshold triggering, ADWIN statistical drift detection) against no-retrain baseline. Experiments across 3,933 runs with varied drift regimes, budgets, latency levels, datasets, and learning modes using unified system model with explicit retraining budgets and latency.
AI.result: Most important factor is whether deployed model learns incrementally. With incremental updates, no policy differs significantly from baseline. Without incremental updates, periodic retraining outperforms reactive policies by 15-55 percentage points in abrupt/gradual drift, while reactive policies only have advantage in recurring drift. Reactive policies have systematic failure modes and latency-budget queueing issues.
AI.conclusion: Incremental learning matters more than retraining strategy choice. Without incremental updates, simple periodic retraining is surprisingly effective for most drift types, while reactive policies have limited value except for recurring drift. The study provides empirical guidance for ML system design.

title: Beyond Imitation: Filtering On-Policy Distillation by Reasoning Progress
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) has emerged as an effective framework for post-training language models by pairing student-generated trajectories with dense token-level supervision from a teacher. However, OPD implicitly assumes that teacher-derived rewards are an appropriate proxy for reasoning progress, and therefore treats all teacher feedback equally during policy optimization. While in practice, this assumption does not always hold. We observe that teacher-derived rewards often conflict with genuine reasoning progress, as reasoning steps with clear reasoning advancement may still receive lower distillation rewards, simply due to deviation from teacher's outputs. To address this mismatch, we propose Reasoning-Progress-Aware Reward Filtering for On-Policy Distillation (R2-OPD), which constructs two within-trajectory rankings of reasoning spans, one from teacher-derived rewards and the other from independently estimated progress reward. Distillation rewards are selectively suppressed whenever the two rankings disagree, reducing supervision that conflicts with reasoning progress while preserving effective teacher guidance. Our approach shows consistent improvement over standard OPD especially regarding reasoning performances.

AI.tldr: R2-OPD improves on-policy distillation by filtering out teacher rewards that conflict with genuine reasoning progress, using two reward rankings to selectively suppress misleading supervision.
AI.motivation: Standard on-policy distillation assumes teacher-derived rewards accurately reflect reasoning progress, but in practice this assumption often fails because reasoning steps that show genuine advancement may still receive low distillation rewards simply due to deviation from teacher outputs, creating a mismatch between supervision and actual reasoning progress.
AI.method: Proposes Reasoning-Progress-Aware Reward Filtering for On-Policy Distillation (R2-OPD), which constructs two within-trajectory rankings of reasoning spans: one from teacher-derived rewards and another from independently estimated progress rewards. Distillation rewards are selectively suppressed whenever these two rankings disagree, preserving effective teacher guidance while reducing supervision that conflicts with reasoning progress.
AI.result: The approach shows consistent improvement over standard on-policy distillation, particularly in reasoning performance metrics.
AI.conclusion: R2-OPD effectively addresses the reward-conflict problem in on-policy distillation by filtering out misleading teacher supervision, leading to better reasoning performance in language models.

title: DeltaMomentum: A Key-Value based Anisotropic Momentum Update via Delta Rule
summary: Most modern optimizers form their momentum as an exponential moving average (EMA) of past gradients, forgetting every direction at one fixed rate. However, the inputs a deep network sees during training can be highly anisotropic, with a few directions queried frequently while most are seen rarely. Recent methods address this anisotropy by wrapping extra processing around this buffer, leaving the momentum update itself unchanged. We propose DeltaMomentum, which builds direction-awareness into the momentum update rule. The main observation is that the gradient of a linear layer splits into an input that acts as a key and an output-side error that acts as a value. Exploiting the key-value structure, DeltaMomentum updates the momentum buffer by the canonical delta rule, so each direction is forgotten at a rate set by how often it appears. We prove that it is a valid momentum, that it applies the input-side curvature correction without matrix inversion, and that it clears stale directions faster than EMA under both a fixed and a drifting optimum. It is a drop-in replacement for the momentum buffer of any optimizer, its coefficient transfers across widths under $μ$P, and its extra compute stays between $22.2\%$ and $25.0\%$ of a gated-MLP block's linear cost with no persistent memory. In FineWeb-Edu pretraining, AdamW with DeltaMomentum (DeltaAdamW) reaches AdamW's validation loss in up to $46.39 \pm 4.32\%$ fewer steps at 67M and $22.12 \pm 0.80\%$ at 370M over three seeds, and the gain persists at 1B on a Chinchilla-optimal budget. A Muon baseline tuned under the same protocol sits above DeltaAdamW at both language-model scales, and the gain holds for SGD, ResNet-18, and ViT-Tiny on CIFAR-10. Training-time diagnostics confirm the predicted mechanism, better gradient tracking and healthier input directions.

AI.tldr: DeltaMomentum introduces a direction-aware momentum update rule that forgets gradient directions at different rates based on their frequency of appearance, improving optimization efficiency compared to standard exponential moving average momentum.
AI.motivation: Standard momentum uses exponential moving average (EMA) that forgets all gradient directions at the same fixed rate, which is suboptimal for anisotropic optimization landscapes where some directions appear frequently while others rarely appear. Recent methods add extra processing but don't change the core momentum update itself.
AI.method: DeltaMomentum exploits the key-value structure of gradients in linear layers (input as key, output-side error as value) and updates the momentum buffer using the canonical delta rule. Each direction is forgotten at a rate proportional to how often it appears, implementing direction-aware momentum without matrix inversion.
AI.result: DeltaMomentum is proven to be a valid momentum, applies input-side curvature correction without matrix inversion, and clears stale directions faster than EMA. As a drop-in replacement, it reduces training steps significantly: 46.39% fewer steps at 67M parameters, 22.12% at 370M parameters, with gains persisting at 1B scale. It transfers across widths under μP and adds only 22.2-25.0% extra compute.
AI.conclusion: DeltaMomentum provides a theoretically grounded, practical improvement to momentum that adapts to input anisotropy, achieves faster convergence across various model architectures and scales, and offers better gradient tracking with healthier input directions compared to standard momentum methods.

title: Symposium: Trust via Auditable Records for Communities of AI Scientist Agents
summary: Symposium is a formal framework and practical implementation to record the operation of AI agents deployed by small scientific research communities. Symposium provides long-term, immutable histories of agent-driven research activity, leaving auditable trails of analyses, hypotheses, data, and scientific discourse. This shared record of published artifacts enables agents to build on prior work and preserves the evidence researchers and agents need to make purpose-dependent trust assessments. Symposium captures scientific argument, including structured claims, fine-grained evidence citations, assumptions, and explicit declarations of what material may and may not be used as evidence. Symposium differs from AI co-scientist agents or integrated AI research environments; it is a framework that separates a scientific community's durable history from the agents and other systems that operate on that history. It assumes that a community will use diverse AI systems in a rapidly evolving environment. A working implementation of the publication infrastructure, agent prompt components, and documentation are provided to enable users to rapidly set up and run their own Symposium community.

AI.tldr: Symposium is a framework for creating immutable, auditable histories of AI agent research activities, enabling scientific communities to build on prior work and make trust assessments through structured argumentation and evidence tracking.
AI.motivation: Scientific research communities using diverse AI agents need durable, shared records of research activities to enable agents to build on prior work and allow researchers to make trust assessments based on auditable evidence trails.
AI.method: Symposium provides a framework and implementation that separates durable research histories from AI agents, capturing scientific arguments with structured claims, evidence citations, assumptions, and usage declarations. It includes publication infrastructure and agent prompt components for rapid deployment.
AI.result: A working implementation of publication infrastructure, agent prompt components, and documentation that enables users to set up and run their own Symposium communities for recording AI-driven scientific research.
AI.conclusion: Symposium offers a practical solution for scientific communities to maintain immutable research histories separate from AI agents, facilitating auditable trails, evidence preservation, and trust assessments in rapidly evolving AI research environments.

title: Beyond Multimodal Alignment: Certifying Physical Language through Response Substitution and Ordered Execution
summary: World models increasingly treat compact multimodal representations as interfaces between perception and physical interaction, yet existing probes do not establish whether different sensors carry the same executable meaning or whether that meaning survives a new action composition. We introduce an operational capability hierarchy and the Disjoint-Bridge Operator-Substitution Certificate (DBOSC), which asks whether independently trained modality compilers enter a frozen response chart interchangeably on evidence outside their training panels. On Cluster Haptic, audio and acceleration representations of the same unseen surface are 4.5x closer in response space than wrong-surface pairings, with the gap holding for all 19 held-out surfaces; unsealing withheld responses confirms that every branch predicts the physics better than the population chart. We then test ordered execution in a controlled elastoplastic system with complementary modality blind spots. At the pre-registered budget, the prerequisite refuses the stack because the frozen executor cannot advance even an exact chart coordinate through a held-out program. At a converged budget, the same rank-three chart executes those programs (oracle NMSE 0.18), fusion improves on both modalities, and 14 of 16 registered checks pass; the two failures arise because a diagonal restriction of the fused information matrix performs as well as the full one. Clearing the gate is a property of the executor, not the chart: an executor emitting whole programs instead of shared per-step dynamics is 38x worse than an entity-blind predictor on the same chart. A matching non-identifiability result explains why compression and fusion alone cannot determine an unseen composition law. These results separate attribute access, response substitution, fusion closure, and ordered execution into distinct, separately testable achievements.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces an operational hierarchy and DBOSC test to verify whether multimodal representations maintain executable meaning across sensor modalities and whether that meaning survives new action compositions in unseen scenarios.
