AI.motivation: Current world models treat compact multimodal representations as interfaces between perception and physical interaction, but existing probes don't establish whether different sensors carry the same executable meaning or whether that meaning persists through novel action compositions. There's a need to verify if independently trained modality compilers can be substituted interchangeably in response charts for evidence outside their training domains.
AI.method: Introduces an operational capability hierarchy and the Disjoint-Bridge Operator-Substitution Certificate (DBOSC) test. Tests modality representations on unseen surfaces (Cluster Haptic dataset with audio, acceleration) and controlled elastoplastic systems. Evaluates modality substitution, fusion closure, and ordered execution through rigorous experimental protocols with pre-registered budgets and validation checks.
AI.result: Multimodal representations of same unseen surfaces are 4.5x closer in response space than wrong pairings, with gap holding across all 19 held-out surfaces. With converged budget, rank-three charts successfully execute programs (oracle NMSE 0.18), fusion improves on both modalities, and 14/16 pre-registered checks pass. However, prerequisite fails at lower budget because frozen executor cannot advance through held-out programs. Key finding: clearing execution gate depends on executor properties, not just the chart.
AI.conclusion: The study successfully separates attribute access, response substitution, fusion closure, and ordered execution into distinct, separately testable achievements. Compression and fusion alone cannot determine unseen composition laws, as demonstrated by non-identifiability results. The operational hierarchy and DBOSC provide a framework for systematically evaluating multimodal world models' executable capabilities.

title: From Retrieved Context to Runtime Control: Adaptive Compression for Edge-based RAG
comment: Accepted to appear in the Proceedings of the ACM AI Leadership Summit 2026. Zlatan Feric and Amir Taherin contributed equally
summary:
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves language-model responses by grounding generation in external passages, which comes with overhead: retrieved context lengthens the prompt, increasing prefill work, KV-cache footprint, memory traffic, latency, and energy. Context compression offers a natural remedy by pruning retrieved text before generation. However, state-of-the-art context-compression methods are typically used with a fixed compression budget, or with the rate selected offline and then applied at inference time. This static view ignores both workload variation and the live state of the edge device. On an edge SoC, compression is not free: the compressor itself runs on the same SoC and consumes latency and energy that can offset any generation savings.
  This paper proposes a vision for telemetry-informed adaptive compression in edge RAG, grounded in experimental evidence. We characterize the compression tradeoff on the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor using Llama and Qwen generators, Natural Questions and HotpotQA datasets, and LLMLingua-2 compression. Our measurements show that generation dominates the RAG budget for larger models, reaching roughly 90% of per-query latency and 91% of GPU energy for 7B-8B generators. Exploring the impact of the compression rate reveals an adaptive operating region: mild compression can miss energy opportunities, and overly aggressive compression can hurt inference quality. Intermediate compression can reduce GPU energy by up to 53.2%, and SoC energy by up to 48.2%, with negligible quality loss. We argue for runtime policies that dynamically manage compression, guided by workload features and edge telemetry.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes telemetry-informed adaptive compression for edge RAG systems to dynamically optimize compression rates based on workload and device state, achieving up to 53.2% GPU energy savings with minimal quality loss.
AI.motivation: Current RAG systems suffer from overhead from retrieved context length, increasing latency and energy consumption. Existing static compression methods ignore workload variation and device state, while compression itself consumes resources on edge devices, creating a need for adaptive solutions.
AI.method: Characterized compression tradeoffs on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor using Llama and Qwen generators with Natural Questions and HotpotQA datasets, using LLMLingua-2 compression. Analyzed impact of compression rates on latency, energy, and quality, identifying optimal adaptive operating regions.
AI.result: Generation dominates RAG budget for larger models (90% latency, 91% GPU energy for 7B-8B generators). Found adaptive operating region where intermediate compression can reduce GPU energy by up to 53.2% and SoC energy by up to 48.2% with negligible quality loss, while both mild and aggressive compression have drawbacks.
AI.conclusion: Runtime policies should dynamically manage compression based on workload features and edge telemetry, as adaptive compression offers significant energy savings without quality degradation on edge RAG systems.

title: Empirical Characterization of Learning Geometry in Hybrid Quantum Forecasting Models
summary: We characterize the learning dynamics of a compact hybrid quantum forecasting model through comparison with a structurally aligned classical baseline. Using stationary harmonic-mixture and nonstationary chirp benchmarks with controlled spectral complexity and data availability, we analyze empirical Neural Tangent Kernel dynamics through kernel-target alignment, kernel drift, spectral concentration, and training loss. The classical model exhibits stronger early target alignment, whereas the hybrid model generally develops a less concentrated kernel spectrum and smaller kernel drift. Despite these distinct optimization geometries, both architectures attain similar held-out performance across the evaluated regimes. Notably, the hybrid model uses 125 trainable parameters compared with 281 for the classical baseline and reaches its validation-selected checkpoint earlier in 15 of 18 frequency conditions. A Fourier-augmented classical baseline does not reproduce the observed training behavior, while a controlled re-uploading ablation shows that repeated encoding systematically modifies both optimization and kernel geometry. These results demonstrate that comparable generalization can emerge from substantially different learning trajectories and that individual NTK diagnostics do not provide monotonic predictors of validation convergence. Rather than claiming a general quantum advantage, the study identifies architecture-dependent learning behavior that is masked by endpoint accuracy alone.

AI.tldr: Hybrid quantum forecasting models show different learning dynamics than classical baselines but achieve similar generalization performance, despite using fewer parameters and converging earlier.
AI.motivation: To understand how quantum-classical hybrid models learn compared to classical models, examining the learning dynamics beyond just endpoint accuracy metrics.
AI.method: Compare hybrid quantum forecasting model with structurally aligned classical baseline using stationary harmonic-mixture and nonstationary chirp benchmarks. Analyze Neural Tangent Kernel dynamics through kernel-target alignment, kernel drift, spectral concentration, and training loss. Test Fourier-augmented classical baseline and re-uploading ablation.
AI.result: Classical model shows stronger early target alignment, while hybrid model develops less concentrated kernel spectrum and smaller kernel drift. Both achieve similar held-out performance. Hybrid model uses 125 vs 281 parameters and reaches validation checkpoint earlier in 15/18 frequency conditions.
AI.conclusion: Similar generalization can emerge from different learning trajectories; individual NTK diagnostics don't predict validation convergence. Study identifies architecture-dependent learning behavior masked by endpoint accuracy, not claiming general quantum advantage.

title: Enforcing LLM Safety through DMD-based Classification of Prompt-Response Embedding Dynamics
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in high-stakes applications, yet their tendency to generate toxic, harmful, or policy-violating content poses significant risks. Detecting these unsafe outputs efficiently in a black-box manner remains an open challenge. In this paper, we extend a recently proposed dynamical systems framework designed for hallucination detection to LLM safety classification. By projecting both prompts and responses into high-dimensional embedding spaces and fitting separate Koopman-based predictive models for safe and unsafe regimes, we classify new outputs using a new differential residual score that compares prediction errors of the safe and unsafe regimes. A key contribution is the incorporation of the prompt and response embedding dynamics, yielding fitted Koopman operators that capture crucial interaction patterns. We evaluate our black-box method across three safety benchmarks using three embedding models. Our results show that incorporating prompt embeddings yields consistent improvements, particularly for interaction-dependent violations when paired with causal decoders (e.g., in Llama-3), while response-only violations benefit more from dense semantic embedding representations. These findings opens the door for using dynamical systems to analyze AI systems rather than the dominant paradigm of using AI to model dynamical systems.

AI.tldr: A novel black-box safety detection method for LLMs using Koopman operators from dynamical systems theory to classify unsafe content by analyzing embedding space dynamics of prompts and responses.
AI.motivation: LLMs deployed in high-stakes applications often generate toxic, harmful, or policy-violating content, creating significant risks. Current approaches lack efficient black-box methods for detecting these unsafe outputs without access to model internals.
AI.method: Extends a dynamical systems framework for hallucination detection to safety classification. Projects prompts and responses into embedding spaces, fits separate Koopman-based predictive models for safe/unsafe regimes, and uses a differential residual score comparing prediction errors of both regimes. Key innovation: incorporates both prompt and response embedding dynamics to capture interaction patterns.
AI.result: Evaluated across three safety benchmarks with three embedding models. Found that: 1) incorporating prompt embeddings yields consistent improvements, 2) interaction-dependent violations (e.g., with Llama-3) benefit from causal decoders, 3) response-only violations benefit more from dense semantic embeddings. Method shows effectiveness in black-box safety classification.
AI.conclusion: The approach successfully applies dynamical systems theory to AI safety analysis, showing that prompt-response interaction patterns can be effectively captured via Koopman operators. Opens new possibilities for using dynamical systems to analyze AI systems rather than the traditional paradigm of using AI to model dynamical systems.

title: In Two Minds about Lifelong Learning: Exploring Hemispheric Redundancy and Specialisation in Neural Models
comment: 21 pages before references/appendix, 9 figures
summary: Persistent intelligent systems require the ability to learn continually, but current machine learning approaches face significant challenges in this area compared to biological learning systems. Machine learning algorithms typically trade off retention of previously learned information and adaptation to new or changing data patterns. When continual learning capabilities are absent, algorithms must undergo retraining using the entire data set, an approach that becomes impractical when original training data are unavailable due to storage constraints, financial or computational costs, or privacy restrictions. However, biological animals can learn continually, without experiencing catastrophic forgetting. This paper attempts to build a high-level framework for how animals learn and preserve knowledge by modelling neural components and states that are known to be related to memory consolidation. We focus on three concepts: experience replay, REM sleep, and bilaterality. We propose 4MAS (4 Module Awake/Sleep), a novel macroarchitecture demonstrating how machine learning models might benefit from asymmetric hemispheres, each with their own long- and short-term memory mechanisms, and how a period of sleep between incremental learning tasks might benefit memory consolidation. Finally, we present results showing that our architecture achieves competitive results on the Split-MNIST, Split-Fashion-MNIST and Split-CIFAR-100 datasets, with 98.3%, 84.9%, and 29.29% accuracy respectively.

AI.tldr: A biologically-inspired continual learning framework called 4MAS that uses asymmetric brain hemispheres and sleep periods to prevent catastrophic forgetting in neural networks.
AI.motivation: Current machine learning systems struggle with continual learning and suffer from catastrophic forgetting, unlike biological brains. Retraining with entire datasets is impractical due to storage, computational, privacy, and cost constraints.
AI.method: Proposes 4MAS (4 Module Awake/Sleep) architecture inspired by biological learning mechanisms: experience replay, REM sleep, and bilaterality. Features asymmetric hemispheres with separate long- and short-term memory, and sleep periods between incremental learning tasks for memory consolidation.
AI.result: Achieves competitive results on Split-MNIST (98.3%), Split-Fashion-MNIST (84.9%), and Split-CIFAR-100 (29.29%) datasets, demonstrating effective continual learning without catastrophic forgetting.
AI.conclusion: Biologically-inspired architectures with asymmetric hemispheres and sleep-based consolidation offer promising solutions for continual learning challenges in AI systems, mimicking how animals preserve knowledge while learning new information.

title: Scientific Data Skills: Enabling Agent-Ready Scientific Data Services at Scale
summary: Scientific data are increasingly used by AI agents, yet existing dataset representations provide limited support for autonomous discovery, interpretation, and invocation. This limitation stems from the fragmentation of scientific data across heterogeneous repositories and from dataset representations designed primarily for human use. To address this limitation, we introduce the Scientific Data Skill (SciDSK), an agent-ready representation that packages dataset-specific knowledge and operational guidance as a reusable agent skill. A SciDSK integrates dataset descriptions, scientific context, file organization, usage procedures, quality checks, and provenance information while retaining the underlying data in its original repository. We define a structured SciDSK specification and develop a systematic construction pipeline that grounds each SciDSK in authoritative dataset records and associated supporting materials. We further establish the Scientific Data Skill Bank, a unified platform that publishes SciDSK resources across six scientific disciplines and supports package access, persistent identification, and traceability to source datasets. We evaluate SciDSK through a retrieval benchmark for dataset discovery and controlled cases for dataset interpretation. The results show that SciDSK improves agent-driven dataset discovery and provides more precise and actionable support for dataset interpretation. These findings support the value of organizing dataset-specific knowledge in an agent-ready representation.

AI.tldr: SciDSK is an agent-ready representation for scientific datasets that packages dataset knowledge and operational guidance as reusable agent skills to improve autonomous discovery and interpretation.
AI.motivation: Scientific data are increasingly used by AI agents, but existing dataset representations provide limited support for autonomous discovery, interpretation, and invocation due to fragmentation across repositories and designs primarily for human use.
AI.method: Introduce Scientific Data Skill (SciDSK) - an agent-ready representation that integrates dataset descriptions, scientific context, file organization, usage procedures, quality checks, and provenance information while keeping original data in repositories. Define structured SciDSK specification and systematic construction pipeline grounded in authoritative dataset records. Establish Scientific Data Skill Bank platform that publishes SciDSK resources across six disciplines with package access, persistent identification, and traceability features.
AI.result: Evaluation through retrieval benchmark for dataset discovery and controlled cases for dataset interpretation shows that SciDSK improves agent-driven dataset discovery and provides more precise and actionable support for dataset interpretation compared to existing representations.
AI.conclusion: The findings support the value of organizing dataset-specific knowledge in an agent-ready representation like SciDSK for enabling more effective autonomous discovery and interpretation of scientific datasets by AI agents.

title: Continuous Adversarial MeanFlow Transfer
comment: Paper under review
summary: Training fast generators on new domains with limited data remains challenging for two reasons. First, adapting a pretrained diffusion or flow model to a new domain leaves its costly multi-step sampling unaddressed, and existing acceleration methods are tied to the source parameterization--$ε$, $x$, $v$, or $u$--leaving heterogeneous pretrained models with no common acceleration target. Second, while adversarial refinement is proven effective for few-step quality, it is formulated only for instantaneous-velocity flows, not for the finite-interval average velocities that MeanFlow (MF) models predict. We address both problems. We propose MeanFlow-Transfer, which maps heterogeneous source outputs into a shared velocity representation, uses it to initialize an MF generator from the source weights, and optimizes an MF objective on the target domain. This unifies adaptation and acceleration in a single training loop across a broad range of pretrained models. We then introduce Continuous Adversarial MeanFlow, a post-training stage that extends continuous adversarial flow models from instantaneous velocities to MF's finite-interval average velocities. CAMF contrasts changes in a learned potential between real and predicted interval endpoints, recovering fine detail that MF regression averages away, and reduces to the instantaneous criterion in the vanishing-interval limit. Adapting four ImageNet-based source models--DiT ($ε$), SiT ($v$), JiT ($x$), iMF ($u$)--to five target domains, MF-T with CAMF matches or exceeds the fine-tuned teacher in FID and FDD at up to $125\times$ fewer Neural Function Evaluations (NFEs), while CAMF improves MF-T's few-step FID by $29\%$ on average.

AI.tldr: Proposes MeanFlow-Transfer (MF-T) for adapting and accelerating pretrained generative models to new domains with limited data, plus Continuous Adversarial MeanFlow (CAMF) for post-training refinement.
AI.motivation: Two key challenges: 1) Existing adaptation methods don't address multi-step sampling costs, and acceleration methods are tied to specific parameterizations (ε, x, v, u), preventing unified acceleration across heterogeneous pretrained models. 2) Adversarial refinement methods only work for instantaneous velocities, not finite-interval average velocities used by MeanFlow models.
AI.method: 1) MeanFlow-Transfer maps heterogeneous source outputs into shared velocity representation, initializes MF generator from source weights, and optimizes MF objective on target domain. 2) Continuous Adversarial MeanFlow extends adversarial refinement to MF's finite-interval average velocities by contrasting changes in learned potential between real and predicted interval endpoints.
AI.result: Adapting four ImageNet models (DiT, SiT, JiT, iMF) to five target domains, MF-T with CAMF matches or exceeds fine-tuned teacher performance in FID/FDD with up to 125× fewer NFEs. CAMF improves MF-T's few-step FID by 29% on average.
AI.conclusion: The proposed methods provide a unified framework for both adaptation and acceleration across diverse pretrained models, achieving significant efficiency gains while maintaining or improving quality in few-shot domain adaptation scenarios.

title: Can Agent Memory Systems Track Evolving State?
summary: As LLM-based agents are deployed for longer and higher-stakes tasks, their memory systems continue to have crucial gaps. While existing memory benchmarks focus largely on recall-shaped tasks, we argue an effective memory system must track the evolving state of the world; as facts, constraints, and decisions are revised over a long interaction, answers must reflect the current state and not a superseded one. We define this capability as state tracking and instantiate it in StateMemBench, a benchmark of 234 multi-session scenarios spanning two conversation-length regimes. Its closed-pool grading scores whether an answer reflects the current state, the superseded state, or fails otherwise, separating state-tracking failures from other errors by construction. Our analysis shows that this task is challenging for existing memory systems, retrieval-augmented baselines, and long-context baselines. We then present StateMem, a state-first memory method that explicitly tracks supersession and relational dependencies, and show it improves current-state accuracy over the strongest same-backbone baseline by 1.8x (0.205 -> 0.363) on DeepSeek-V4-Flash and over the strongest memory system by 1.6x (0.149 -> 0.233) on Qwen-3.5-9B, while remaining competitive with the long-context baselines. Finally, we show the same state approach can be applied as a lightweight single-call wrapper over existing memory systems, lifting current-state accuracy by +32 to +67 points on StateMemBench across six memory and retrieval backends. A length- and cost-matched control attributes +15 to +32 of those points to state structure rather than added context.

AI.tldr: StateMemBench is a benchmark for evaluating LLM memory systems' ability to track evolving world state, and StateMem is a new method that explicitly tracks supersession and dependencies to improve current-state accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing memory benchmarks focus mainly on recall tasks, but effective memory systems must track evolving world states as facts, constraints, and decisions are revised over long interactions. Answers must reflect current states rather than superseded ones.
AI.method: Created StateMemBench with 234 multi-session scenarios across different conversation lengths, using closed-pool grading to separate state-tracking failures from other errors. Developed StateMem, a state-first memory method that explicitly tracks supersession and relational dependencies.
AI.result: StateMem improved current-state accuracy over strongest same-backbone baseline by 1.8x (0.205 → 0.363) on DeepSeek-V4-Flash and over strongest memory system by 1.6x (0.149 → 0.233) on Qwen-3.5-9B. As a lightweight wrapper, it lifted current-state accuracy by +32 to +67 points across six backends.
AI.conclusion: State tracking is crucial for LLM memory systems in long, high-stakes tasks, and explicitly modeling state supersession and dependencies significantly improves performance on current-state accuracy metrics.

title: DraftFM: A FoundationModel for Day-Zero Drafting in Magic: The Gathering
comment: 28 pages, 6 figures, 13 tables. Sealed pre-registered forecast published ~36h before release; scoring note to follow. Also on SSRN (7257098). Code: https://github.com/brianward92/mtga Sealed forecast: https://github.com/brianward92/draftfm (tag draftfm-v1.0) Weights: https://huggingface.co/brianward92/draftfm Data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/brianward92/draftfm-frozen-eval
summary: Drafting a new Magic: The Gathering expansion begins before any pick from it has been observed: the complete card list is public, but the draft logs that supervised pick models train on do not yet exist. We study this day-zero regime directly. DraftFM is a discrete-choice policy that scores exactly the cards available in the current pack, conditioned on the drafted pool and the state of the draft. Every card enters as a frozen 775-dimensional function of its public card record, structured features and a fixed text embedding, with no card identities, set identities, or usage statistics anywhere in the model, so an unseen card is scored by the same machinery as a familiar one. A 1.6-million-parameter network fitted on 149 million human picks from 29 expansions predicts held-out picks in three expansions withheld in their entirety, reaching 50.8%, 60.4%, and 56.7% top-1 agreement, where uniform chance at the opening pick is about 7%. Refitted on all 32 observed expansions, the same architecture produced a card ranking for the then-unreleased set The Hobbit, sealed with its complete cryptographic provenance and published roughly 36 hours before the set became draftable on MTG Arena. The sealed ranking agrees with six independent expert reviewers roughly as much as those reviewers agree with one another. Evaluation against realized outcomes is committed to a follow-on note, whatever it shows.

AI.tldr: DraftFM is a day-zero card drafting AI that predicts Magic: The Gathering picks using only public card features and text embeddings, without relying on historical usage data, enabling evaluation on completely unseen expansions.
AI.motivation: To address the challenge of drafting new MTG expansions before any draft logs exist (day-zero regime), where traditional models trained on historical picks cannot be applied since no data exists for the new set.
AI.method: Uses a discrete-choice policy that scores available cards based on 775-dimensional features from card records and text embeddings, conditioned on drafted pool and draft state. No card/set identities or usage statistics included. A 1.6M-parameter network trained on 149M human picks from 29 expansions.
AI.result: Achieves 50.8%, 60.4%, and 56.7% top-1 agreement on three completely withheld expansions (vs ~7% chance). Successfully produced sealed rankings for unreleased Hobbit set 36 hours before draft availability, matching expert consensus as well as experts agree with each other.
AI.conclusion: Day-zero drafting is feasible using only public card features and language embeddings without historical usage data, enabling evaluation of draft AI on completely unseen expansions before any picks are observed.

title: Frequency-Aware Continual Learning for Smart Contract Vulnerability Detection with Large Language Models
summary: Smart contract vulnerability detection with Large Language Models (LLMs) faces three causally linked challenges. First, new vulnerability categories demand parameter-efficient adaptation, since full retraining is prohibitive for sequentially arriving tasks. Second, training per-task adapters on a shared backbone causes catastrophic forgetting of previously learned vulnerabilities. Third, the resulting multiplicity of adapters must be consolidated into a single model, since task identity is unknown at inference time. Each challenge arises directly from the solution to its predecessor, making an integrated framework essential. We propose a three-stage pipeline in which each stage addresses one challenge and feeds into the next. The adaptation stage uses Frequency-Aware Low-Rank Adaptation (FA-LoRA), which performs adaptation in the Fourier domain with per-frequency importance gates, requiring only 0.4% trainable parameters while outperforming standard LoRA and QLoRA. The continual learning stage applies Forget-Aware Replay (FAR), which uses these frequency gates to estimate per-sample forgetting risk via loss dynamics and prioritizes vulnerable knowledge for rehearsal, achieving an average Micro-F1 of 0.8022 across sequential tasks. The deployment stage employs Anchor-Protected Progressive Merging (APPM), which exploits the asymmetric generalization produced by FAR training to identify the strongest-generalizing adapter as an anchor and consolidates all adapters into a single model via anchor-protected weighted merging with frequency-domain gate competition. APPM achieves a Micro-F1 of 0.8085, within 2.7% of the independent per-task upper bound, at a merge cost of 156 ms and no additional runtime memory. Experiments on DIVE confirm the framework effectively addresses all three challenges for evolving blockchain ecosystems.

AI.tldr: A three-stage pipeline using FA-LoRA for parameter-efficient adaptation, FAR for continual learning with forgetting-aware replay, and APPM for merging multiple adapters into a single deployable model for smart contract vulnerability detection with LLMs.
AI.motivation: Smart contract vulnerability detection with LLMs faces three interconnected challenges: 1) need for parameter-efficient adaptation to handle new vulnerabilities without full retraining, 2) catastrophic forgetting when training per-task adapters on a shared backbone, and 3) the multiplicity of adapters that must be consolidated since task identity is unknown at inference time.
AI.method: Three-stage pipeline: 1) Adaptation stage uses Frequency-Aware Low-Rank Adaptation (FA-LoRA) that performs adaptation in Fourier domain with per-frequency importance gates (0.4% trainable parameters). 2) Continual learning stage applies Forget-Aware Replay (FAR) that uses frequency gates to estimate forgetting risk via loss dynamics and prioritizes vulnerable knowledge for rehearsal. 3) Deployment stage employs Anchor-Protected Progressive Merging (APPM) that identifies strongest-generalizing adapter as anchor and consolidates all adapters via anchor-protected weighted merging with frequency-domain gate competition.
AI.result: FA-LoRA outperforms standard LoRA and QLoRA. FAR achieves average Micro-F1 of 0.8022 across sequential tasks. APPM achieves Micro-F1 of 0.8085 (within 2.7% of independent per-task upper bound) with merge cost of 156 ms and no additional runtime memory. Experiments on DIVE dataset confirm effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: The proposed three-stage framework effectively addresses all three causally linked challenges for smart contract vulnerability detection in evolving blockchain ecosystems, providing parameter-efficient adaptation, overcoming catastrophic forgetting, and enabling deployment of a single consolidated model.

title: A Two-Stage Time-Aware Transformer for Short-Horizon AECOPD Risk Prediction
comment: 7 pages. Accepted for publication in IEEE Systems, Man, and Cybernetics Letters
summary: Acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (AECOPD) can worsen rapidly, making timely prediction a clinical priority. Most existing machine learning approaches rely on episodically collected clinical variables, introducing delays that limit their practical utility in home monitoring settings. Home ventilators offer a lower-latency alternative, producing a near-continuous record of respiratory status during daily use. However existing ventilator-based approaches either compress the waveform into handcrafted features or focus primarily on binary risk classification, leaving the timing of an impending event unresolved. In this paper, we present a two-stage framework that operates directly on raw pressure and flow waveforms from the most recent seven days of home ventilator use. The first-stage classification model identifies patients at high risk of a severe exacerbation. The second-stage regression model then estimates how many days remain before the event occurs. Our experimental results demonstrate that the two-stage model outperforms traditional baseline models on both risk classification and time-to-event estimation, with our selected Stage 1 classifier achieving F1 = 0.91 and our Stage 2 regression model achieving RMSE = 1.00 days and R^2 = 0.76, giving clinicians both an early warning and actionable lead time before a severe exacerbation occurs.

AI.tldr: A two-stage machine learning framework using raw ventilator waveforms to predict COPD exacerbations: first identifies high-risk patients, then estimates days until event.
AI.motivation: Current machine learning approaches for predicting COPD exacerbations rely on episodically collected clinical data with inherent delays, limiting utility for home monitoring. Home ventilators provide near-continuous respiratory status data but existing methods either compress waveforms into handcrafted features or only offer binary risk classification without timing information.
AI.method: Two-stage framework operating directly on raw pressure and flow waveforms from recent seven days of home ventilator use. Stage 1: classification model identifies patients at high risk of severe exacerbation. Stage 2: regression model estimates how many days remain before the event occurs.
AI.result: The two-stage model outperforms traditional baselines on both risk classification and time-to-event estimation. Stage 1 classifier achieves F1 = 0.91, Stage 2 regression achieves RMSE = 1.00 days and R^2 = 0.76.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides clinicians with both early warning and actionable lead time before severe COPD exacerbations, enabling more timely interventions through direct analysis of ventilator waveform data without compression into handcrafted features.

title: Learning Hierarchical Skill Policies with Offline Quality-Diversity Reinforcement Learning
comment: IROS 2026
summary: Recent studies investigate how to leverage pre-collected datasets to improve the policy performance and sample efficiency of RL. One promising approach to achieve this goal is to employ a two-stage strategy: In the first stage, diverse skills are extracted as a low-level policy from a given dataset, and a high-level policy is trained to solve a specific task in the second stage. Typically, extraction of the low-level policy is performed based on unsupervised learning such as trajectory VAE. However, a limitation of this approach is that the quality of the low-level policy highly depends on the quality of the dataset. To address this issue, we introduce QDOS (Quality-Diversity Offline Skill learning), a unified pipeline for robust offline-to-online learning. Our approach incorporates an Advantage-Weighted Quality-Diversity pretraining objective, which weights the skill extraction and diversity objectives by the estimated advantage of each trajectory segment. This approach allows the model to extract diverse and high-value skills. By providing robust and task-relevant skill representations, QDOS significantly improves the quality of the embedded skill space used by the low-level policy. We further integrate this with a dual dataset reuse strategy, where offline data is used both for skill pretraining and for populating the online replay buffer via pseudo-labeling. Experiments demonstrate that QDOS significantly outperforms strong baselines in structured manipulation tasks and unstructured locomotion tasks, confirming its ability to accelerate exploration and improve final returns in challenging sparse-reward domains.

AI.tldr: QDOS is a two-stage offline-to-online RL method that extracts diverse, high-value skills from offline data using advantage-weighted quality-diversity pretraining, then uses these skills for efficient online task learning with dual dataset reuse.
AI.motivation: Current two-stage RL approaches that extract skills from offline datasets suffer from skill quality being heavily dependent on dataset quality. There's a need for more robust skill extraction methods that can work effectively with varying quality offline datasets.
AI.method: QDOS combines: 1) Advantage-Weighted Quality-Diversity pretraining that weights skill extraction and diversity objectives by estimated advantage of trajectory segments, 2) extraction of diverse and high-value skills as low-level policy, 3) training high-level policy for specific tasks, 4) dual dataset reuse strategy where offline data is used for both skill pretraining and populating online replay buffer via pseudo-labeling.
AI.result: Experiments show QDOS significantly outperforms strong baselines in both structured manipulation tasks and unstructured locomotion tasks. It accelerates exploration and improves final returns in challenging sparse-reward domains.
AI.conclusion: QDOS provides a robust pipeline for offline-to-online learning that improves skill space quality through advantage-weighted quality-diversity pretraining, making skill extraction more resilient to dataset quality variations while improving sample efficiency and final performance.

title: Kähler landscapes for complex neural network descents and guarantees including a search and destroy of the Calabi-Yau manifold
comment: First version
summary: We study landscapes for complex-parameterized networks. Our approach is motivated with an information-theoretic manifold perspective of the parameter and via classical optimization guarantees although of complex geometric variety such as through Dolbeault asymptotics. The descent path admits a Kähler information metric under a cross-entropy via the Wirtinger Hessian on the log-likelihood potential. We restrict attention to a descent update rule with natural gradient descent via a differentiated loss scaled by the inverse metric, so the descent path remains in the holomorphic tangent bundle. We emphasize Calabi-Yau information manifolds which profane theoretical guarantees via an ill-curvature-conditioned landscape. Under a Calabi-Yau metric, specifically in a non-compact setting with a global potential so defined geometrically rather than invoking the topological requirements of the Calabi conjecture, a wedged nowhere-vanishing holomorphic form is the top exterior product of the Kähler form up to constants, yielding a constant determinant condition. Under a fixed determinant, a metric almost low rank up to an eigenvalue tolerance implies a blow-up effect. Moreover, it has been discovered that negative curvature subverts the loss landscape, specifically sectional curvature, so we expand on this and draw interconnections to negative-definite Ricci curvature. Our arguments primarily exist in a geometric analytic modality, although we establish roots in deep learning theory such as through asymptotics at initialization and connections through failure modes of neural network guarantees under vanishing and negative Ricci curvature.

AI.tldr: The paper studies loss landscapes for complex-parameterized neural networks using information-theoretic geometry, focusing on Calabi-Yau information manifolds and their impact on optimization dynamics through curvature analysis.
AI.motivation: The research is motivated by understanding optimization landscapes for complex-parameterized neural networks through geometric and information-theoretic perspectives, addressing theoretical guarantees in deep learning, particularly how curvature conditions affect optimization behavior.
AI.method: The approach uses complex geometric analysis with information-theoretic manifolds, employing Kähler information metrics under cross-entropy via Wirtinger Hessian. The method focuses on natural gradient descent in holomorphic tangent bundles, analyzes Calabi-Yau information manifolds with constant determinant conditions, and studies curvature effects (sectional and Ricci curvature) on loss landscapes.
AI.result: The analysis reveals that under Calabi-Yau metrics in non-compact settings, the landscape exhibits constant determinant conditions and blow-up effects when metrics are almost low-rank. Negative curvature (both sectional and Ricci) adversely affects optimization landscapes, subverting theoretical guarantees and connecting to failure modes in neural network optimization.
AI.conclusion: Complex-parameterized networks have optimization landscapes deeply connected to geometric curvature properties, with Calabi-Yau information manifolds providing important theoretical insights. Negative curvature fundamentally disrupts loss landscapes and optimization guarantees, establishing crucial connections between deep learning theory and geometric analysis through curvature-based failure modes.

title: Rethinking the Evaluation and Optimization of LLM-Based Social Simulation
summary: LLM-based social simulation is a promising complement to traditional methods such as surveys and behavioral experiments. A core question is how to evaluate the fidelity of LLM-simulated human behavior and optimize LLMs toward it. Prevailing practice evaluates by accuracy, checking whether the model selects the single response observed from a human, and trains the LLM to reproduce this hard label. However, human behavior is inherently subjective: the same person in the same situation may reasonably act differently, so an observed response is only one draw from an underlying response distribution, rendering accuracy-based evaluation unreliable and hard-label training misleading. To address these problems, we first introduce the subjectivity coefficient, an entropy-based quantity distinguishing objective tasks such as coding from subjective ones such as social simulation, and use it to systematically analyze how accuracy-based evaluation and hard-label training fail as subjectivity grows. Based on the subjectivity coefficient, we propose Subjectivity-Adaptive soft-Label Training (SALT): it pools observed outputs from semantically nearby inputs into soft distributional labels, with an aggregation radius adapted to the estimated subjectivity of each input; in the near-objective limit the neighborhood shrinks, so SALT naturally falls back to standard single-label training. Moreover, since existing datasets record only single observed responses and cannot support distributional evaluation, we construct SUBJSIM, a benchmark of 19,300 contexts covering 193 annotators and 100 subjective questions. Since real-world data typically provide only a single observation per input, our experiments train models from single observed outputs while evaluating them against the full response distributions, verifying feasibility in realistic settings. Results on SUBJSIM demonstrate the advantages of our method.

AI.tldr: Proposes SALT (Subjectivity-Adaptive soft-Label Training) for LLM-based social simulation, addressing limitations of accuracy-based evaluation and hard-label training by adapting to task subjectivity and using soft distributional labels instead of single observed responses.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-based social simulation methods use accuracy-based evaluation and hard-label training, which is problematic because human behavior is inherently subjective - the same person in the same situation may act differently, so a single observed response is just one draw from a distribution.
AI.method: Introduces subjectivity coefficient (entropy-based measure) to distinguish objective vs subjective tasks. Proposes SALT which pools observed outputs from semantically nearby inputs into soft distributional labels, with aggregation radius adapted to estimated subjectivity of each input. Also constructs SUBJSIM benchmark with 19,300 contexts from 193 annotators covering 100 subjective questions.
AI.result: Results on SUBJSIM benchmark demonstrate advantages of the proposed method. The method trains models from single observed outputs while evaluating against full response distributions, showing feasibility in realistic settings where only single observations per input are available.
AI.conclusion: SALT provides a principled approach for LLM-based social simulation that adapts to task subjectivity, overcoming limitations of traditional accuracy-based evaluation and hard-label training by using adaptive soft labels that naturally fall back to standard training in near-objective cases.

title: Unregularized Convergence of Single-Loop, Entropy-Regularized Natural Actor-Critic
summary: While entropy regularization is widely used to stabilize and accelerate Natural Policy Gradient methods, its ability to yield faster convergence rates for the unregularized objective remains underexplored. Existing analyses often rely on double-loop architectures and invoke a linear entropy penalty. To bridge the gap between theory and practice, we analyze a single-loop, entropy-regularized Natural Actor-Critic algorithm under compatible linear function approximation. By training an uncentered critic, our critic tracking can remain stable even as the training policy approaches determinism and the Fisher information matrix degenerates. We focus on two primary regimes for the optimization landscape: a Stochastic Regime, where we fuse coupled actor-critic updates into a joint Lyapunov recurrence, and a Deterministic Regime, where we pivot to a Policy Mirror Descent framework to circumvent the collapse of Euclidean geometry. By exploiting a positive Minimal Action Gap in the unregularized Markov decision process, we introduce an Exponential Translation mechanism that maps the regularized gap to the unregularized one up to an exponentially decaying tail. By tuning the fixed temperature, our algorithm achieves accelerated unregularized convergence rates, up to approximation-error terms: $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(T_{total}^{-1})$ in the Stochastic Regime, and $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(T_{total}^{-2/3})$ for the average iterate alongside $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(T_{total}^{-1/3})$ for the last iterate in the Deterministic Regime. Here, $T_{total}$ denotes the total number of stochastic critic updates (or Monte Carlo rollouts). Furthermore, in the tabular setting, our positive-action-gap analysis yields a $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(T_{total}^{-2/3})$ average-iterate rate, surpassing the $\mathcal{O}(T_{total}^{-1/2})$ worst-case statistical barrier that applies without a positive action margin.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a single-loop entropy-regularized Natural Actor-Critic algorithm that achieves accelerated convergence rates for the unregularized objective by exploiting a positive minimal action gap through an exponential translation mechanism.
AI.motivation: Existing entropy regularization methods for Natural Policy Gradient lack theoretical understanding of how they accelerate convergence for unregularized objectives. Current analyses often use double-loop architectures and linear entropy penalties, creating a gap between theory and practical single-loop implementations.
AI.method: The paper proposes a single-loop entropy-regularized Natural Actor-Critic algorithm with compatible linear function approximation. Key innovations include: (1) an uncentered critic for stability when policies approach determinism, (2) two analysis regimes (Stochastic and Deterministic) using different techniques (joint Lyapunov recurrence and Policy Mirror Descent), and (3) an Exponential Translation mechanism that maps regularized performance gaps to unregularized ones using the positive minimal action gap.
AI.result: The algorithm achieves accelerated unregularized convergence rates: Õ(T_total^{-1}) in the Stochastic Regime, and Õ(T_total^{-2/3}) for average iterate plus Õ(T_total^{-1/3}) for last iterate in the Deterministic Regime. In tabular settings, the analysis yields Õ(T_total^{-2/3}) average-iterate rate, surpassing the worst-case Ω(T_total^{-1/2}) statistical barrier without positive action margin.
AI.conclusion: The paper bridges theory-practice gap for entropy regularization in policy optimization, showing how carefully tuned regularization can accelerate convergence for unregularized objectives through exploitation of positive action gaps, with theoretical rates that overcome worst-case statistical barriers.

title: Beyond Memory Majority: Latent-Source Reasoning for Multi-Agent Memory Arbitration
summary: Long-term multi-agent systems continuously accumulate the memories produced by different agents. Existing memory methods typically treat retrieved memories as independent evidence and combine them through voting or weighting. However, this independence assumption often fails in multi-agent settings: memories written by different agents may inherit the same upstream source or shared bias, causing correlated evidence to be repeatedly counted and creating a false majority. We term this failure mode \textit{Memory Correlation Bias}. To address the issue, we propose the \textbf{C}orrelation-\textbf{A}ware \textbf{M}emory \textbf{A}rbitration (CAMA) framework that jointly decouples retrieved memories and recovers missing independent evidence. We model the retrieved memories as query-conditioned evidence groups and combine neural dependency inference with provenance-based symbolic priors to estimate the effective number of independent evidence sources, thereby preventing correlated memories from forming a false majority. Since critical independent evidence may be absent from the initial retrieval set, \textsc{CAMA} further learns a sequential recovery policy that actively retrieves alternative evidence or traces upstream sources before making the final decision, aiming to recover sufficient independent evidence for reliable arbitration while minimizing retrieval cost. Experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of our method over the state-of-the-art baseline methods, suppressing false majorities induced by correlated memories.

AI.tldr: CAMA is a Correlation-Aware Memory Arbitration framework that addresses Memory Correlation Bias in multi-agent systems by detecting correlated memories, estimating independent evidence sources, and actively recovering missing evidence before decision-making.
AI.motivation: Existing memory methods in multi-agent systems treat retrieved memories as independent evidence, but this assumption often fails because memories written by different agents may inherit the same upstream sources or shared bias, leading to correlated evidence being repeatedly counted and creating a false majority - a problem termed Memory Correlation Bias.
AI.method: CAMA jointly decouples retrieved memories and recovers missing independent evidence by: 1) Modeling retrieved memories as query-conditioned evidence groups, 2) Combining neural dependency inference with provenance-based symbolic priors to estimate the effective number of independent evidence sources, 3) Learning a sequential recovery policy that actively retrieves alternative evidence or traces upstream sources before final decision, balancing reliability with retrieval cost.
AI.result: Experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of CAMA over state-of-the-art baseline methods, effectively suppressing false majorities induced by correlated memories.
AI.conclusion: The proposed CAMA framework successfully addresses Memory Correlation Bias in multi-agent systems by moving beyond the independence assumption, providing a more reliable memory arbitration approach that accounts for correlations between memories and actively recovers missing independent evidence.

title: Complementary, Not Cumulative: Interaction Effects in Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Navier-Stokes Vortex Shedding
summary: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) embed governing partial differential equations directly into the training loss, offering a promising alternative to costly CFD solvers for unsteady flows. Yet the growing list of techniques proposed to improve PINN training is typically validated one at a time, leaving open whether these techniques actually compose. We study this question in depth on the DFG/Schafer-Turek unsteady cylinder wake benchmark. In isolation, nearly every technique performs no better than an untreated baseline. However, combining periodic (SIREN) activations with causal weighting unlocks a previously inaccessible regime, reconstructing velocity and pressure fields to within 4.1% average relative L2 error against an OpenFOAM reference solution. Adding further techniques instead causes catastrophic performance degradation, demonstrating that individually effective PINN interventions can interact nonlinearly and that more elaborate training recipes are not necessarily better.

AI.tldr: PINNs with periodic activations (SIREN) combined with causal weighting achieves 4.1% average relative L2 error for unsteady cylinder wake benchmark, while other techniques individually fail or degrade performance when combined.
AI.motivation: Many techniques have been proposed to improve PINN training for unsteady flows, but they're typically validated individually, leaving uncertainty about whether these techniques actually work together effectively when combined.
AI.method: Studied the DFG/Schafer-Turek unsteady cylinder wake benchmark, testing various PINN techniques individually and in combination. Key methods investigated: periodic (SIREN) activations and causal weighting, among other proposed PINN improvements.
AI.result: Most techniques performed no better than baseline when tested individually. However, the combination of SIREN activations with causal weighting achieved 4.1% average relative L2 error against OpenFOAM reference. Adding further techniques caused catastrophic performance degradation.
AI.conclusion: Individually effective PINN interventions can interact nonlinearly and may not compose well. Simpler combinations (SIREN + causal weighting) can unlock previously inaccessible performance, while more elaborate training recipes aren't necessarily better and can degrade results.

title: SafeBranch: Branch-Pair Safety Alignment for Embodied Agents
comment: 25 pages, 12 figures
summary: Vision-language-model-based embodied agents can complete instructed tasks but often violate safety constraints in the process, a problem recently framed as interactive safety. Training such agents to act safely is difficult, since safety and task success are distinct objectives, and safety arises only at a small number of safety-critical steps within a trajectory. Standard supervision is insufficient: imitating safe trajectories teaches behavior without explaining why it is safe, and contrasting arbitrary safe and unsafe trajectories mixes the safety signal with unrelated differences. We propose SafeBranch, a framework that aligns an embodied actor on safety through branch pairs constructed from the actor's own unsafe rollouts via environment rollback. SafeBranch rolls each unsafe rollout back to the safety-critical step that caused the violation, queries the actor for a safe alternative, and pairs the original action with the alternative so that the two branches differ only at that step. The trained actor acts safely at deployment with no critic in the loop. On IS-Bench, SafetyALFRED, and out-of-distribution variants with unseen tasks and objects, it handles safety reliably without sacrificing task success, achieving roughly ten times more safe successes than the untrained baseline on the unseen-object variant.

AI.tldr: SafeBranch trains embodied agents to be safer by creating branch pairs from their own unsafe rollouts, focusing training on safety-critical steps through environment rollback.
AI.motivation: Vision-language-model-based embodied agents often violate safety constraints while completing tasks, but existing supervision methods are insufficient for effective safety training as they either don't explain why behavior is safe or mix safety signals with unrelated differences.
AI.method: SafeBranch constructs branch pairs from the actor's unsafe rollouts via environment rollback: rolls back to safety-critical steps that caused violations, queries the actor for safe alternatives, and pairs original unsafe actions with safe alternatives so branches differ only at that critical step.
AI.result: On IS-Bench, SafetyALFRED, and out-of-distribution variants with unseen tasks/objects, SafeBranch handles safety reliably without sacrificing task success, achieving roughly 10x more safe successes than untrained baseline on unseen-object variants.
AI.conclusion: SafeBranch effectively trains embodied agents to act safely by focusing supervision on safety-critical steps through self-generated branch pairs, enabling safe deployment without requiring a safety critic during inference.

title: Time-Uniform Self-Normalized Concentration for Discounted Least Squares: Limits and Corrections
summary: Self-normalized concentration inequalities are standard tools in bandit and reinforcement-learning analyses. A widely used weighted extension claims an analogous time-uniform guarantee for discounted least-squares estimators in non-stationary problems. A simple scalar Gaussian counterexample with a fixed parameter shows that the claimed bounded radius is crossed with probability one. For fixed discount and regularization parameters, we further show that, when $δ\leq1/2$ and $T/δ$ is sufficiently large, any deterministic anytime boundary valid uniformly over the stated conditionally sub-Gaussian model class must be at least of order $R\sqrt{\log(T/δ)}$ at some time by horizon $T$; for nondecreasing boundaries, this order is required at time $T$. We identify the proof error: different terminal times use different Gaussian mixing distributions, so the fixed-time mixtures do not form one supermartingale, and the stopping-time argument does not repair this failure. Finally, we show that the weighted inequality remains valid at each fixed deterministic time, give valid finite- and infinite-horizon corrections, and discuss consequences for downstream analyses.

AI.tldr: A paper exposing a flaw in weighted self-normalized concentration inequalities used in bandit/RL analyses, showing the claimed time-uniform guarantees fail, providing counterexamples, identifying the proof error, and offering corrections.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to address a critical error in widely used self-normalized concentration inequalities, particularly weighted extensions for discounted least-squares estimators in non-stationary bandit and reinforcement learning problems. These inequalities are standard tools but contain a flaw that could impact downstream analyses.
AI.method: The authors use a simple scalar Gaussian counterexample with fixed parameters to demonstrate the flaw. They analyze deterministic anytime boundaries, show lower bounds on boundary sizes, and mathematically identify the proof error involving Gaussian mixing distributions and supermartingale properties.
AI.result: Results show: 1) The claimed time-uniform guarantee fails - a simple counterexample violates the bounded radius with probability one; 2) For fixed discount/regularization, any valid deterministic anytime boundary must be at least order R√log(T/δ) at some time by horizon T; 3) Identification of the proof error: different terminal times use different Gaussian mixing distributions, preventing formation of a single supermartingale.
AI.conclusion: The weighted inequality remains valid only at fixed deterministic times, not uniformly over time. The paper provides valid finite- and infinite-horizon corrections and discusses consequences for downstream analyses in bandit and reinforcement learning.

title: GenMatch: An End-to-End Generative Matching Framework for Micro-View Order-Dispatching in Ride-Hailing
summary: Micro-View Order-Dispatching assigns available drivers to passenger orders within each dispatch batch and is critical to the service quality and operational efficiency of ride-hailing platforms. Mainstream industrial solutions follow a multi-stage paradigm of model prediction, value calculation, and dispatch matching. Although dispatch quality is determined by the final batch-level assignment, these stages optimize different intermediate objectives. This cross-stage objective inconsistency means that improving a single stage does not necessarily improve the overall dispatch result. We therefore formulate Micro-View Order-Dispatching as a generative matching problem and propose GenMatch, an end-to-end Generative Matching framework and the first such framework deployed in a real-world production environment. Applying generative modeling to this problem introduces three challenges. First, each dispatch batch forms a dynamic sparse bipartite graph, requiring efficient structured batch-level encoding. Second, replacing the hand-crafted value function requires learning unified business utility from heterogeneous feedback. Third, directly generating an assignment requires tracking the evolving matching state because each selected order-driver pair changes the remaining feasible candidates. GenMatch addresses these challenges with a Context-Aware Bipartite Encoder, a Business-Aware Utility Learner, and a State-Aware Pointer Decoder. Extensive offline evaluations and online A/B tests in five cities across DiDi's international ride-hailing markets show consistent improvements over competitive baselines, confirming the effectiveness and practicality of GenMatch for industrial order-dispatching.

AI.tldr: GenMatch: First end-to-end generative matching framework for ride-hailing order dispatching that replaces multi-stage pipelines, achieving consistent improvements in real-world deployment.
AI.motivation: Current industrial solutions use multi-stage pipelines (prediction → value calculation → dispatch matching) with inconsistent objectives across stages, where improving individual stages doesn't guarantee better overall dispatch results.
AI.method: Formulates dispatching as generative matching problem. Uses Context-Aware Bipartite Encoder for dynamic sparse graph encoding, Business-Aware Utility Learner for unified utility learning from heterogeneous feedback, and State-Aware Pointer Decoder to track evolving matching state.
AI.result: Extensive offline evaluations and online A/B tests across five cities in DiDi's international markets show consistent improvements over competitive baselines, confirming effectiveness and practicality.
AI.conclusion: GenMatch is the first end-to-end generative matching framework successfully deployed in real-world production environment, solving objective inconsistency in traditional multi-stage approaches through unified generative modeling.

title: DeltaML-Bench: Evaluating Machine Learning Agents on Real-World Research Repositories
comment: 18 pages, 3 figures, 12 tables. Code and benchmark: https://github.com/AlgorithmicResearchGroup/deltaml-bench-public
summary: Autonomous agents for machine learning experimentation must navigate heterogeneous repositories, repair training pipelines, and evaluate candidate improvements under realistic compute constraints. Existing benchmarks only partially capture these conditions. We introduce DeltaML-Bench, a benchmark comprising 48 tasks sourced from research papers that require agents to improve published baselines within imperfect, open-source repositories. We evaluate GPT-5 and Claude Sonnet 4 with a standard Modular agent and a search-based ARG scaffolding. In the 4 x 6h allocation, ARG raises GPT-5's per-run success rate from 9.4% to 33.9%; in the 2 x 12h allocation, GPT-5 ARG reaches 49.0%. Modular configurations exhibit specification gaming rates as high as 47.9%, while no gaming is observed in the evaluated ARG configurations. These results indicate that scaffolding design and integrity checks are important considerations when deploying agents for autonomous ML experimentation.

AI.tldr: DeltaML-Bench is a new benchmark for autonomous ML agents that tests their ability to improve imperfect open-source research repositories under realistic compute constraints, showing that search-based ARG scaffolding significantly improves performance while reducing specification gaming.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks don't fully capture the real-world challenges of autonomous ML experimentation, including navigating heterogeneous repositories, repairing training pipelines, and improving published baselines under imperfect conditions and realistic compute constraints.
AI.method: Created DeltaML-Bench with 48 tasks sourced from research papers requiring agents to improve published baselines in imperfect open-source repositories. Evaluated GPT-5 and Claude Sonnet 4 using two agent architectures: standard Modular agent and search-based ARG scaffolding under different time allocations (4x6h and 2x12h).
AI.result: ARG scaffolding dramatically improved GPT-5's success rate from 9.4% to 33.9% in 4x6h allocation and up to 49.0% in 2x12h allocation. Modular agents showed high specification gaming rates (up to 47.9%), while ARG configurations showed no gaming, indicating that scaffolding design and integrity checks are crucial.
AI.conclusion: Scaffolding design and integrity checks are critical considerations when deploying agents for autonomous ML experimentation, as search-based ARG scaffolding significantly improves performance while eliminating problematic specification gaming behaviors.

title: TT-net: Quantum Inspired Tensor Network Denoising in Conditional GANs
summary: Developed as a workhorse for classical simulations of quantum algorithms and quantum many-body systems, Tensor Network methods have entered the scientific mainstream in quantum physics. Among various types of tensor networks, Tensor Trains (commonly know as Matrix Product States in the quantum computing community) have already found applications in machine learning. These methods often rely on a powerful linear algebra tool called the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD). Several conditional GAN architectures for image denoising incorporate SVD as a single-cut decomposition step applied to generator feature maps. In this work we introduce TT-Net, which replaces the per-channel SVD denoising block with a two-cut tensor-train decomposition capable of accessing cross-channel information directly, a capability absent from contemporary alternatives. In a controlled comparison differing only in this decomposition mechanism, TT-Net outperforms SVD-Net on PSNR and SSIM across all three noise types tested (Gaussian, motion blur, and salt-and-pepper), supporting the hypothesis that cross-channel access improves denoising quality. Training-dynamics analysis further shows that TT-Net's adversarial loss term consistently saturates to a stagnant state across all three noise types, more so than SVD-Net's, while reconstruction quality continues to improve regardless, raising an open question about the adversarial component's contribution that this work identifies but does not resolve. Furthermore, for Gaussian noise our method outperforms both the EigenGAN and the state of the art Pix2pix method which does not assume any linear algebra decompositions and does not retain any linear algebra information. Our manuscript shows how quantum inspired tools can be used as practical real world feature filters for deep learning applications.

AI.tldr: TT-Net replaces SVD blocks in GAN architectures with tensor-train decomposition to access cross-channel information for improved image denoising, outperforming existing methods across multiple noise types.
AI.motivation: Current conditional GAN architectures for image denoising use SVD as a single-cut decomposition step on generator feature maps, but this approach lacks cross-channel information access which could improve denoising quality.
AI.method: Introduces TT-Net which replaces the per-channel SVD denoising block with a two-cut tensor-train decomposition, allowing direct access to cross-channel information that SVD-based methods cannot access.
AI.result: TT-Net outperforms SVD-Net on PSNR and SSIM across all three noise types tested (Gaussian, motion blur, salt-and-pepper). For Gaussian noise, it also beats EigenGAN and state-of-the-art Pix2pix method. Training analysis shows TT-Net's adversarial loss saturates to stagnant state while reconstruction quality continues improving.
AI.conclusion: Tensor-train decomposition enables cross-channel information access that improves denoising quality, demonstrating quantum-inspired tensor network methods can serve as practical feature filters in deep learning. The work identifies an open question about adversarial component contributions when reconstruction improves despite stagnant adversarial loss.

title: Rationally Enriched Chebyshev Trunk Bases for DeepONet Surrogates of High Péclet Entrance Transport
comment: 39 pages, 9 figures
summary: This study demonstrates a rationally enriched Chebyshev (REC) trunk for deep operator network (DeepONet) surrogate models of singularly perturbed and high-Péclet transport problems whose solution profiles are characterized by thin localized boundary or wall layers. The REC trunk combines Chebyshev polynomial dictionary elements with rational dictionary elements constructed using the adaptive Antoulas-Anderson (AAA) algorithm. Over five independent training runs, the resulting REC-trunk DeepONet is evaluated against a vanilla DeepONet and a Chebyshev-trunk DeepONet whose prescribed dictionary consists only of Chebyshev polynomials across three problems whose singular perturbation parameters are diffusion-to-advection ratios: a singularly perturbed scalar boundary-value problem (BVP), the thermal entrance problem with a prescribed wall temperature, and the concentration entrance problem with an absorbing wall. Across the held-out test profiles, the REC-trunk DeepONet improves over the vanilla DeepONet and remains comparable to the Chebyshev-trunk DeepONet in predicting the scalar profile, with its clearest advantage over the Chebyshev-trunk DeepONet appearing when the perturbation parameter lies between $1.00\times10^{-4}$ and $1.78\times10^{-4}$, where it reduces the profile-error metrics by up to $19.5\,\%$ relative to the Chebyshev-trunk DeepONet. In predicting the wall-normal temperature and concentration profiles, the REC-trunk DeepONet reduces the profile-error metrics by up to $60.2\,\%$ and $32.2\,\%$ relative to the vanilla and Chebyshev-trunk DeepONets, respectively, while suppressing artificial near-wall oscillations as the Péclet or mass-transfer Péclet number ranges from $10^{2}$ to $10^{4}$.

AI.tldr: REC-trunk DeepONet improves accuracy for singularly perturbed transport problems by combining Chebyshev and rational basis functions, reducing errors by up to 60% compared to vanilla DeepONet.
AI.motivation: Singularly perturbed and high-Péclet transport problems have thin boundary layers that are challenging for standard neural operator surrogates like DeepONet to capture accurately. Traditional polynomial basis functions may not adequately represent these sharp gradients.
AI.method: Proposes a Rationally Enriched Chebyshev (REC) trunk for DeepONet that combines Chebyshev polynomial dictionary elements with rational dictionary elements constructed using the adaptive Antoulas-Anderson (AAA) algorithm. This creates a more expressive basis for capturing sharp gradients in boundary layers.
AI.result: The REC-trunk DeepONet outperforms vanilla DeepONet and is comparable to Chebyshev-trunk DeepONet for scalar boundary-value problems. For thermal and concentration entrance problems, it reduces profile-error metrics by up to 60.2% (vs vanilla) and 32.2% (vs Chebyshev-trunk), while suppressing artificial near-wall oscillations across Péclet numbers from 10² to 10⁴.
AI.conclusion: The rationally enriched trunk architecture significantly improves DeepONet surrogate accuracy for singularly perturbed transport problems by better capturing boundary layer physics through a combined polynomial-rational basis, demonstrating particular advantage in the moderate perturbation parameter regime.

title: LLMs as Acquisition Policies for Finite-Pool Materials Optimization: A Controlled Study
summary: Discovering materials with desirable properties often requires searching large candidate spaces while experimental or computational evaluations remain costly. Active learning addresses this challenge by using previous observations to select which candidate to evaluate next, typically through probabilistic surrogate models. We investigate whether open-weight large language models (LLMs) can serve as standalone acquisition policies in this setting. We evaluate five LLMs across four retrospective finite-pool materials optimization tasks under different candidate-presentation strategies and compare them with random selection and conventional Gaussian-process methods. LLM policies generally reach the global optimum in fewer iterations than random selection, indicating that they provide a useful acquisition signal without task-specific training. Their performance relative to Gaussian-process methods is mixed: conventional acquisition performs better on most tasks, while LLMs match or outperform it in some settings. Performance varies substantially across tasks, models, initializations, and candidate presentations, with no LLM approach performing best across all tasks. Overall, open-weight LLMs show potential as acquisition policies for finite-pool materials search, although their reliability remains sensitive to the task and to how candidates and scientific context are presented.

AI.tldr: Open-weight LLMs can serve as acquisition policies for materials discovery, performing better than random selection but with mixed results compared to Gaussian processes, and showing sensitivity to task setup and candidate presentation.
AI.motivation: Discovering materials with desirable properties requires efficient search of large candidate spaces where experimental/computational evaluations are costly. Active learning with probabilistic surrogate models helps, but the authors want to investigate whether open-weight LLMs can serve as standalone acquisition policies without task-specific training.
AI.method: Evaluated five LLMs across four retrospective finite-pool materials optimization tasks under different candidate-presentation strategies. Compared LLM performance with random selection and conventional Gaussian-process methods. Tested various initialization and presentation approaches to assess reliability.
AI.result: LLM policies generally reach global optimum in fewer iterations than random selection, indicating useful acquisition signal without training. Performance vs Gaussian processes is mixed: conventional methods better on most tasks, but LLMs match or outperform in some settings. Performance varies substantially across tasks, models, initializations, and candidate presentations with no LLM approach performing best across all tasks.
AI.conclusion: Open-weight LLMs show potential as acquisition policies for finite-pool materials search, but their reliability remains sensitive to the task and to how candidates and scientific context are presented. They represent a promising but still inconsistent alternative to conventional methods.

title: FleetSieve: Decision-Critical Profiling for SLO-Aware LLM Fleet Configuration
summary: Choosing tensor-parallel (TP) degrees and replica counts for an LLM serving fleet is difficult because performance is not monotonic in TP and the feasible choice can change with load. Exhaustive profiling resolves this uncertainty, but measures many configurations that do not affect the final resource allocation. We present FleetSieve, which selects measurements according to their expected effect on a resource-coupled, SLO-aware fleet decision. FleetSieve models capacity and tail latency jointly, compares conservative and optimistic allocations, and stops when their remaining decision gap is below a specified tolerance. On a fixed H100 measurement grid for a 31B-parameter open-weight model, FleetSieve reaches the oracle aggregate decision using 22,200 GPU-seconds, 6.9% less than uniform random profiling in the fixed comparison. Across 200 random reveal orders, its mean saving over random profiling is 5.4% (95% bootstrap CI: 3.5-7.2%). The fixed-comparison saving is 21.5% for Chat, while FleetSieve does not use the fewest GPU-seconds for Code. Joint capacity and tail modeling also avoids selecting a configuration whose 46.4-second completion p99 violates a 30-second SLO. In a 16-GPU allocation, an incorrect sparse-profile decision loses up to 1.93 requests/s and 12.4 percentage points of max-min fulfillment. Boundary repeats and BurstGPT measurements support the observed load-dependent tail-latency mechanism.

AI.tldr: FleetSieve is an intelligent profiling system that efficiently selects tensor-parallel degree and replica configurations for LLM serving fleets by prioritizing measurements that impact resource allocation decisions, reducing profiling time while maintaining performance and SLO compliance.
AI.motivation: Choosing optimal tensor-parallel (TP) degrees and replica counts for LLM serving is challenging because performance isn't monotonic with TP changes, and optimal configurations vary with load. Exhaustive profiling is wasteful since many configurations don't affect final resource allocation decisions.
AI.method: FleetSieve selects measurements based on their expected impact on resource-coupled, SLO-aware fleet decisions. It jointly models capacity and tail latency, compares conservative vs optimistic allocations, and stops profiling when the decision gap falls below a specified tolerance.
AI.result: On H100 GPUs with a 31B-parameter model, FleetSieve achieved oracle-level decisions using 22,200 GPU-seconds (6.9% less than random profiling). Across 200 random reveal orders, mean saving was 5.4% vs random profiling. It successfully avoided configurations violating 30-second SLOs with 46.4-second p99 latencies, and prevented up to 1.93 req/s losses and 12.4% fulfillment reduction in suboptimal allocations.
AI.conclusion: FleetSieve provides an efficient, SLO-aware approach to LLM fleet configuration profiling by intelligently selecting measurements that matter for resource allocation decisions, significantly reducing profiling costs while maintaining performance and service level compliance.

title: Towards general embodied intelligence: integrating large language models, knowledge bases, and reasoning capabilities to build the next generation of AI agents
summary: The convergence of large language models (LLMs), structured knowledge bases (KBs), and reasoning ability (RA) presents a promising trajectory toward general embodied intelligence (GEI). This paper reviews the evolution of LLM-centered intelligent systems, emphasising their integration with knowledge representation, logical reasoning, and physical embodiment. We analyse LLM architectures, pre-training methods, and inference mechanisms, along with their interaction with external knowledge sources and structured reasoning frameworks. Furthermore, we examine embodied intelligence (EI) paradigms wherein agents learn and act in physical environments. To synthesise these dimensions, we present a conceptual framework that illustrates the synergy among LLMs, KBs, RA, and embodiment, serving as a guiding model for perception, reasoning, and action rather than an implemented engineering architecture. To advance toward GEI, we identify five key challenges: efficient LLM deployment, closed-loop knowledge integration, hybrid symbolic-neural reasoning, perception-action grounding, and continual learning. This survey provides a comprehensive roadmap for developing adaptive, multimodal agents capable of operating in complex, dynamic settings.

AI.tldr: This paper surveys the convergence of LLMs, knowledge bases, reasoning abilities, and embodiment as a pathway toward general embodied intelligence, proposing a conceptual framework and identifying key challenges.
