AI.motivation: The paper is motivated by the need to understand how large language models, when integrated with structured knowledge bases, reasoning abilities, and physical embodiment, can progress toward general embodied intelligence in complex environments.
AI.method: The paper reviews the evolution of LLM-centered intelligent systems, analyzes LLM architectures and their integration with external knowledge sources and reasoning frameworks, examines embodied intelligence paradigms, and proposes a conceptual framework illustrating the synergy among these components.
AI.result: The paper presents a conceptual framework showing how LLMs, knowledge bases, reasoning abilities, and embodiment can work together for perception, reasoning, and action. It identifies five key challenges: efficient LLM deployment, closed-loop knowledge integration, hybrid symbolic-neural reasoning, perception-action grounding, and continual learning.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that integrating LLMs with structured knowledge, reasoning abilities, and embodiment provides a promising path toward general embodied intelligence, and offers a roadmap for developing adaptive, multimodal agents for complex, dynamic environments.

title: SAGE-XGBoost: Spatially Augmented Graph Embeddings--Machine Learning Framework for Natural Hazards Susceptibility Mapping under Data Scarcity
summary: Natural hazard susceptibility mapping is often constrained by limited labeled data, reducing the generalizability of conventional machine learning and limiting the applicability of complex deep learning models. This study proposes SAGE (Spatially Augmented Graph Embeddings), a structurally informed feature-engineering framework that combines controlled noise-based data augmentation with neighborhood-based graph embeddings to improve prediction under data-scarce conditions. A K-nearest neighbor graph is constructed to derive local spatial statistics, which are reduced using principal component analysis and integrated with environmental covariates and spatial coordinates. The resulting features are used with XGBoost to develop the SAGE-XGBoost model. The framework was evaluated for landslide and wildfire susceptibility mapping. SAGE-XGBoost consistently outperformed conventional and spatially explicit machine learning models. Compared with Spatial XGBoost, it achieved an absolute improvement of above 33 percentage points across the two case studies. The model reached AUC values of approximately 0.97 for landslide susceptibility and 0.95 for wildfire susceptibility. Feature importance analysis confirmed the contribution of graph embeddings to prediction, while their integration improved spatial coherence and reduced local noise amplification. Overall, SAGE-XGBoost provides an efficient and transferable alternative to deep representation learning for environmental hazard assessment and other geospatial prediction tasks under limited supervision.

AI.tldr: SAGE-XGBoost framework combines graph embeddings with spatial data augmentation to improve natural hazard susceptibility mapping under limited labeled data conditions, outperforming conventional approaches.
AI.motivation: Natural hazard susceptibility mapping is constrained by limited labeled data, which reduces the generalizability of conventional machine learning and limits the applicability of complex deep learning models that require large datasets.
AI.method: Proposes SAGE (Spatially Augmented Graph Embeddings) framework that constructs K-nearest neighbor graphs to derive local spatial statistics, reduces them with PCA, and integrates them with environmental covariates and spatial coordinates. Uses XGBoost for modeling, evaluated for landslide and wildfire susceptibility mapping.
AI.result: SAGE-XGBoost consistently outperformed conventional and spatially explicit machine learning models, achieving above 33 percentage points improvement over Spatial XGBoost. Model reached AUC values of ~0.97 for landslide susceptibility and ~0.95 for wildfire susceptibility. Feature importance confirmed contribution of graph embeddings.
AI.conclusion: SAGE-XGBoost provides an efficient and transferable alternative to deep representation learning for environmental hazard assessment and geospatial prediction tasks under limited supervision, with improved spatial coherence and reduced local noise amplification.

title: ADAPT: Physics-Aware Diffusion-based World Models for Adaptive Predictive Transferable HVAC Control
summary: Buildings account for roughly one-third of global energy consumption and CO$_2$ emissions. Optimizing indoor climate systems plays a critical role for urban climate mitigation aligned with UN Sustainable Development Goals 11 and 13. However, indoor delayed thermodynamic responses and partial observability severely hinder existing methods, which are primarily limited by implicit thermal inertia, occupancy dynamic prediction, and cumulative prediction errors, especially for out-of-distribution environments. In practice, these challenges are further exacerbated by the high cost and privacy burden of dense indoor sensing, forcing operators to collect only limited data in a single operating regime while expecting controllers to generalize reliably across unseen seasons and climate regions. To address this problem, we propose ADAPT, a physics-aware conditional diffusion indoor environmental world model for HVAC control. The model predicts a short-horizon held-action thermal baseline to capture the latent thermal inertia of the buildings. The diffusion backbone utilizes the robustness of generative models, while a learnable multi-zone heat-balance regularizer constrains generated trajectories to satisfy transferable building thermodynamics without requiring known building geometry or manually calibrated thermal parameters. A credit assignment is then design for the downstream reinforcement learning. Extensive experiments on SemibuildingSim and Sinergym demonstrate that ADAPT reduces HVAC energy consumption by 7.3\% and occupant discomfort by 30.2\% compared with state-of-the-art baselines under IID control. Under OOD control scenarios spanning unseen seasons and climate regions, ADAPT maintains robust performance with only marginal degradation relative to its IID performance, substantially outperforming existing methods in transfer robustness.

AI.tldr: ADAPT: A physics-aware conditional diffusion world model for HVAC control that combines generative modeling with building thermodynamics to achieve robust energy-efficient control across unseen seasons and climate regions.
AI.motivation: Buildings account for significant global energy and emissions, but indoor climate control faces challenges from delayed thermodynamic responses, partial observability, and the high cost/privacy burden of dense sensing. Existing methods struggle with implicit thermal inertia, occupancy dynamics, and cumulative prediction errors, especially in out-of-distribution environments where limited data from single operating regimes must generalize to unseen conditions.
AI.method: ADAPT uses a physics-aware conditional diffusion indoor environmental world model. It predicts short-horizon held-action thermal baselines to capture latent thermal inertia. The diffusion backbone provides robustness, while a learnable multi-zone heat-balance regularizer constrains generated trajectories to satisfy transferable building thermodynamics without requiring known geometry or calibrated parameters. Includes credit assignment design for downstream reinforcement learning.
AI.result: Experiments on SemibuildingSim and Sinergym show ADAPT reduces HVAC energy consumption by 7.3% and occupant discomfort by 30.2% compared to SOTA baselines under IID control. Under OOD control (unseen seasons/climate regions), ADAPT maintains robust performance with only marginal degradation, substantially outperforming existing methods in transfer robustness.
AI.conclusion: ADAPT successfully addresses key challenges in HVAC control by combining physics-aware modeling with generative approaches, enabling reliable generalization across diverse environmental conditions without extensive sensing infrastructure, supporting climate mitigation goals.

title: A Locally Tokenized Generative Model for Robust Time-Series Watermarking
comment: Submitted to NeurIPS 2026
summary: Watermarking is a central tool for provenance in generative models, yet its application to multivariate time series remains hindered by reliability failures under post-editing attacks. We show that existing detectors, which rely on globally coupled re-encoding, suffer from bidirectional drift of the null distribution: post-editing attacks can shift the z-score of non-watermarked samples in either direction, invalidating clean-calibrated thresholds. We argue that this instability is a property of the re-encoding, and that reliable detection requires each recovered unit to depend only on a bounded temporal neighborhood. Guided by this principle, we propose L-VQVAE, a generative model in which each discrete token is produced from a short contiguous window, and LVQMark, a watermarking method over this token space that combines logit-bias injection with robust re-encoding for attack-time detection. Experiments on four benchmarks spanning finance, energy, and neuroimaging show that our approach preserves generation quality while stabilizing both detection power and false-positive behavior under post-editing attacks.

AI.tldr: Watermarking method for multivariate time series that maintains reliable detection under post-editing attacks by using local temporal dependencies instead of global re-encoding.
AI.motivation: Existing watermarking methods for multivariate time series fail under post-editing attacks due to unreliable detection caused by bidirectional drift of the null distribution when using globally coupled re-encoding.
AI.method: Propose L-VQVAE (a generative model producing discrete tokens from short contiguous windows) and LVQMark (a watermarking method combining logit-bias injection with robust re-encoding for attack-time detection over this token space).
AI.result: Experiments on four benchmarks (finance, energy, neuroimaging) show the approach preserves generation quality while stabilizing both detection power and false-positive behavior under post-editing attacks.
AI.conclusion: Reliable watermark detection for multivariate time series requires local temporal dependencies rather than global re-encoding to prevent instability under post-editing attacks, and the proposed L-VQVAE/LVQMark framework successfully addresses this limitation.

title: When Saying No Makes Better Videos: Designing Dual Gatekeeping for Pedagogically Grounded AI Content Creation
comment: 4 pages, 1 figure. Presented at the CHI 2026 Workshop on Understanding and Engaging Critical Resistance to AI in Education
summary: To prevent the adoption of aesthetically polished but pedagogically flawed AI content, we study a video authoring pipeline featuring two layers of structured refusal. The first layer empowers educators to iteratively reshape AI scripts based on multimedia learning theory, while the second employs automated metrics to flag violations in instructional coherence and narrative-visual synchronization. While neither layer is exhaustive, their synergy ensures that principled resistance--the act of deferring AI output until it meets rigorous standards--becomes a catalyst for higher quality. Evaluation combining a study with 23 educators across 3 topics and automated metrics across 7 topics drawn from established science and philosophy curricula shows that both layers independently improve the same instructional dimensions, suggesting that thoughtful resistance and generative AI are not opposites but partners.

AI.tldr: A video authoring pipeline with two layers of structured refusal improves AI-generated educational content quality by combining educator-guided refinement based on multimedia learning theory with automated metrics that flag instructional coherence issues.
AI.motivation: To prevent the adoption of aesthetically polished but pedagogically flawed AI-generated educational content. Current AI systems can produce visually appealing content that may lack proper instructional design and pedagogical soundness.
AI.method: A video authoring pipeline with two layers of structured refusal: 1) Educators iteratively reshape AI scripts based on multimedia learning theory; 2) Automated metrics flag violations in instructional coherence and narrative-visual synchronization. The approach emphasizes "principled resistance" - deferring AI output until it meets rigorous standards.
AI.result: Evaluation involved 23 educators across 3 topics and automated metrics across 7 topics from science and philosophy curricula. Both layers independently improved the same instructional dimensions, demonstrating that structured refusal mechanisms enhance AI-generated educational content quality.
AI.conclusion: Thoughtful resistance and generative AI are not opposites but partners. The synergy between educator-guided refinement and automated metrics ensures principled resistance becomes a catalyst for higher quality educational content, preventing adoption of pedagogically flawed but aesthetically polished AI-generated materials.

title: RecPFN: Prior-Fitted Networks for In-Context-Based Recommendations
comment: 12 pages, 4 figures, 8 tables
summary: We introduce RecPFN, a prior-fitted network that brings in-context learning to sequential recommendation. RecPFN is pretrained entirely on synthetic clickstream environments sampled from a broad structural causal prior, enabling it to amortize Bayesian-style inference from a small support set. At inference, a lightweight decoder-only transformer conditions on a handful of domain sequences and produces next-item predictions for queries in a single forward pass, without any weight updates. Across eight public benchmarks, RecPFN achives state-of-the-art zero-shot performance while remaining strongly competitive with supervised methods in low-compute and low-data regimes. It is deployment-efficient and robust to domain shift, outperforming strong zero-shot baselines that rely on large real-interaction corpora. RecPFN provides a practical path toward generalizable, data-efficient recommenders and opens avenues for richer priors, longer-context ICL, and multimodal extensions. Code for training and evaluation is publicly available at https://github.com/SAP-samples/tabular-ai-recpfn/.

AI.tldr: RecPFN is a prior-fitted network for sequential recommendation that uses in-context learning, pretrained entirely on synthetic data from structural causal priors, achieving strong zero-shot performance without weight updates.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to create more generalizable, data-efficient recommenders that can learn from minimal real data without expensive fine-tuning, addressing challenges of domain shift and compute/data constraints in traditional recommendation systems.
AI.method: RecPFN uses a decoder-only transformer pretrained on synthetic clickstream environments generated from broad structural causal priors. It employs in-context learning where the model conditions on a small support set of domain sequences and produces predictions in a single forward pass without weight updates.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot performance across eight public benchmarks, remains competitive with supervised methods in low-data/low-compute regimes, demonstrates deployment efficiency and robustness to domain shift, and outperforms zero-shot baselines that rely on large real-interaction corpora.
AI.conclusion: RecPFN provides a practical path toward generalizable, data-efficient recommenders and opens avenues for richer priors, longer-context in-context learning, and multimodal extensions. The approach enables amortized Bayesian-style inference and efficient deployment.

title: Causal Reasoning with Bipartite Graphical Causal Models
comment: Figure 2 was added w.r.t. to the published version at Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence (UAI) 2026
summary: Causal Bayesian networks (CBNs) and structural causal models (SCMs) are the dominant frameworks for graphical causal reasoning, but they cannot adequately represent all real-world causal systems. In particular, systems at equilibrium---where feedback mechanisms create cyclic causal dependencies---can exhibit causal semantics that are fundamentally incompatible with these frameworks: different interventions that enforce the same variable value may have different effects, rendering the standard ``perfect intervention'' do($X = x$) ambiguous. We propose bipartite graphical causal models (BGCMs), in which the structure of a system of equations is encoded by a bipartite graph with variable and equation nodes. In this framework, a hard intervention do($f_j : X_v = ξ_v$) specifies which equation is replaced, which variable is targeted, and at what value---resolving the ambiguity of the standard notion. We demonstrate, through a detailed case study of a physical system, that this representation naturally corresponds to distinct real-world interventions. We formulate a Markov property in terms of a new graphical separation criterion (B-separation) that exploits the functional determinism inherent in the equations, and we extend it to settings with non-random inputs. We show how this gives rise to a do-calculus for reasoning about domain invariances. BGCMs strictly generalize CBNs and SCMs while retaining the ability to perform graphical causal reasoning.

AI.tldr: BGCMs (bipartite graphical causal models) address limitations of standard causal frameworks by using bipartite graphs with variable and equation nodes to properly represent systems with feedback cycles and equilibrium dynamics, resolving ambiguities in standard interventions.
AI.motivation: Standard causal frameworks (CBNs and SCMs) cannot adequately represent real-world causal systems with feedback mechanisms and equilibrium dynamics. In such systems, different interventions that enforce the same variable value may have different effects, making the standard "perfect intervention" do(X=x) ambiguous and inadequate.
AI.method: Proposes bipartite graphical causal models (BGCMs) that encode system structure using bipartite graphs with variable and equation nodes. Introduces a refined intervention concept do(f_j: X_v = ξ_v) that specifies which equation is replaced, which variable is targeted, and at what value. Develops a new graphical separation criterion (B-separation) that exploits functional determinism in equations.
AI.result: BGCMs provide a framework that naturally corresponds to distinct real-world interventions in systems with feedback cycles. The proposed B-separation criterion enables graphical causal reasoning even in settings with non-random inputs, giving rise to a do-calculus for reasoning about domain invariances.
AI.conclusion: BGCMs strictly generalize both CBNs and SCMs while retaining the ability to perform graphical causal reasoning, offering a more comprehensive framework for modeling causal systems with feedback mechanisms and equilibrium dynamics that standard frameworks cannot adequately represent.

title: Truncate Bad, Upweight Good: BoN-Style Distillation via Rank-Based Classification
summary: Inference-time selection methods, such as Best-of-N, improve generation by sampling a pool of candidates and selecting the top-ranked completion according to a reward model. Distillation seeks to amortize this procedure into a single policy by replacing raw rewards with in-pool ranks and learning a policy that upweights higher-ranked completions. However, existing rank-based policies typically use smooth full-support reweighting, so low-ranked completions receive less mass but remain in the target support. Although a sharper reweighting reduces lower-tail mass, it also increases reliance on brittle ranking at the top made by a single reward model. We propose TUP: a Truncate-bad, Upweight-good Policy that removes low-ranked completions from the support and reweights only the retained upper tail with a tunable sharpness. TUP admits a closed-form, prompt-independent normalization and can be trained fully offline via binary cross-entropy, using shifted-truncated win-rates as soft labels and distilled-to-reference log-likelihood ratios as logits. Theoretically, under certain assumptions, we show that for any unknown oracle reward, the best monotone rank-reweighting can be matched by a lower-tail truncation rule, providing formal support for removing the lower tail rather than merely downweighting it. Empirically, we show that TUP is competitive with strong offline alignment baselines.

AI.tldr: TUP proposes a novel offline alignment method that truncates bad completions instead of downweighting them, improving policy distillation by focusing only on top-ranked candidates with tunable sharpness.
AI.motivation: Existing rank-based distillation methods use smooth full-support reweighting where low-ranked completions receive less mass but remain in the target support. This approach has limitations: sharper reweighting reduces lower-tail mass but increases brittle reliance on single reward model rankings.
AI.method: TUP (Truncate-bad, Upweight-good Policy) removes low-ranked completions from the support entirely and reweights only the retained upper tail with tunable sharpness. It admits closed-form, prompt-independent normalization and can be trained fully offline via binary cross-entropy, using shifted-truncated win-rates as soft labels and distilled-to-reference log-likelihood ratios as logits.
AI.result: Theoretically, TUP shows that for any unknown oracle reward, the best monotone rank-reweighting can be matched by a lower-tail truncation rule. Empirically, TUP is competitive with strong offline alignment baselines.
AI.conclusion: TUP provides a principled approach to offline alignment by truncating low-ranked completions rather than downweighting them, offering formal justification for removing the lower tail and practical benefits in policy distillation.

title: Specification-delta-driven data governance: an empirical study of the «spec-delta» as the unit of change in lakehouse data platforms
summary: Spec Driven Development SDD has consolidated the idea that the specification rather than the code should be the primary artefact governing AI assisted work. Tools such as GitHub Spec Kit, and proposals such as Constitutional SDD, have formalised this principle in the software domain, while the executable data-contracts literature has extended it to schema and quality enforcement at run time. Nevertheless, the treatment of the specification delta OpenSpec's core idea that every change should produce a reviewable increment of requirements as the unit of change in data platforms remains empirically unexplored, even though many data-platform changes are contractual (new datasets, service-level agreements, metric semantics, access policies) rather than purely code changes. This work formalises the spec-delta concept, proposes a taxonomy of data platform changes according to their suitability for incremental specification, and defines a controlled experiment comparing a spec-delta-driven workflow against a conventional code pull-request workflow without a delta. The response variables are discovery to deployment time, the density of defects reaching the Silver and Gold lakehouse layers, cross-tool metric divergence, and reviewer cognitive load measured with NASA TLX. The paper explicitly reserves a demonstration-and-laboratory section for instantiation on a real lakehouse environment. The contribution is not a tool but reproducible evidence and an applicability guide that helps to avoid the up front over specification antipattern.

AI.tldr: Spec-driven development (SDD) emphasizes specifications over code for AI-assisted work, but the spec-delta concept (requirements as the unit of change) hasn't been empirically tested for data platforms. This paper formalizes spec-deltas, proposes a taxonomy of data platform changes, and conducts a controlled experiment comparing spec-delta workflows against conventional pull-request workflows.
AI.motivation: While spec-driven development has gained traction in software development with tools like GitHub Spec Kit and concepts like Constitutional SDD, the core idea of treating specification deltas (requirements changes as the unit of change) remains unexplored empirically for data platforms. Many data platform changes are contractual (new datasets, service-level agreements, metric semantics, access policies) rather than purely code changes, making spec-driven approaches particularly relevant.
AI.method: The paper formalizes the spec-delta concept, proposes a taxonomy of data platform changes according to their suitability for incremental specification, and defines a controlled experiment comparing a spec-delta-driven workflow against a conventional code pull-request workflow without deltas. The study measures discovery-to-deployment time, defect density in Silver and Gold lakehouse layers, cross-tool metric divergence, and reviewer cognitive load using NASA TLX. Includes a demonstration section for real lakehouse environment instantiation.
AI.result: The paper positions itself to provide reproducible evidence and an applicability guide rather than a new tool. The controlled experiment will measure concrete outcomes including time savings, defect reduction, metric consistency improvements, and cognitive load reduction. The demonstration section will show practical instantiation on real lakehouse environments.
AI.conclusion: The contribution is evidence-based guidance for when and how to use spec-delta workflows in data platforms, helping teams avoid upfront over-specification antipatterns while improving development efficiency, quality, and consistency across data platform changes.

title: Credit Without Ground Truth: Auditing Step-Level Credit Assignment in LLM Agents Against Executed Replay
comment: 49 pages, 7 figures. Pre-registered; frozen analysis plans and prompts included in the appendices. Under review
summary: Audited against causal ground truth from executed replay in a single-agent tool environment (ALFWorld), none of the step-level credit signals used to train LLM agents -- LLM-judge scores, outcome-conditioned logprob ratios, or the policy's own confidence -- identifies which steps causally matter better than chance. Existing evaluations grade these signals against annotated step *correctness*; we audit them against step *contribution* -- what re-sampling the policy's own alternatives at each decision point and rolling forward actually changes about the outcome -- and the two come apart. The ground truth itself is structured: causal contribution is sparse (30.5% of decision points where ground truth is defined carry measurable effect), and measurability is model-dependent -- the fraction of points with no policy-supported counterfactual differs by a factor of two (13.1% vs. 26.8%) between two similar-scale policies. The failure mode is identifiable: implicit credit echoes the policy's fluency (median rank correlation +0.75, replicating at +0.70 in a second family under a corrected instrument), while conditioning on the outcome adds no causal information (partial correlation -0.004, Qwen). A confidence-only router recovers pivotal steps at chance level, but cuts judge cost by 13.1% per turn (14.0% per trajectory). In a seven-arm pre-registered training experiment, no arm reliably outperforms the untrained policy, and the checkpoints' apparent instrument signature is fully explained by training dose -- sparser credit retains fewer examples, an order-of-magnitude spread in optimizer steps -- not credit content. Comparisons of credit rules must therefore match effective sample size, or they measure dose, not credit.

AI.tldr: Existing LLM agent training signals (judge scores, outcome-conditioned logprob ratios, policy confidence) fail to identify which steps actually causally matter for task outcomes, performing no better than chance when evaluated against causal ground truth.
AI.motivation: Current evaluations of LLM agent credit assignment signals only measure step correctness annotations, but this paper argues we need to audit against causal contribution - what actually changes outcomes when re-sampling policy alternatives at each decision point.
AI.method: Used causal ground truth from executed replays in ALFWorld single-agent tool environment. Measured causal contribution by re-sampling policy's own alternatives at each decision point and rolling forward to see outcome changes. Compared existing credit signals against this ground truth.
AI.result: No existing credit signal (LLM-judge scores, outcome-conditioned logprob ratios, policy confidence) identifies causally important steps better than chance. Causal contribution is sparse (30.5% of decision points matter). Implicit credit correlates with policy fluency (+0.75 rank correlation) rather than causality. Outcome conditioning adds no causal information (-0.004 partial correlation). Training experiments show no signal reliably outperforms untrained policy when matched for effective sample size.
AI.conclusion: Current LLM agent credit assignment methods fail to capture causal contribution. Credit signals merely echo policy fluency rather than true causality. Comparisons of credit rules must match effective sample size to avoid confounding with training dose effects.

title: SAPO: Single-Rollout Autoregressive Policy Optimization for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
summary: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) has become a critical stage in the post-training of large language models. Existing critic-free, group-relative methods estimate policy advantages from multiple rollouts, avoiding the substantial memory overhead of conventional proximal policy optimization (PPO) and achieving strong performance on long-horizon interactive tasks. Despite their success, recent studies revealed three limitations: (1) Lack explicit value generalization and effective temporal credit assignment; (2) Suffer from potential advantage collapse in long-horizon complex tasks; (3) Require a costly trade-off between sampling budget and policy performance. In this work, we propose Single-rollout Autoregressive Policy Optimization (SAPO), a low-memory and compute-efficient framework in which the policy and value functions share a single autoregressive backbone. SAPO exploits the autoregressive structure of LLMs to produce policy and value predictions at distinct causal boundaries with shared parameters, while independently optimizing the PPO objectives and auxiliary on-policy SARSA objectives. To robustly estimate the contribution of each turn, we further introduce a trajectory-level generalized advantage estimator that combines lambda-returns with batch normalization. Experiments across ALFWorld and WebShop with Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B show that SAPO trains stably and outperforms PPO and GRPO by mean +15.1 and +12.1 percentage points, respectively, while eliminating the memory cost of a separate critic model and reducing per-iteration runtime by 33.2% over PPO.

AI.tldr: SAPO is a memory-efficient reinforcement learning framework that uses a single autoregressive backbone for both policy and value functions, outperforming PPO and GRPO while reducing computational overhead.
AI.motivation: Existing critic-free, group-relative RL methods for LLM post-training have three limitations: lack of explicit value generalization and temporal credit assignment, potential advantage collapse in long-horizon tasks, and a costly trade-off between sampling budget and policy performance.
AI.method: Proposes Single-rollout Autoregressive Policy Optimization (SAPO) with: 1) a shared autoregressive backbone for policy and value functions, 2) independent optimization of PPO and on-policy SARSA objectives, and 3) a trajectory-level generalized advantage estimator combining lambda-returns with batch normalization.
AI.result: SAPO outperforms PPO by mean +15.1 percentage points and GRPO by +12.1 percentage points on ALFWorld and WebShop with Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B, eliminates critic model memory costs, and reduces per-iteration runtime by 33.2% over PPO.
AI.conclusion: SAPO provides a memory-efficient, compute-efficient RL framework that addresses limitations of existing methods while achieving superior performance on long-horizon interactive tasks with LLMs.

title: Finite-Horizon Input-Output Dynamics of Minibatch Perturbations in AdamW
summary: A minibatch can influence training beyond the update at which it is observed because AdamW stores past gradient information in its optimizer states. We study this delayed effect through paired trajectories that differ only in one gradient update and share the same subsequent training sequence. We formulate AdamW as a finite-horizon input--state--output (ISO) system whose state contains the model parameters and first- and second-moment estimates. Linearizing the joint dynamics yields a signed response operator that maps a localized gradient perturbation to its future loss effects, revealing how optimizer memory shapes their magnitude, timing, and sign. We further derive an exact multistep error decomposition and establish first-order finite-horizon accuracy under local smoothness and controlled activation switching. Experiments validate the response mechanism and optimizer-state effects, while repeated-future analyses reveal substantial prospective structure in delayed influence that can be partially recovered from ISO approximations. Code is available at https://github.com/Kanyooo/Loss_ISO.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how minibatches have delayed effects on training in AdamW due to optimizer state memory, using input-state-output system analysis to track gradient perturbations' future impacts.
AI.motivation: Minibatches can influence training beyond their immediate update because AdamW stores past gradient information in optimizer states (first/second-moment estimates), creating delayed effects that aren't well understood.
AI.method: Formulates AdamW as a finite-horizon input-state-output system, linearizes the joint dynamics to create a signed response operator mapping gradient perturbations to future loss effects, derives exact multistep error decomposition, and establishes first-order finite-horizon accuracy conditions.
AI.result: Developed a framework to analyze how optimizer memory shapes the magnitude, timing, and sign of delayed gradient effects, validated through experiments showing substantial prospective structure in delayed influence that can be partially recovered from ISO approximations.
AI.conclusion: The input-state-output system approach successfully captures how AdamW's optimizer states create delayed training effects from minibatches, revealing systematic patterns in gradient perturbation propagation that provide insights into optimization dynamics.

title: PolicyGuide: From Guarding One Action to Guiding the Whole Workflow for Policy-Compliant LLM Agents
comment: 26 pages, 15 figures, including appendices
summary: Customer-service LLM agents must follow organizational policy when acting on a user's behalf. Compliance failures arise from either forbidden actions, such as granting an ineligible change, or omitted procedural requirements, such as identification or confirmation. Runtime safeguards can intervene on risky actions, but action-local checks do not guide an agent through a multi-step procedure. Workflow-following systems support prescribed process execution, but primarily target workflow completion rather than safeguarding agent behavior. PolicyGuide instead compiles each domain policy into a workflow graph and invokes a proactive verifier at user-turn boundaries. From persisted graph state, the verifier reconciles open requests and returns step-specific remediation along a policy-compliant path. Across the $τ^2$-bench airline, retail, and telecom domains with a GPT-5.4 agent and verifier, PolicyGuide raises mean $\mathrm{Pass}^4$ from $0.42$ to $0.62$, with the largest gain on telecom ($0.19$ to $0.61$), the most workflow-structured domain. The same workflows transfer to Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Gemini 2.5 Pro agents. Complementary evaluations find the lowest observed attack-success rate under adversarial users and the strongest procedural compliance in an author-designed workflow-level validation.

AI.tldr: PolicyGuide is a system that compiles domain policies into workflow graphs and uses proactive verification to guide customer-service LLM agents through policy-compliant procedures, significantly improving compliance across multiple domains.
AI.motivation: Customer-service LLM agents often fail to follow organizational policies, either by performing forbidden actions or omitting required procedural steps. Existing approaches either use runtime safeguards that only check individual risky actions (missing multi-step guidance) or workflow systems focused on completion rather than policy compliance.
AI.method: PolicyGuide compiles each domain policy into a workflow graph and invokes a proactive verifier at user-turn boundaries. The verifier reconciles open requests from persisted graph state and returns step-specific remediation along policy-compliant paths to guide the agent.
AI.result: Across airline, retail, and telecom domains using GPT-5.4 agents and verifiers, PolicyGuide raised mean Pass⁴ from 0.42 to 0.62, with the largest gain in telecom (0.19 to 0.61). The workflows transferred successfully to Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Gemini 2.5 Pro agents, showing the lowest attack-success rate under adversarial users and strongest procedural compliance.
AI.conclusion: PolicyGuide effectively addresses policy compliance in customer-service LLM agents by combining policy compilation into workflow graphs with proactive verification, demonstrating significant improvements across domains and agent models while maintaining security against adversarial users.

title: Unsupervised Anomaly Detection Using Flow Matching on Tabular Data
summary: Financial anomaly detection often relies on large unlabeled transaction logs, where anomalous samples may already be present during training. Such training-set contamination violates the clean-normal data assumption underlying many anomaly detection methods. Although flow matching has demonstrated strong performance in generative modeling, its robustness in unsupervised tabular anomaly detection remains underexplored. In this work, we study flow-matching-based anomaly detection under contaminated training data by comparing Time-Conditioned Contraction Matching (TCCM) with Forest-Flow and evaluating multiple anomaly scoring functions. Our results show that the choice of anomaly score is critical. The original single-step Decision score used by TCCM is sensitive to contamination, whereas trajectory-based Deviation and Reconstruction scores provide more stable anomaly signals. With these scores, Forest-Flow becomes competitive with, and in some cases outperforms, TCCM. These findings highlight the importance of anomaly scoring for flow-matching methods in financial anomaly detection under severe class imbalance.

AI.tldr: Flow-matching-based anomaly detection in financial data shows that anomaly scoring function choice is critical, with trajectory-based scores outperforming original single-step scores when training data is contaminated.
AI.motivation: Financial anomaly detection often uses unlabeled transaction logs where anomalous samples may be present during training, violating the clean-normal data assumption of many methods. Flow matching shows promise but its robustness to contaminated training data is underexplored.
AI.method: Study flow-matching-based anomaly detection under contaminated training data by comparing Time-Conditioned Contraction Matching (TCCM) with Forest-Flow and evaluating multiple anomaly scoring functions including Decision, Deviation, and Reconstruction scores.
AI.result: Choice of anomaly score is critical: original single-step Decision score used by TCCM is sensitive to contamination, while trajectory-based Deviation and Reconstruction scores provide more stable anomaly signals. With these better scores, Forest-Flow becomes competitive with and sometimes outperforms TCCM.
AI.conclusion: Anomaly scoring function selection is crucial for flow-matching methods in financial anomaly detection under severe class imbalance and contaminated training data, with trajectory-based scores offering better robustness.

title: EnvHarness: Awakening Static Worlds for Agent Learning
summary: LLM agents learn by interacting with environments, yet these environments are hand-built and static: blind to an agent's weaknesses, and quickly left behind as it improves. While recent environment generation methods attempt to address this, they require domain-specific pipelines, rely on expensive or unreliable verifiers, and still produce static environments. To alleviate the engineering burden of rebuilding environments from scratch, we propose Environment Harness (EnvHarness), a programmable layer of plug-in components that wraps a static environment to reshape its behavior without modifying the underlying logic. Operating through standard interfaces, EnvHarness applies across diverse domains while ensuring every reshaped environment retains its original verifier. To automate this process, we introduce EnvRigger, which treats the target policy as a black box, observing its execution trajectories to synthesize EnvHarness components targeting diagnosed flaws, and validating them via fresh rollouts. Across five benchmarks in four domains, EnvHarness outperforms both original environments and domain-specific environment generation pipelines, achieving up to a 9.0-point improvement on held-out instances with 9.8% fewer execution steps. Furthermore, EnvHarness provides a superior optimization signal for reinforcement learning, enabling continuous, targeted co-evolution of the policy and its environment.

AI.tldr: EnvHarness is a programmable layer that dynamically reshapes static environments to target agent weaknesses, enabling automated environment adaptation without domain-specific engineering.
AI.motivation: Current LLM agent environments are hand-built, static, and blind to agent weaknesses, requiring expensive domain-specific pipelines for environment generation that still produce static environments.
AI.method: EnvHarness provides plug-in components that wrap static environments to reshape behavior without modifying underlying logic, and EnvRigger automates component synthesis by observing policy execution trajectories to diagnose flaws and validate via fresh rollouts.
AI.result: Across five benchmarks in four domains, EnvHarness outperforms original environments and domain-specific environment generation pipelines, achieving up to 9.0-point improvement on held-out instances with 9.8% fewer execution steps, and provides superior optimization signal for RL.
AI.conclusion: EnvHarness alleviates engineering burdens, enables continuous co-evolution of policy and environment through targeted reshaping, and maintains original verifier reliability while operating across diverse domains.

title: MileGPO: Milestone Inference with Local Evidence for Graph-Based Policy Optimization of Long-Horizon LLM Agents
summary: Credit assignment is challenging in long-horizon agentic reinforcement learning, where supervision often comes only from final rewards. Existing methods refine trajectory-level signals into step-level credits through step grouping or graph-based advantage estimation, but can overlook meaningful intermediate milestones. We propose MileGPO (Milestone Inference with Local Evidence for Graph-Based Policy Optimization), which derives process-level credit from grouped on-policy rollouts through three designs. Milestone Discovery identifies candidate milestones on successful rollouts and recurring traps on failed ones. Reliability-Calibrated Shaping (RCS) weights these candidates by outcome-based confidence, strengthening reliable milestones and traps while down-weighting uncertain ones. Progress-Contrastive Calibration (PCC) further tests whether a candidate reflects local progress and whether its incoming ansition outperforms observed alternatives from the same state.MileGPO requires neither auxiliary models nor additional environment interaction. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop show state-of-the-art performance and a small in-distribution to out-of-distribution gap on ALFWorld. Ablations and credit diagnostics indicate that reliability weighting, local progress, and same-state branch evidence complement milestone discovery and resolve ambiguous intermediate credit.

AI.tldr: MileGPO is a new method for credit assignment in long-horizon reinforcement learning that identifies meaningful intermediate milestones in successful trajectories and recurring traps in failed ones, using reliability calibration and progress contrastive calibration to refine step-level credits without requiring additional models or environment interactions.
AI.motivation: Credit assignment is challenging in long-horizon agentic reinforcement learning where supervision typically comes only from final rewards. Existing methods refine trajectory-level signals into step-level credits through step grouping or graph-based advantage estimation, but often overlook meaningful intermediate milestones that could provide better credit assignment.
AI.method: MileGPO (Milestone Inference with Local Evidence for Graph-Based Policy Optimization) proposes three key designs: 1) Milestone Discovery identifies candidate milestones on successful rollouts and recurring traps on failed ones; 2) Reliability-Calibrated Shaping (RCS) weights these candidates by outcome-based confidence, strengthening reliable milestones/traps while down-weighting uncertain ones; 3) Progress-Contrastive Calibration (PCC) tests whether a candidate reflects local progress and whether its incoming transition outperforms observed alternatives from the same state. The method requires neither auxiliary models nor additional environment interaction.
AI.result: Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop show state-of-the-art performance and a small in-distribution to out-of-distribution gap on ALFWorld. Ablations and credit diagnostics indicate that reliability weighting, local progress, and same-state branch evidence complement milestone discovery and effectively resolve ambiguous intermediate credit assignment.
AI.conclusion: MileGPO successfully addresses the credit assignment challenge in long-horizon RL by discovering meaningful intermediate milestones and calibrating them with reliability and progress-based evidence, providing superior performance compared to existing methods while maintaining efficiency by not requiring additional models or environment interactions.

title: TESTNAV: Pareto-Guided Search for Compositional Robustness Testing
summary:
Deep learning models remain vulnerable to real-world input perturbations, especially when multiple corruptions co-occur in the same input (e.g., brightness shifts and motion blur). Compositional testing reveals these interaction effects but introduces two challenges: combinatorial growth of the perturbation space as dimensions and severity levels increase, and uneven diagnostic value-many combinations yield unrealistically degraded inputs with limited practical relevance.
  We present TESTNAV, 1 a Pareto-guided robustness testing framework for efficiently exploring discrete, compositional perturbation spaces when only a limited number of perturbation configurations can be evaluated. TESTNAV prioritises severe yet realistic failures by formulating robustness testing as bi-objective optimisation: maximise performance degradation while preserving input fidelity measured by modality-specific metrics (e.g., SSIM and KID for vision; chrF and BERT-F1 for language and code). It uses NSGA-II to approximate the bi-objective Pareto front. Across four benchmarks spanning vision, natural language, and code generation, TESTNAV recovers Pareto fronts up to 2.15x faster than search-based baselines, using 35.8%-89.3% of the discrete perturbation space defined by four perturbation dimensions with six levels each.

AI.tldr: TESTNAV is a Pareto-guided robustness testing framework that efficiently explores compositional perturbation spaces by balancing performance degradation and input fidelity, using multi-objective optimization to find severe yet realistic failures.
AI.motivation: Deep learning models are vulnerable to real-world input perturbations, especially when multiple corruptions co-occur. Compositional testing reveals interaction effects but faces two challenges: combinatorial explosion of perturbation space (dimensions × severity levels) and many unrealistic combinations with limited practical relevance.
AI.method: TESTNAV formulates robustness testing as bi-objective optimization: maximize performance degradation while preserving input fidelity using modality-specific metrics (SSIM/KID for vision, chrF/BERT-F1 for language/code). It uses NSGA-II to approximate the bi-objective Pareto front, prioritizing severe yet realistic failures.
AI.result: TESTNAV recovers Pareto fronts up to 2.15× faster than search-based baselines, using only 35.8%-89.3% of the discrete perturbation space across four benchmarks spanning vision, natural language, and code generation.
AI.conclusion: TESTNAV provides an efficient framework for exploring compositional perturbation spaces with limited evaluations, focusing on practical, realistic failures rather than exhaustive testing of all unrealistic combinations.

title: Answer-Level Trust Selection for Physical Vision-Language Reasoning
comment: Preprint
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) can estimate physical quantities such as duration, speed, and acceleration from visual observations, but existing benchmarks primarily assess overall model performance against annotated ground truth. In deployment, a key question is whether an individual prediction can be trusted when its ground truth is unavailable. Self-consistency alone may fail to capture important failure modes: a VLM may produce stable-but-wrong estimates or rely on textual priors rather than visual evidence. We formulate answer-level selective prediction for quantitative physical reasoning and propose Answer-Level Trust Selection (ATS), a post-hoc, model-agnostic framework for accepting or rejecting individual VLM predictions. ATS requires no fine-tuning, auxiliary verifier, or access to the model's internal logits. Instead, it aggregates eight interpretable behavioral diagnostic scores derived from repeated queries and controlled interventions into a unified trust score. We evaluate ATS in depth on Qwen2.5-VL-7B and across 20 VLM backbones, examining selective performance, diagnostic behavior, and targeted failure modes. Our results show that intervention-based diagnostics help identify stable-but-wrong and prior-tracking predictions that repeated agreement alone may miss. However, improved failure-case rejection can come at the cost of lower retention of correct predictions. ATS therefore complements model-level capability evaluation with answer-level reliability assessment for quantitative VLM predictions. Code will be released upon publication.

AI.tldr: ATS is a post-hoc framework that aggregates behavioral diagnostic scores from repeated queries and interventions to assess trustworthiness of individual VLM predictions for quantitative physical reasoning, without needing fine-tuning or model internals.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks assess overall VLM performance but don't help determine trustworthiness of individual predictions when ground truth is unavailable. Self-consistency alone may fail to identify stable-but-wrong predictions or text-based priors over visual evidence.
AI.method: Answer-Level Trust Selection (ATS) aggregates eight interpretable behavioral diagnostic scores derived from repeated queries and controlled interventions into a unified trust score. It's post-hoc, model-agnostic, requiring no fine-tuning, auxiliary verifier, or access to internal logits.
AI.result: ATS was evaluated on Qwen2.5-VL-7B and 20 VLM backbones. Intervention-based diagnostics identified stable-but-wrong and prior-tracking predictions that repeated agreement alone missed, but improved failure-case rejection sometimes reduced retention of correct predictions.
AI.conclusion: ATS complements model-level capability evaluation with answer-level reliability assessment for quantitative VLM predictions, providing a practical framework for trust selection in deployment where ground truth is unavailable.

title: Write Once, Run Everywhere: The Axon DSL for Shape-Safe and Framework-Agnostic LLM Architectures
summary: The entire ecosystem of open-source language models effectively relies on a single platform. What if this platform was forced to shut down tomorrow? Implementing and maintaining efficient model definitions and translating them between different training and inference regimes is a resource-heavy task that severely limits model efficiency and portability, hindering both scaling and deployment. Here, we present Axon, a strongly typed domain-specific language with Haskell-like syntax, that enables a write-once, run everywhere paradigm for LLM architectures. By basing collaboration on a language specification rather than a specific framework's vision, Axon fosters open cooperation and empowers researchers to implement highly specialized architectures without giving up optimization infrastructure or accepting deployment lock-in. Axon allows for concise, auditable specifications that can be automatically compiled to standalone implementations for leading frameworks: PyTorch, PyTorch with Triton, JAX, MLX and vLLM. In 467 inference benchmarking experiments on models ranging from 135M to 32B parameters, we demonstrate median speedups of 7% on PyTorch, 12% on PyTorch with Triton, 91% on JAX, and 107% on MLX, compared to the reference implementations from Transformers. When deployed as native vLLM architectures with PagedAttention and KV-cache, Axon models achieve a 58% median speedup over Transformers implementations.

AI.tldr: Axon is a Haskell-like domain-specific language for LLM architectures that enables write-once, run-everywhere portability across frameworks (PyTorch, JAX, MLX, vLLM) with significant performance improvements.
AI.motivation: The open-source LLM ecosystem relies on a single platform, creating vulnerability if it shuts down. Current implementations require heavy resources to maintain and translate between frameworks, limiting model efficiency, portability, scaling, and deployment.
AI.method: Axon is a strongly typed domain-specific language with Haskell-like syntax that enables write-once, run-everywhere paradigm. It compiles concise, auditable specifications to standalone implementations for multiple frameworks: PyTorch, PyTorch with Triton, JAX, MLX, and vLLM.
AI.result: In 467 inference benchmarking experiments on models from 135M to 32B parameters: median speedups of 7% on PyTorch, 12% on PyTorch with Triton, 91% on JAX, and 107% on MLX vs. Transformers. As native vLLM architectures with PagedAttention and KV-cache: 58% median speedup over Transformers implementations.
AI.conclusion: Axon enables open cooperation through language specification rather than framework-specific implementations, empowering researchers to implement specialized architectures without sacrificing optimization infrastructure or accepting deployment lock-in, while achieving substantial performance improvements.

title: FAR-DPO: Feasibility-Aware and Robust Direct Preference Optimization for Cyclic Peptide Design
comment: 16 pages, 6 figures, and 7 tables. Includes supplementary materials
summary: Cyclic peptides are emerging as promising molecular scaffolds in drug discovery due to their high binding affinity and structural stability. However, extending generative models from linear to cyclic peptide design remains challenging, as cyclization sharply restricts the feasible design space through coupled geometric and biophysical constraints. Moreover, limited training data has led existing approaches to rely largely on zero-shot generation or post hoc filtering, resulting in low yields of feasible designs and limited control over multi-objective trade-offs. To address these limitations, we propose FAR-DPO (Feasibility-Aware and Robust Direct Preference Optimization), an architecture-agnostic framework that steers generative models toward structurally and biophysically feasible cyclic peptide designs, particularly for challenging targets. FAR-DPO integrates feasibility-aware preference construction with difficulty-aware group-robust optimization. Specifically, it constructs within-target preference pairs through feasibility-gated multi-objective dominance and adaptively reweights predefined difficulty groups according to their current preference losses. On the CPSea LNR benchmark, under a fixed generation budget, FAR-DPO increases overall success rate from 46.89% to 57.79% on PepGLAD and from 47.96% to 49.57% on PepFlow. These gains also extend to the hardest target quartile and are accompanied by more favorable best-per-target binding scores. Together, these results demonstrate FAR-DPO's effectiveness in improving feasibility and target-wise robustness.

AI.tldr: FAR-DPO is a new framework that improves generative models for designing cyclic peptides by incorporating feasibility constraints and robust optimization, achieving higher success rates in generating viable peptide structures for challenging drug targets.
AI.motivation: Cyclic peptides are promising for drug discovery due to high binding affinity and stability, but generative models struggle with cyclic peptide design because cyclization imposes strict geometric and biophysical constraints. Existing methods have low yields and poor control over multi-objective trade-offs due to limited training data.
AI.method: FAR-DPO (Feasibility-Aware and Robust Direct Preference Optimization) integrates feasibility-aware preference construction through feasibility-gated multi-objective dominance and difficulty-aware group-robust optimization. It constructs within-target preference pairs and adaptively reweights difficulty groups based on their current preference losses.
AI.result: On the CPSea LNR benchmark, FAR-DPO increased overall success rate from 46.89% to 57.79% on PepGLAD and from 47.96% to 49.57% on PepFlow. Improvements extended to the hardest target quartile with more favorable best-per-target binding scores.
AI.conclusion: FAR-DPO effectively improves feasibility and target-wise robustness for cyclic peptide design, addressing key limitations in generative modeling for drug discovery applications involving constrained molecular scaffolds.

title: EXIMO: VLM Guided Exploration of VLA Policies
summary: How to efficiently finetune robot policies to learn new tasks on the fly? State of the art robotic manipulation policies are based on behaviour cloning of large vision-language-action (VLA) models with billions of parameters on huge teleoperation datasets. While this simple approach has enabled significant advances for robotic manipulation, finetuning of VLA policies for learning new tasks still remains an open problem. In particular, collecting teleoperation datasets requires hundreds of hours of expensive human labour and the alternative, reinforcement learning (RL), can be notoriously sample-inefficient especially for long-horizon tasks. In addition, RL with VLAs imposes several challenges due to the model's size and architectural design. In this work, we propose EXIMO, an efficient algorithm for finetuning of VLA policies. EXIMO operates in three stages: explore, imitate, and optimize. During the explore phase, EXIMO equips the VLA with a vision language model (VLM) that acts as a planner. The VLM thinks and breaks down challenging long-horizon problems into shorter ones for the VLA. The VLM, together with the VLA, is used to collect an orchestrated dataset on new tasks. During the imitate phase, the VLA is finetuned with the orchestrated data. Finally, during the optimize stage, we use residual off-policy RL to further finetune the policy. In our experiments, we ablate all three stages of EXIMO and show that it outperforms existing approaches significantly in terms of sample-efficiency and final performance.

AI.tldr: EXIMO is an efficient three-stage algorithm (explore-imitate-optimize) for fine-tuning large vision-language-action models on new robot manipulation tasks with improved sample efficiency over existing methods.
AI.motivation: Current VLA-based robotic manipulation policies struggle with fine-tuning for new tasks due to: 1) high cost of collecting human teleoperation data (hundreds of hours), 2) sample inefficiency of reinforcement learning for long-horizon tasks, and 3) architectural challenges of applying RL to large VLAs.
AI.method: Three-stage approach: 1) EXPLORE - VLA equipped with VLM planner breaks long-horizon tasks into shorter subproblems and collects orchestrated dataset; 2) IMITATE - VLA fine-tuned on orchestrated data; 3) OPTIMIZE - residual off-policy RL further fine-tunes the policy.
AI.result: EXIMO significantly outperforms existing approaches in both sample-efficiency and final performance across experimental evaluations, with comprehensive ablation studies validating all three stages.
AI.conclusion: EXIMO provides an effective solution to the challenging problem of fine-tuning VLA policies for new robot manipulation tasks, addressing data efficiency challenges through its explore-imitate-optimize framework that combines planning, imitation learning, and residual RL.

title: Adaptive Probabilistic Shielding by Learning MDPs for Safe Reinforcement Learning
comment: 19 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. To be published in the proceedings of RV 2026
summary: Probabilistic shielding is a technique for safe reinforcement learning (RL). Typically, a static observer -- called the shield -- constrains the learning agent's actions to those for which acting safely remains feasible. Traditionally, the shield is computed from the transition probabilities of the underlying Markov decision process (MDP). Thus, this technique is not applicable when the MDP model is not given a priori, which, unfortunately, is the case in typical RL applications. In this paper, we study the problem of computing a shield in the setting where the transition graph of the MDP is known, but the transition probabilities are unknown. Our approach integrates probabilistic shielding with online model learning: as the RL agent explores the environment, we estimate the transition probabilities. From this estimate, we compute a shield. While the shield may be conservative initially, it adapts as the model estimate becomes more precise. Thus, the shield improves in tandem with the RL agent. This paradigm of adaptive probabilistic shielding raises a number of challenges, such as when to recompute the shield and how to balance between exploration and safety during learning. We empirically evaluate multiple variants of this paradigm across several environments.

AI.tldr: Adaptive probabilistic shielding integrates online model learning with safety constraints in reinforcement learning when transition probabilities are unknown, enabling safe exploration while adapting the shield as models improve.
AI.motivation: Traditional probabilistic shielding requires known transition probabilities, which limits its application in typical RL settings where the MDP model is not given a priori. The paper addresses this gap by developing an adaptive shielding approach for environments with known transition graphs but unknown probabilities.
AI.method: The approach combines probabilistic shielding with online model learning: as the RL agent explores, transition probabilities are estimated, and shields are computed from these estimates. The method addresses challenges like when to recompute shields and balancing exploration vs safety during learning.
AI.result: The paper empirically evaluates multiple variants of the adaptive probabilistic shielding paradigm across several environments, demonstrating that the shield adapts and improves alongside the RL agent as model estimates become more precise.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive probabilistic shielding enables safe RL in environments with unknown transition probabilities by integrating online model learning, allowing shields to evolve from potentially conservative initial estimates to more precise safety constraints as learning progresses.

title: Bringing analytic rigor to agentic AI for science: The Brain Researcher platform for neuroimaging data analysis
comment: 103 pages, 19 figures; Supplementary Information included
summary: AI agents can execute scientific analyses, but an analytic output becomes a defensible claim only after alternatives are weighed and the claim is limited to what the evidence supports. Agents may reproduce failures including selective analysis, premature declarations of success and optimization of imperfect criteria. We present Brain Researcher, an agentic research harness operating in a neuroimaging researcher's computational environment under rules for admissible analyses, required checks and claim scope. In benchmarks, Brain Researcher increased first-choice tool-selection accuracy across seven models by 70.2 percentage points (23.3% without it versus 93.6% with it) and verifiable grounding from 4.6% to 22.0%. In collaborator-led and self-evolving studies, multiverse analyses exposed analytic-choice sensitivity, and scientific review classified claims as accepted, qualified, revised, blocked, rejected or deferred. By linking decisions to evidence and provenance, Brain Researcher embeds methodological judgment within the workflow, not after it.

AI.tldr: Brain Researcher is an agentic research harness that enforces scientific rigor in AI-driven neuroimaging analysis by implementing rules for admissible analyses, required checks, and proper claim scoping to prevent common methodological failures.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to address scientific reliability issues in AI-driven research. While AI agents can execute analyses, they often reproduce human scientific failures like selective analysis, premature success declarations, and optimizing imperfect criteria. These practices undermine scientific rigor and produce claims that lack proper evidentiary support.
AI.method: The authors developed Brain Researcher, an agentic research harness that operates in a neuroimaging researcher's computational environment. It implements rules governing admissible analyses, required checks, and claim scope limitations. The system links decisions to evidence and provenance, embedding methodological judgment within the workflow rather than as a post-hoc process.
AI.result: In benchmarks, Brain Researcher increased first-choice tool-selection accuracy across seven models by 70.2 percentage points (from 23.3% without it to 93.6% with it) and improved verifiable grounding from 4.6% to 22.0%. In collaborator-led and self-evolving studies, multiverse analyses exposed analytic-choice sensitivity, and scientific review classified claims as accepted, qualified, revised, blocked, rejected, or deferred.
AI.conclusion: Brain Researcher successfully embeds methodological judgment within AI-driven scientific workflows, transforming analytic outputs into defensible claims by enforcing rigorous scientific practices. It addresses key reliability issues in automated research and provides a framework for making AI-generated scientific claims more transparent, evidence-based, and properly scoped.

title: Inadvertent Context Leakage in Language Models
summary:
For AI agents to be useful beyond simple chat, they must hold sensitive user context such as calendars, credentials, health records, and financial data. We study whether the mere presence of such secrets in a model's context window introduces hidden correlations into the model's benign outputs, allowing reconstruction even when the model correctly refuses direct extraction. We further study whether an adversary can actively engineer prompts that amplify this effect, using the model as a covert carrier to transmit secrets through seemingly innocuous text. In both cases, this limited leakage is exploited using a novel adaptive attack that assumes black-box access to the underlying model.
  In controlled experiments across eight proprietary models, we find that 2-digit in-context secrets are reconstructed with near-perfect accuracy and 4-digit secrets at 82\% exact match, all from outputs the model produces in response to ordinary, non-adversarial requests. We observe that more capable models leak more: stronger instruction-following amplifies sensitivity to in-context secrets, suggesting leakage is a byproduct of capability as opposed to a patchable bug. We show this leakage enables two practical attacks: (1) a trained classifier that infers semantic predicates about user memories (e.g., health conditions, financial events) from routine natural-language outputs, and (2) an RL-trained adversary that extracts full Social Security Numbers from a production-style agent.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that AI models leak sensitive information from their context windows through seemingly innocent outputs, showing that even when models refuse direct extraction, hidden correlations allow adversaries to reconstruct secrets, with stronger models leaking more information.
AI.motivation: As AI agents handle sensitive user data (calendars, credentials, health records, financial data), there's a need to understand whether the mere presence of such secrets in a model's context window creates hidden correlations that can be exploited, even when models correctly refuse direct extraction.
AI.method: Researchers conducted controlled experiments across eight proprietary models, using a novel adaptive attack with black-box access. They tested both passive leakage from benign outputs and active prompting engineered to amplify the effect. They developed two practical attacks: a trained classifier for semantic predicate inference and an RL-trained adversary for extracting sensitive information.
AI.result: Results show significant leakage: 2-digit secrets reconstructed with near-perfect accuracy, 4-digit secrets at 82% exact match from ordinary outputs. More capable models leak more information, suggesting leakage correlates with capability rather than being a patchable bug. Practical attacks successfully inferred health conditions and financial events, and extracted full Social Security Numbers from production-style agents.
AI.conclusion: AI models inherently leak sensitive information from context windows through hidden correlations, with stronger models being more vulnerable. This presents a fundamental security challenge that cannot be easily patched, requiring new approaches to secure AI systems handling sensitive user data.

title: Spike-based Belief Propagation in Nonlinear Dynamical Systems
comment: Accepted at NCTA 2026 (18th Int'l Conf. on Neural Computation Theory and Applications), part of IJCCI 2026, Angers, France. Pre-peer-review submitted version
summary: This paper presents a Bayesian control framework that integrates spike-based dynamics with probabilistic inference for adaptive control. Bayesian inference is widely regarded as a core computational principle of brain function, providing a normative framework for perception, decision-making, and learning under uncertainty. By combining a biologically inspired spiking neural model with Bayesian inference principles, we propose a brain-like control algorithm capable of operating in uncertain environments. We use the mountain car parking problem as a benchmark with non-linear dynamics. Our results demonstrate that the proposed controller can successfully update states in real time and generate goal-directed action plans through spike-driven dynamics. The results highlight the proposed model's potential as a bridge between computational neuroscience and probabilistic control theory.

AI.tldr: Bayesian control framework integrates spiking neural models with probabilistic inference for adaptive control in uncertain environments.
AI.motivation: Bayesian inference is considered a core computational principle of brain function, providing a normative framework for perception, decision-making, and learning under uncertainty. There's a need to bridge computational neuroscience with probabilistic control theory.
AI.method: Proposes a brain-like control algorithm that combines biologically inspired spiking neural models with Bayesian inference principles. The framework integrates spike-based dynamics with probabilistic inference for adaptive control. Uses the mountain car parking problem with non-linear dynamics as a benchmark.
AI.result: The proposed controller successfully updates states in real time and generates goal-directed action plans through spike-driven dynamics. The model demonstrates effective operation in uncertain environments.
AI.conclusion: The results highlight the proposed model's potential as a bridge between computational neuroscience and probabilistic control theory, showing that spike-based Bayesian control can enable adaptive behavior in complex environments.

title: Online Test-Time Adaptation for Generalizable Dynamic Graph Anomaly Detection
summary: Generalizable dynamic graph anomaly detection (DGAD) enables pretrained detectors to identify anomalies in unseen target domains without costly retraining. However, existing methods often fail for two reasons. First, they mainly rely on domain-agnostic patterns and miss domain-specific patterns that keep evolving. Second, they assume access to the full target domain data, whereas in more practical online test-time adaptation settings, target data arrive sequentially in unlabeled chunks. To address these limitations, we formulate online test-time adaptation for generalizable DGAD and propose OTTA-DGAD. OTTA-DGAD first extracts dynamic prototypes, i.e., evolving representations of normal and anomalous patterns, from temporal ego-graphs and stores them in a memory buffer. The buffer selectively retains general patterns shared across the source domains used for pretraining while incorporating new patterns from the target domain. An anomaly scorer then compares incoming edge representations against these prototypes to identify both general and domain-specific anomalies. During adaptation, OTTA-DGAD updates the memory buffer using reliable pseudo-labels identified through confidence-based detection. It further enriches each target chunk with relevant representations retained from previous chunks, compensating for information loss resulting from the sequential arrival of data. Extensive experiments under strict test-then-adapt OTTA settings demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on ten real-world datasets from diverse domains.

AI.tldr: OTTA-DGAD enables online test-time adaptation for dynamic graph anomaly detection by extracting evolving prototypes, maintaining a memory buffer of normal/anomalous patterns, and using confidence-based pseudo-labels for adaptation to unseen target domains without retraining.
AI.motivation: Existing generalizable dynamic graph anomaly detection methods fail because they: 1) mainly rely on domain-agnostic patterns and miss evolving domain-specific patterns, and 2) assume access to full target domain data rather than dealing with the more practical online test-time adaptation setting where data arrives sequentially in unlabeled chunks.
AI.method: OTTA-DGAD extracts dynamic prototypes (evolving representations of normal/anomalous patterns) from temporal ego-graphs and stores them in a memory buffer. The buffer selectively retains general patterns from source domains while incorporating new patterns from target domains. It uses an anomaly scorer to compare incoming edge representations against prototypes, and updates the buffer using reliable pseudo-labels identified through confidence-based detection. It also enriches each target chunk with relevant representations from previous chunks to compensate for sequential data arrival.
AI.result: Extensive experiments under strict test-then-adapt OTTA settings demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on ten real-world datasets from diverse domains.
AI.conclusion: OTTA-DGAD successfully addresses the limitations of existing methods by enabling online test-time adaptation for generalizable dynamic graph anomaly detection, handling both general and domain-specific patterns while accommodating practical sequential data arrival scenarios.

title: A Strong Linear Baseline for Whole-Heart Cardiac Shape Completion on CT, with an Open Eleven-Structure Statistical Shape Model
summary: Public cardiac cohorts annotate different subsets of the heart, so shapes from separate sources cannot be pooled without shared correspondence. Among released cardiac shape resources, none we identified carries the atrial appendage, pulmonary veins, and caval stumps as separate blocks in one mesh. Completion benchmarks also compare deep models against a least-squares projection onto shape modes, not the conditional estimator the same fitted model implies. We release an eleven- structure cardiac computed-tomography (CT) statistical shape model, built from 383 automatically labelled cases in 11 571-vertex correspondence, and compare completion estimators under one frozen internal split and endpoint. On a 76-case internal list held out from fitting, a closed-form conditional-Gaussian estimator reconstructed the missing non-chamber structures at 3.717 mm mean per-vertex error, averaged equally over one, three, five, and nine observed structures. A five-refit mask-conditioned graph variational autoencoder reached 5.248 mm and nearest-neighbour retrieval 8.931 mm. The paired difference was 1.531 mm (95% confidence interval 1.384 to 1.711), and the ordering held in a raw-coordinate sensitivity arm. Expert manual labels exist for 58 external CT cases, but our registered reference is close enough to score only five structures. There the closed-form estimator again had lower average surface distance, 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance, and Chamfer error for both completed atria. On a second public benchmark of 20 cases the reference was close enough for three of four completed structures, and the same ordering held there. Four structures have no expert reference. The released model and its completion operator support cohort-unification research on aligned CT, not clinical use.

AI.tldr: Researchers created a comprehensive 11-structure cardiac CT statistical shape model with 383 automatically labeled cases, showing that a closed-form conditional-Gaussian estimator outperforms deep learning and nearest-neighbor approaches for reconstructing missing cardiac structures.
AI.motivation: Existing cardiac shape resources lack comprehensive anatomical structures (atrial appendage, pulmonary veins, caval stumps) as separate blocks in one mesh, and completion benchmarks use inappropriate baselines (least-squares projection) rather than proper conditional estimators.
AI.method: Built an 11-structure cardiac CT statistical shape model from 383 automatically labeled cases with 11,571-vertex correspondence.
