Compared completion estimators including: 1) closed-form conditional-Gaussian estimator, 2) five-refit mask-conditioned graph variational autoencoder, 3) nearest-neighbor retrieval. Evaluated on internal held-out cases (76 cases) and external benchmarks.
AI.result: The closed-form conditional-Gaussian estimator achieved 3.717 mm mean per-vertex error, outperforming the graph VAE (5.248 mm) and nearest-neighbor (8.931 mm). This superiority held across internal validation and external benchmarks, with consistent ordering in performance. External validation was limited to 5 of 11 structures due to registration issues.
AI.conclusion: The released comprehensive cardiac shape model with its optimal conditional-Gaussian completion operator enables better cohort-unification research on aligned CT data, though it's not suitable for clinical use. Traditional statistical methods outperform deep learning approaches for this shape completion task.

title: Separating Covariate Shift from Mechanism Change with Two Discriminators: CJSD, a Conditional Discrepancy with an Exact Covariate-Concept Decomposition
comment: 11 pages, 7 figures
summary: Streaming systems that maintain a pool of expert models must repeatedly decide whether to reuse an existing expert for arriving data, spawn a new one, or defer. We present a decision layer that makes all three outcomes statistically meaningful. Reuse and spawn are posed as one-sided sequential hypotheses on a conditional (mechanism-level) discrepancy, separated by an indifference zone; defer is exactly the state in which neither betting e-process has accumulated sufficient evidence. We prove finite-time anytime validity for the observable surrogate discrepancy of a predictable discriminator sequence, and an unconditional one-sided transfer to the population quantity in which each side's slack is the excess risk of a single discriminator; an empirically observed downward-bias regularity makes the spawn side exactly conservative. Recency without sacrificing the guarantee is obtained by a restarted e-detector: a bank of unwindowed betting supermartingales at geometrically spaced restart times (O(log t) memory), with the error budget spent over restart instances, which preserves lifetime anytime validity; spending over expert-creation order likewise controls multiplicity for unboundedly many experts. On synthetic multi-concept streams, Electricity, Covertype, and the recurrence-heavy INSECTS benchmark, the instance-accounted restarted bank achieves zero false spawns and zero false reuses after switches and matches or exceeds the retired windowed heuristic (INSECTS-reoccurring accuracy 0.675), making the deployed algorithm and the guaranteed algorithm one and the same.

AI.tldr: A statistical decision layer for streaming expert systems that provides guaranteed control over false spawns and reuses using e-processes with geometric restarts and recency mechanisms.
AI.motivation: Streaming systems maintaining expert pools need principled statistical decisions about when to reuse existing experts, spawn new ones, or defer decisions, while ensuring reliability and avoiding false expert creation or reuse errors.
AI.method: A decision layer using one-sided sequential hypotheses on conditional discrepancy with indifference zone; employs e-processes for reuse/spawn decisions with deferral when insufficient evidence. Uses restarted e-detectors with geometrically spaced restart times (O(log t) memory) for recency while maintaining guarantees, and controls multiplicity via error budget spending over expert-creation order.
AI.result: Achieves zero false spawns and zero false reuses after concept switches on synthetic multi-concept streams, Electricity, Covertype, and INSECTS benchmarks. Matches or exceeds performance of retired windowed heuristics (INSECTS-reoccurring accuracy 0.675).
AI.conclusion: The method provides statistically meaningful decisions with finite-time anytime validity guarantees for expert management in streaming systems, unifying the deployed and guaranteed algorithms while maintaining recency without sacrificing statistical guarantees.

title: Learning Early-to-Final Solution Consistency for MILP Acceleration
summary: Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) is a fundamental problem class in operations research and combinatorial optimization, with broad applications to industrial decision-making. Owing to their NP-hardness, however, modern solvers may struggle to find high-quality solutions for challenging MILP instances within practical time limits. Recent learning-based approaches seek to accelerate MILP solving by directly predicting high-quality solutions from static instance-level features, such as variable-constraint bipartite graphs. Yet accurate solution prediction from instance features alone is difficult, and these methods largely overlook the information revealed during the solver's search process. In this paper, we find that solutions produced at the early search stage of MILP solvers, which are computationally cheap to obtain, are often structurally close to the solutions found after full-budget search. Motivated by this observation, we propose a new solver-informed paradigm that shifts the learning target from variable assignment to early-to-final consistency: for each variable, we predict whether its early-stage assignment should persist in full-budget solutions. The predicted consistency naturally guides downstream search, for instance by fixing the assignments deemed consistent. At inference time, we further ensemble consistency predictions across multiple early-stage solutions to improve robustness. Experiments across four MILP benchmarks show our method improves prediction-guided search across diverse downstream pipelines. With Gurobi, our proposed method reduces the primal gap by 56.9% on average and closes it completely on combinatorial auction instances. Besides, we transferred the Gurobi-trained model zero-shot to SCIP without adaptation, achieving a 36.4% average gap reduction across benchmarks.

AI.tldr: A new MILP solver-informed paradigm that predicts consistency between early-stage and final solutions, improving solution quality by 56.9% gap reduction with Gurobi and enabling zero-shot transfer to SCIP.
AI.motivation: Existing learning-based approaches for MILP acceleration rely on predicting solutions from static instance features, which is difficult and overlooks valuable search process information revealed during solving.
AI.method: Proposes shifting learning target from variable assignment to early-to-final consistency prediction. For each variable, predicts whether its early-stage assignment persists in final solutions. Uses multiple early-stage solutions for ensemble predictions to guide downstream search by fixing consistent assignments.
AI.result: Experiments across four MILP benchmarks show 56.9% average primal gap reduction with Gurobi, complete gap closure on combinatorial auction instances. Zero-shot transfer of Gurobi-trained model to SCIP achieves 36.4% average gap reduction.
AI.conclusion: The solver-informed paradigm leveraging early-to-final consistency prediction effectively accelerates MILP solving, improves solution quality, and demonstrates strong transferability across different solvers.

title: Evidence Before Expansion: Reuse, Spawn, or Defer in Lifelong Expert Pools
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures
summary: Streaming systems that maintain a pool of expert models must repeatedly decide whether to reuse an existing expert for arriving data, spawn a new one, or defer. We present a decision layer that makes all three outcomes statistically meaningful. Reuse and spawn are posed as one-sided sequential hypotheses on a conditional (mechanism-level) discrepancy, separated by an indifference zone; defer is exactly the state in which neither betting e-process has accumulated sufficient evidence. We prove finite-time anytime validity for the observable surrogate discrepancy of a predictable discriminator sequence, and an unconditional one-sided transfer to the population quantity in which each side's slack is the excess risk of a single discriminator; an empirically observed downward-bias regularity makes the spawn side exactly conservative. Recency without sacrificing the guarantee is obtained by a restarted e-detector: a bank of unwindowed betting supermartingales at geometrically spaced restart times (O(log t) memory), with the error budget spent over restart instances, which preserves lifetime anytime validity; spending over expert-creation order likewise controls multiplicity for unboundedly many experts. On synthetic multi-concept streams, Electricity, Covertype, and the recurrence-heavy INSECTS benchmark, the instance-accounted restarted bank achieves zero false spawns and zero false reuses after switches and matches or exceeds the retired windowed heuristic (INSECTS-reoccurring accuracy 0.675), making the deployed algorithm and the guaranteed algorithm one and the same.

AI.tldr: A streaming system with expert pools uses statistically grounded decisions (reuse, spawn, defer) based on sequential hypothesis testing with e-processes, achieving guaranteed finite-time validity and handling concept drift via restarted e-detectors with logarithmic memory.
AI.motivation: Streaming systems maintaining expert pools need principled statistical methods to decide when to reuse existing experts versus spawn new ones, while maintaining anytime validity guarantees and handling concept drift without sacrificing statistical rigor.
AI.method: Proposes a decision layer framing reuse/spawn as one-sided sequential hypotheses on conditional discrepancy with indifference zone. Uses e-processes for statistical evidence, restarted e-detectors with geometrically spaced restart times (O(log t) memory) for handling concept drift while preserving lifetime anytime validity, and controls multiplicity for unbounded experts.
AI.result: Achieves zero false spawns and zero false reuses after concept switches on synthetic and real datasets (Electricity, Covertype, INSECTS). Matches or exceeds windowed heuristic performance (INSECTS-reoccurring accuracy 0.675) while providing formal statistical guarantees.
AI.conclusion: The method provides statistically meaningful decisions for expert reuse/spawn/defer in streaming systems with guaranteed anytime validity, handles concept drift efficiently via restarted e-detectors with logarithmic memory, and makes the deployed algorithm identical to the guaranteed algorithm.

title: Rethinking Patch Based Multivariate Time Series Forecasting with Semantic Structured Partitioning
summary: Multivariate time series forecasting (MTSF) is a fundamental task in many real world applications. Existing patch based forecasting methods generally fall into three categories: fixed partitioning, multi-scale partitioning, and extendable partitioning. Fixed partitioning often breaks meaningful temporal boundaries, multi-scale partitioning may introduce redundant representations across scales, and extendable partitioning improves flexibility but still lacks an explicit mechanism for organizing semantic structure and modeling interactions among heterogeneous temporal patterns. To address these limitations, we propose SCPaT, a Transformer based framework built on semantic structured partitioning. SCPaT first decomposes input sequences into semantically consistent units through adaptive semantic unit generation, then constructs a dynamic semantic graph to model directed dependencies among these units and organize them into higher order semantic blocks. Based on these structured representations, an importance aware routing mechanism adaptively dispatches different semantic blocks to different experts for customized modeling. Extensive experiments on 12 real world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of SCPaT.

AI.tldr: SCPaT is a Transformer-based framework for multivariate time series forecasting that uses semantic structured partitioning to organize temporal patterns into meaningful units and model their interactions through adaptive routing to specialized experts.
AI.motivation: Existing patch-based forecasting methods have limitations: fixed partitioning breaks temporal boundaries, multi-scale partitioning creates redundant representations, and extendable partitioning lacks mechanisms for organizing semantic structure and modeling interactions among heterogeneous temporal patterns.
AI.method: 1) Decomposes input sequences into semantically consistent units through adaptive semantic unit generation; 2) Constructs a dynamic semantic graph to model directed dependencies among units and organize them into higher-order semantic blocks; 3) Uses an importance-aware routing mechanism to adaptively dispatch different semantic blocks to different experts for customized modeling.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on 12 real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of SCPaT compared to existing methods, showing improved forecasting performance through better organization and modeling of semantic temporal patterns.
AI.conclusion: SCPaT addresses limitations of existing patch-based forecasting methods by introducing semantic structured partitioning with adaptive routing, providing a more effective framework for multivariate time series forecasting that better captures and organizes meaningful temporal patterns.

title: Reliable Neural Collapse Approximation for Open-World Test-Time Adaptation
summary: Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) methods aim to bridge the domain gap between the source and target domains. However, traditional TTA methods become ineffective when the label distribution shift occurs, a challenge commonly referred to as an open-world scenario. In this paper, we introduce a new method named Reliable Neural Collapse approximation (ReNC) for Open-World Test-Time Adaptation (OWTTA). Specifically, we leverage neural collapse as a structural prior for reliable target-domain adaptation. Guided by this prior, we justify that the pre-trained classifier weights can serve as the prototypes of the source domain. By measuring the similarity between samples and prototypes, we filter out the Out-Of-Distribution~(OOD) samples for reliable updates. Furthermore, we propose a neural collapse approximation mechanism to refine these prototypes, ensuring they can gradually adapt to the target domain while maintaining the neural collapse structure. Extensive experiments on several open-world benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method. Our empirical analysis suggests that ReNC better preserves NC-related properties in the target domain, providing useful evidence for explaining reliable OWTTA and offering new insights for model design. Code is available at https://github.com/JiaqiLin-AI/ReNC.

AI.tldr: ReNC is a test-time adaptation method that uses neural collapse as a structural prior to handle open-world scenarios where label distribution shifts occur, enabling reliable adaptation by filtering out-of-distribution samples and refining prototypes.
AI.motivation: Traditional Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) methods fail when label distribution shifts occur (open-world scenarios), creating a need for methods that can reliably adapt to target domains even when class distributions differ from the source domain.
AI.method: The method leverages neural collapse as a structural prior, using pre-trained classifier weights as source domain prototypes. It measures similarity between samples and prototypes to filter out-of-distribution samples for reliable updates, and employs a neural collapse approximation mechanism to refine prototypes while maintaining the neural collapse structure as they adapt to the target domain.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on open-world benchmarks demonstrate superior performance. Empirical analysis shows ReNC better preserves neural collapse-related properties in the target domain, providing evidence for explaining reliable Open-World TTA and offering new insights for model design.
AI.conclusion: ReNC effectively addresses open-world test-time adaptation by incorporating neural collapse as a structural prior, enabling reliable target-domain adaptation through prototype refinement and OOD filtering, with empirical results validating its superiority and providing new design insights for TTA methods.

title: ReguSim: Evaluating LLM Agent Rule Grounding in Financial Compliance
summary: LLM agents in financial markets may cite rules yet still submit orders that violate executable constraints or misread surveillance evidence. We introduce ReguSim, a controlled financial-compliance environment, and ReguBench, a target-marked monitoring benchmark, to separate four artifacts: stated reasoning, attempted action, execution enforcement, and monitor evidence. In trader runs with DeepSeek V4 Pro and Gemini 3.5 Flash, visible rules reduce but do not eliminate rejected actions, and incentive or persona framing shifts behavior. A bridge study shows that trader rationales can mislead an independent monitor unless enforcement evidence is shown. In monitoring, simple structured baselines either match or exceed prompt-only LLMs. The results frame financial compliance evaluation as an audit of rule-grounded actions and evidence use, rather than a single compliance score.

AI.tldr: Financial LLM agents often violate executable constraints despite citing rules. The paper introduces ReguSim environment and ReguBench benchmark to evaluate compliance through reasoning, actions, enforcement, and evidence artifacts.
AI.motivation: Current LLM agents in financial markets can cite compliance rules but still submit orders that violate executable constraints or misread surveillance evidence, creating a gap between stated knowledge and actual behavior.
AI.method: Introduces ReguSim (controlled financial-compliance environment) and ReguBench (target-marked monitoring benchmark) to separate four artifacts: stated reasoning, attempted action, execution enforcement, and monitor evidence. Tests with DeepSeek V4 Pro and Gemini 3.5 Flash trader agents under various framing conditions.
AI.result: Visible rules reduce but don't eliminate rejected actions; incentive/persona framing shifts behavior. Trader rationales can mislead independent monitors unless enforcement evidence is shown. In monitoring, simple structured baselines match or exceed prompt-only LLMs.
AI.conclusion: Financial compliance evaluation should be framed as an audit of rule-grounded actions and evidence use rather than a single compliance score, requiring multi-faceted assessment of reasoning, actions, enforcement, and evidence.

title: PETA:Parameter-Efficient Test-Time Adaptation for Virtual Screening
summary: Accurately ranking active ligands for a target protein pocket from massive chemical libraries remains a central challenge in virtual screening. DrugCLIP and its recent extensions substantially accelerate this process by encoding protein pockets and molecules into a shared embedding space. Despite this progress, further performance improvements typically require retraining the entire model, incurring substantial computational overhead and making target-specific customization inefficient. In this work, we formulate the specialization of pretrained virtual screening models to individual pockets as a test-time adaptation problem and propose PETA, a parameter-efficient framework that directly adapts pretrained model at test time. Given a target pocket, PETA constructs pocket-specific negatives through molecular diffusion and chemical validity filtering, and further moves them toward the reference ligand retrieved from structural databases via embedding-space mixup to create more challenging ranking tasks. A ranking objective then places greater emphasis on suppressing high-scoring invalid candidates that could contaminate the top-ranked screening results, providing structured supervision for lightweight adaptation. Experiments across diverse benchmarks demonstrate that this lightweight, pocket-specific adaptation outperforms both pretrained and fully retrained baselines while updating only the LayerNorm parameters, which account for approximately $0.03\%$ of the full model.

AI.tldr: PETA enables parameter-efficient test-time adaptation of pretrained virtual screening models for individual protein pockets, outperforming both pretrained and fully retrained baselines while updating only 0.03% of model parameters.
AI.motivation: Current virtual screening models like DrugCLIP require full retraining for performance improvements, which is computationally expensive and inefficient for target-specific customization. There's a need for efficient adaptation to individual protein pockets without full retraining overhead.
AI.method: PETA formulates specialization as test-time adaptation: 1) constructs pocket-specific negatives via molecular diffusion and chemical validity filtering, 2) moves them toward reference ligands via embedding-space mixup to create challenging ranking tasks, 3) uses ranking objective emphasizing suppression of high-scoring invalid candidates, 4) updates only LayerNorm parameters (~0.03% of full model).
AI.result: PETA outperforms both pretrained and fully retrained baselines across diverse benchmarks while being lightweight and computationally efficient, demonstrating effective pocket-specific adaptation with minimal parameter updates.
AI.conclusion: PETA provides a parameter-efficient framework for test-time adaptation of virtual screening models to individual protein pockets, enabling target-specific customization without expensive retraining while maintaining or improving performance.

title: Optimal Skill Selection for LLM Agents with Provable Bicriteria Guarantees
summary: Loading reusable skill documents into a bounded context window is now the primary way large language model (LLM) agents acquire task-specific capabilities, which makes skill selection a first-order determinant of task performance and token cost. Yet current agents score skills independently by semantic relevance and assemble the set by top-$k$ or greedy packing, with no quality guarantee or cost awareness on the selected set. As a result, redundant or poorly chosen skills waste scarce context tokens and can even degrade performance. We give the first model of how the selected skill set shapes execution outcomes and cast skill selection as an optimization problem: choose a skill set under a hard token budget to maximize a monotone submodular benefit minus context penalty. For this problem, we develop Best Prefix Selection (BPS), a polynomial-time algorithm, and prove, to our knowledge, the first performance guarantee for skill selection: a bicriteria $(1-1/e,1)$ approximation whose benefit coefficient is optimal in polynomial time. On a contamination-controlled BigCodeBench variant, BPS outperforms all the baselines, reaching $0.73$ measured task success versus $0.20$--$0.52$ for released skill routers, text retrievers, and the executor's own selection, on $28\%$ fewer tokens than the strongest released router.

AI.tldr: BPS algorithm solves skill selection for LLM agents with theoretical guarantees, outperforming baselines on coding tasks while using fewer tokens.
AI.motivation: Current LLM agents select skills independently based on semantic relevance using top-k or greedy packing, lacking quality guarantees, cost awareness, and often selecting redundant or poor skills that waste context tokens and degrade performance.
AI.method: Formalizes skill selection as optimization: maximize monotone submodular benefit minus context penalty under token budget constraints. Develops Best Prefix Selection (BPS) polynomial-time algorithm.
AI.result: BPS achieves (1-1/e,1) bicriteria approximation with optimal benefit coefficient. On BigCodeBench variant: 0.73 task success vs 0.20-0.52 for baselines, using 28% fewer tokens than strongest released router.
AI.conclusion: BPS provides first theoretical guarantees for skill selection, significantly improving performance and efficiency by treating skill selection as optimization rather than independent scoring.

title: Multi-Source Wasserstein Distributionally Robust Graph Learning
summary: Network topology inference from graph signals is central to graph signal processing with applications in neuroscience, sensor, and social networks. In practice, target-domain samples are scarce while heterogeneous source-domain data are abundant. Fusing these sources is challenging: Euclidean averaging works for homogeneous sources but degrades sharply as inter-source divergence grows, collapsing distinct geometries into an inflated, biased consensus. We exploit the Wasserstein metric's distribution-preserving properties to counter heterogeneity while preserving each source's intrinsic geometry. We propose MS-WDRO, a multi-source Wasserstein distributionally robust graph learning framework that fuses heterogeneous sources via their weighted Wasserstein barycenter, a geometrically principled nominal distribution, then builds an ambiguity ball around it to hedge residual uncertainty. Minimizing worst-case risk yields a tractable regularized Laplacian estimator solved efficiently via a provably convergent ADMM scheme. We establish non-asymptotic guarantees: a finite-sample concentration bound for the empirical barycenter, a pooling bias lower bound proving naive aggregation is suboptimal, and an out-of-sample excess risk bound decaying at a parametric rate with only logarithmic dependence on source count. To calibrate hyperparameters governing robustness, sparsity, and source fusion, we unroll the solver into a differentiable architecture trained end-to-end, achieving data-adaptive calibration beyond cross-validation while retaining interpretability. Experiments on synthetic benchmarks and the multi-site ABIDE~I neuroimaging dataset show MS-WDRO consistently outperforms seven baselines in graph recovery, sample efficiency, and downstream diagnostic utility, with the largest gains in the sample-scarce regime.

AI.tldr: Multi-source Wasserstein distributionally robust graph learning framework (MS-WDRO) that fuses heterogeneous graph signal sources via Wasserstein barycenters and ambiguity sets to infer network topologies with improved sample efficiency and robustness.
AI.motivation: Network topology inference from graph signals is important for applications like neuroscience, sensor networks, and social networks. In practice, target-domain samples are scarce while heterogeneous source-domain data are abundant. Traditional Euclidean averaging methods degrade with heterogeneous sources, collapsing distinct geometries into biased consensus.
AI.method: Proposed MS-WDRO framework: 1) Fuse heterogeneous sources via their weighted Wasserstein barycenter as a geometrically principled nominal distribution, 2) Build an ambiguity ball around it to hedge residual uncertainty, 3) Minimize worst-case risk to get tractable regularized Laplacian estimator, 4) Solve via convergent ADMM scheme, 5) Use unrolled differentiable architecture for end-to-end hyperparameter calibration.
AI.result: Established non-asymptotic guarantees: finite-sample concentration bound for empirical barycenter, pooling bias lower bound proving naive aggregation is suboptimal, out-of-sample excess risk bound decaying at parametric rate with logarithmic dependence on source count. Experiments show MS-WDRO outperforms 7 baselines in graph recovery, sample efficiency, and downstream diagnostic utility, especially in sample-scarce regimes.
AI.conclusion: MS-WDRO provides an effective framework for fusing heterogeneous graph signal sources using Wasserstein geometry, offering theoretical guarantees, computational efficiency, and superior performance over existing methods, particularly when target-domain samples are scarce.

title: ExPhy: A Benchmark for Explicit Physical Property Learning in Multi-Object Trajectory Forecasting
summary: Understanding object dynamics requires not only predicting future trajectories but also examining whether a model captures the physical properties that govern motion. However, existing benchmarks rarely expose object-level physical properties as explicit evaluation targets alongside trajectory forecasting. To address this gap, we introduce \emph{ExPhy}, a multi-object trajectory forecasting benchmark containing 24,000 simulated physical scenes with explicit object-level labels for mass, friction, and restitution. ExPhy provides observed and future trajectories together with an in-distribution (ID) split and two out-of-distribution (OOD) splits over physical parameters (OOD-Parameter) and initial states (OOD-Initial) for jointly evaluating trajectory forecasting and physical property estimation. We further instantiate \textsc{PhyODE}, a physics-guided model with an explicit property interface that estimates physical properties from observed trajectories and uses them for differentiable future rollout. On the long-horizon OOD-Initial setting, \textsc{PhyODE} reduces ADE and FDE by 33.1\% and 31.0\%, respectively, compared with the strongest baseline. Zero-shot evaluation on ComPhy further assesses cross-benchmark transfer. Property-level analyses reveal that accurate trajectory forecasting does not necessarily imply accurate recovery of the underlying physical properties. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Zest86/ExPhy.

AI.tldr: ExPhy is a new multi-object trajectory forecasting benchmark with explicit physical property labels (mass, friction, restitution), enabling joint evaluation of trajectory prediction and physical property estimation. The paper also introduces PhyODE, a physics-guided model that estimates properties from observed trajectories and uses them for differentiable rollouts.
AI.motivation: Current trajectory forecasting benchmarks lack explicit object-level physical properties as evaluation targets. Understanding object dynamics requires examining whether models capture the physical properties governing motion, not just predicting trajectories.
AI.method: The authors create ExPhy benchmark with 24K simulated scenes with physical property labels. They also develop PhyODE, which estimates physical properties from observed trajectories and uses these for differentiable future rollouts through a physics-guided approach. The benchmark includes ID and OOD splits for comprehensive evaluation.
AI.result: PhyODE reduces ADE and FDE by 33.1% and 31.0% respectively in long-horizon OOD-Initial settings compared to strongest baselines. Zero-shot evaluation on ComPhy shows cross-benchmark transfer capability. Analysis reveals trajectory forecasting accuracy doesn't guarantee accurate physical property recovery.
AI.conclusion: ExPhy enables joint evaluation of trajectory forecasting and physical property estimation, revealing gaps between trajectory prediction and understanding underlying physics. PhyODE demonstrates the value of explicit physical modeling for better generalization, especially in OOD scenarios.

title: Auditing Recorded Predictive Lead Service-Line Classifications Against Physical Verification: A Statewide Study of New York
comment: 14 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. Analysis code and data provenance: https://github.com/msarmadsohail/predictive-lead-service-line-audit
summary: Under the US Lead and Copper Rule Revisions, a utility may determine a service line's material with a predictive model instead of inspecting it. New York State publishes, per address, which method was used. Almost no address carries both a model classification and a physical verification, so the check is between populations within a utility rather than paired addresses. We screen all 153 New York localities that classified at least 100 addresses this way. Seventy-five (49%), covering 125,990 addresses or 57% of those screened, record one value. Zero variance alone is not misconduct: 68 of the 75 match their own verification or have too little to test. Seven are contradicted by their own crews, six beyond any sampling explanation. Five are boroughs of New York City, which file as one system; one is East Rochester, 550 km away. New York City is the largest case: a predictive model is the recorded basis for 43,215 addresses, and on all of them the recorded material is "Known Other". The city records "Unknown" on 121,779 addresses, 1,880 already excavated, and lead on 120,692. In the model bucket both counts are zero, and the 95% upper bound on the rate is 0.0085%. Across the rest of New York the same method records lead or the hedge "Unknown but could be lead" on 12.21% of 176,888 addresses, a comparison whose weaknesses we report. The model-cleared population is newer, median year built 1984 against 1930, and construction era accounts for about a third of the gap and not the rest: holding era fixed, records-based classification finds lead at 4.3-31.9%, physical verification at 1.5-14.5%, the model in no era. Six era-aware estimators place the expected lead lines among them at 1,150-1,450. Two findings need no comparison: 7,782 of these addresses are in pre-1940 buildings, and the archived 2025 snapshot shows the public-side determination was copied from a customer-side model output.

AI.tldr: New York State utilities use predictive models instead of physical inspections for lead service line identification, and researchers found statistical anomalies suggesting potential issues with model implementation, particularly in New York City where the model cleared 43,215 addresses as "Known Other" with zero lead detections despite evidence suggesting some should contain lead.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether utilities in New York State are properly implementing predictive models for lead service line identification as permitted under the US Lead and Copper Rule Revisions, and to examine statistical anomalies in model-reported results that suggest potential issues.
AI.method: Screened all 153 New York localities that classified at least 100 addresses using predictive models; analyzed data from NYS public records showing which method was used per address; examined populations with model classifications vs physical verifications; used statistical methods to identify zero-variance cases and conducted era-aware analysis of building construction dates.
AI.result: Found 75 localities (49%) with zero variance in model predictions, covering 125,990 addresses; identified 7 localities where model results contradicted their own verification crews; New York City's model classified 43,215 addresses as "Known Other" with zero lead detections while other methods found lead on 12.21% of addresses elsewhere; model-cleared addresses were newer buildings (median 1984 vs 1930); estimated 1,150-1,450 expected lead lines among model-cleared addresses.
AI.conclusion: There are significant statistical anomalies in how predictive models are being implemented for lead service line identification in New York, with evidence suggesting some utilities may not be properly using the models, particularly in cases where zero variance or implausible results (like New York City's 43,215 addresses all classified as "Known Other") raise concerns about potential non-compliance or improper implementation.

title: Manifold Drift in Flow Preference Optimization: A Root Cause of Reward Hacking
summary: Preference optimization is a standard alignment method for generative models, yet extending it to continuous-time dynamics remains non-trivial. In flow matching, reward-driven updates modify transport trajectories without an inherent constraint to the pretrained data manifold and can move terminal samples off the pretrained support. We formalize this failure mode as manifold drift. Theoretically, we show that optimal flow matching recovers the terminal data distribution, whereas a preference update leaves the pretrained manifold whenever its induced terminal displacement has a nonzero normal component. As a remedy, we propose ThermoDPO, a temperature-controlled objective that anchors pairwise preference optimization on preferred samples. Across temperature regimes, this objective connects rejection sampling fine-tuning and FlowDPO and controls a pointwise reconstruction-based surrogate for manifold distance. To counteract diminished signals at low temperatures, we further introduce a weighted variant, ThermoDPO-weighted. On the main toy benchmark, ThermoDPO-weighted attains a StrictScore of 0.899, compared with 0.629 for FlowDPO and 0.857 for FlowDPO+RFT. On SD3.5-M at CFG = 4.5, it improves OCR by 47.5% and the average of four metrics by 16.0%.

AI.tldr: ThermoDPO is a temperature-controlled preference optimization method for flow matching models that prevents "manifold drift" by anchoring optimization on preferred samples and controlling reconstruction-based distance to the pretrained data manifold.
AI.motivation: Standard preference optimization methods for generative models face challenges when extended to continuous-time dynamics in flow matching. The "manifold drift" problem occurs where reward-driven updates can move terminal samples off the pretrained data manifold support, breaking alignment with the original training distribution.
AI.method: Proposes ThermoDPO, a temperature-controlled objective that anchors pairwise preference optimization on preferred samples. It connects rejection sampling fine-tuning (RFT) and FlowDPO across temperature regimes and controls a pointwise reconstruction-based surrogate for manifold distance. Also introduces ThermoDPO-weighted variant to handle diminished signals at low temperatures.
AI.result: On the main toy benchmark, ThermoDPO-weighted achieves StrictScore of 0.899, significantly outperforming FlowDPO (0.629) and FlowDPO+RFT (0.857). On SD3.5-M at CFG = 4.5, it improves OCR by 47.5% and the average of four metrics by 16.0%.
AI.conclusion: The temperature-controlled ThermoDPO framework effectively addresses manifold drift in continuous-time preference optimization, enabling better preservation of the pretrained data manifold while improving preference alignment metrics across various benchmarks.

title: G-MARK: Grounded Multi-Agent Reasoning for Cooperative Driving via Knowledge Graphs
comment: Accepted for oral presentation at the 25th IEEE International Conference on Machine Learning and Applications (ICMLA'26)
summary: Autonomous driving systems must operate under partial observability, where safety-critical objects may be occluded or visible only to neighboring connected vehicles. Vehicle-to-vehicle cooperation can reduce this uncertainty, but existing cooperative driving methods often compress multi-agent evidence into latent features or hidden multimodal states. As a result, they obscure which agent observed each object, whether the object is visible to the ego vehicle, and how conflicting evidence affects downstream decisions. We propose G-MARK, a grounded multi-agent reasoning framework that converts cooperative object-centric observations into explicit provenance-aware knowledge graphs (KGs). The resulting KGs preserve object hypotheses together with their source attribution, ego-versus-partner visibility, uncertainty, conflicts, spatial relations, and planning-relevant context. G-MARK then derives a shared feature representation from these KGs, enabling lightweight task heads to support object reasoning, motion prediction, control selection, and trajectory forecasting. Compared with the state-of-the-art baseline, GMARK improves occlusion reasoning accuracy by 42.2%, reduces control-selection error by 13.1%, and achieves comparable trajectory-planning accuracy with a 25.6x smaller structured communication payload. Our code is available at https://github.com/bhavyagupta98/g-mark.

AI.tldr: G-MARK is a grounded multi-agent reasoning framework for autonomous driving that converts cooperative object-centric observations into provenance-aware knowledge graphs to preserve source attribution, visibility, and conflicts for better occlusion reasoning and decision making.
AI.motivation: Autonomous driving systems face partial observability where safety-critical objects may be occluded or only visible to neighboring vehicles. Existing cooperative driving methods compress multi-agent evidence into latent features, obscuring which agent observed each object, visibility status, and how conflicting evidence affects decisions.
AI.method: G-MARK converts cooperative object-centric observations into explicit provenance-aware knowledge graphs (KGs) that preserve object hypotheses with source attribution, ego-vs-partner visibility, uncertainty, conflicts, spatial relations, and planning context. The framework then derives shared feature representations from these KGs to support various downstream tasks.
AI.result: Compared to state-of-the-art baseline, G-MARK improves occlusion reasoning accuracy by 42.2%, reduces control-selection error by 13.1%, and achieves comparable trajectory-planning accuracy while using 25.6x smaller structured communication payload.
AI.conclusion: G-MARK provides an effective framework for cooperative autonomous driving by explicitly preserving and reasoning about multi-agent evidence through provenance-aware knowledge graphs, enabling better occlusion reasoning and decision-making with reduced communication overhead.

title: Contrastive Mixed Prompt Learning for Incomplete Multimodal Sentiment Analysis with Unseen Modality Combination
summary: Incomplete multimodal sentiment analysis has garnered significant attention in recent years. Existing approaches typically assume that data is missing at random or are designed specifically for certain missing patterns, ignoring the modality combination inconsistency between training and testing phases. However, in real-world scenarios, the testing phase often encounters modal combinations that were not present during the training phase, which leads to insufficient generalization capabilities and unstable performance. In this paper, we introduce the problem of Incomplete Multimodal Sentiment Analysis with Unseen Modality Combinations (IMSAUMC), aiming to enhance model generalization for unseen modality combinations. To address this challenge, we propose the model named $\textbf{C}$ontrastive $\textbf{M}$ixed $\textbf{P}$rompt $\textbf{L}$earning ($\textsf{CMPL}$) for IMSAUMC. It introduces a label-guided contrastive feature learning mechanism to learn robust and discriminative cross-modal representations. Additionally, we design modality-combination prompts with a soft router to facilitate better learning of various modality combinations. Furthermore, we introduce three prompt contrastive learning strategies, which enable effective learning of prompts corresponding to unseen modality combinations, thereby significantly strengthening the model's generalization capabilities in diverse testing scenarios. Extensive experiments on three widely used datasets demonstrate that $\textsf{CMPL}$ achieves more than a 5% improvement in accuracy compared to state-of-the-art approaches.

AI.tldr: A new approach called Contrastive Mixed Prompt Learning (CMPL) addresses incomplete multimodal sentiment analysis for unseen modality combinations, achieving over 5% accuracy improvement over state-of-the-art methods.
AI.motivation: Current incomplete multimodal sentiment analysis methods assume random missing data or work only with specific missing patterns, ignoring that real-world testing often encounters modality combinations not seen during training. This leads to poor generalization and unstable performance.
AI.method: Proposes CMPL with three key components: 1) label-guided contrastive feature learning for robust cross-modal representations, 2) modality-combination prompts with soft router to learn various combinations, 3) three prompt contrastive learning strategies to enable effective learning for unseen modality combinations.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on three widely used datasets show CMPL achieves more than 5% improvement in accuracy compared to state-of-the-art approaches.
AI.conclusion: The proposed CMPL framework effectively addresses the Incomplete Multimodal Sentiment Analysis with Unseen Modality Combinations (IMSAUMC) problem, significantly enhancing model generalization capabilities for diverse testing scenarios with unseen modality combinations.

title: Green BOA: Determining the environmental break-even point for ML-based data compression
comment: 3 pages, 1 figure. Accepted as a lightning-talk contribution at the 2nd International Workshop on Low Carbon Computing (LOCO 2026), Lancaster University, United Kingdom, 10-11 September 2026. Part of the LOCO 2026 proceedings, arXiv:LOCO2026/L05
summary: We summarise the outcome of two summer internship projects based at the University of Manchester, focused on the break-even point in terms of environmental sustainability for ML-based data compression algorithms. Using the example of a ML-based lossless compression algorithm, we compare estimates for the carbon-equivalent of the infrastructure needed for ML training and inference with the carbon-equivalent savings from reduced disk storage requirements, and discuss their break-even point.

AI.tldr: ML-based compression algorithms need to reach a break-even point where energy savings from reduced storage offset the environmental costs of training and inference
AI.motivation: As ML-based data compression algorithms become more prevalent, there's a need to understand when their environmental benefits (from reduced storage) outweigh the environmental costs of their training and inference infrastructure
AI.method: Used a case study approach with a ML-based lossless compression algorithm, comparing carbon-equivalent estimates for ML training/infrastructure with carbon-equivalent savings from reduced disk storage requirements
AI.result: Identified and discussed the break-even point where environmental savings from compression equal or exceed the environmental costs of the ML system
AI.conclusion: Understanding the break-even point is crucial for making environmentally sustainable choices in ML-based compression, ensuring that the technology's benefits justify its environmental footprint

title: A three-dimensional typology of agency for advanced AI systems
summary: Research on the agency of advanced artificial intelligence (AI) systems focuses on agency as a normative concept and on the agency of particularly agentic AI systems. While recent work also focuses on the different profiles of agentic systems, no framework exists to address the question of the type of agency instantiated by advanced AI systems, particularly when considering non-moral forms of agency. Based on established theoretical positions in philosophy, ethics, legal theory and sociology, we develop a typology of agency for frontier AI systems consisting of three dimensions: the nature of agency (moral or legal), its mode (individual or collective) and its locus (human or non-human). Combining these dimensions produces eight possible instantiations of agency, which we classify as conventional, contested or controversial. The typology separates legal from moral agency and thereby creates conceptual space for considering individual, legal, non-human agency without presupposing that advanced AI systems are moral agents. We argue that this distinction is increasingly relevant where instrumental goal pursuit complicates the attribution of AI actions to particular human actors.

AI.tldr: A typology framework for understanding different types of agency in advanced AI systems across three dimensions: nature (moral/legal), mode (individual/collective), and locus (human/non-human).
AI.motivation: Existing research focuses on agency as a normative concept or on particularly agentic AI systems, but lacks frameworks to address different types of agency, especially non-moral forms of agency. The attribution of AI actions to human actors becomes complex with instrumental goal pursuit.
AI.method: Developed a typology based on established theoretical positions from philosophy, ethics, legal theory, and sociology. The framework consists of three dimensions: nature of agency (moral or legal), mode (individual or collective), and locus (human or non-human), producing eight possible instantiations classified as conventional, contested, or controversial.
AI.result: Created a three-dimensional typology that separates legal from moral agency, creating conceptual space for considering individual, legal, non-human agency without presupposing advanced AI systems as moral agents.
AI.conclusion: The distinction between legal and moral agency is increasingly relevant as instrumental goal pursuit complicates attribution of AI actions to human actors, providing a useful framework for analyzing frontier AI systems' agency beyond traditional moral agency concepts.

title: Scale-Aware Pretraining of Time Series Foundation Models via Multi-Patch Token Alignment and Hybrid Masking
summary: Pretraining time series foundation models across heterogeneous datasets necessitates effective handling of varying sampling frequencies. Current methods either employ dataset-specific patch sizes and separate FFNs, leading to fragmented representations, or enforce a fixed patch size that neglects inherent temporal variations. To address this, we propose SATS, featuring a scale-aware token alignment mechanism that treats patch size as an explicit notion of scale. By incorporating a contrastive-inspired alignment regularizer, SATS aligns representation spaces across scales while preserving distinct modeling capacities. Furthermore, a hybrid masking strategy combining random and contiguous masking is introduced to capture multi-scale temporal structures. Experimental results on LSTF benchmarks demonstrate that SATS achieves a 9.2% improvement in MSE and an 8.3% gain in GIFT-Eval MASE compared to competitive baselines. Notably, SATS consistently delivers SOTA performance while achieving a 65.6% increase in model efficiency over advanced baselines, highlighting its effectiveness and scalability in time series pretraining.

AI.tldr: SATS is a scale-aware time series pretraining method that aligns representation spaces across different sampling frequencies using a contrastive-inspired alignment regularizer and hybrid masking strategy, achieving SOTA performance with improved efficiency.
AI.motivation: Current time series pretraining methods either use dataset-specific patch sizes/FFNs (leading to fragmented representations) or enforce fixed patch sizes (neglecting inherent temporal variations), creating challenges for handling heterogeneous sampling frequencies.
AI.method: SATS introduces a scale-aware token alignment mechanism treating patch size as an explicit scale notion, incorporates contrastive-inspired alignment regularizer to align representation spaces across scales, and uses hybrid random+contiguous masking to capture multi-scale temporal structures.
AI.result: Achieves 9.2% MSE improvement and 8.3% gain in GIFT-Eval MASE on LSTF benchmarks, with consistent SOTA performance and 65.6% increase in model efficiency over advanced baselines.
AI.conclusion: SATS effectively addresses scale heterogeneity in time series pretraining, demonstrating superior performance and efficiency through explicit scale modeling and cross-scale representation alignment.

title: On the Applicability of Safety Nets: A Safety-By-Design Solution for Certifying Neural Networks
summary: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in safety-critical aviation systems presents significant challenges for certification and deployment. Aviation, often regarded as the safest form of transportation, relies on numerous safety-critical systems. For future safety-critical AI-based systems, EASA requires a Safety-by-Design approach, which can be achieved by using Safety Nets that combine neural network compression with lookup tables to ensure 100 % correct runtime behavior across the discretized operational design domain. Although Safety Nets have been studied, no comprehensive study of their performance characteristics and system design trade-offs has been conducted. This work presents the first systematic analysis of the trade-off between neural network and lookup table size in Safety Nets. By systematically comparing neural networks with diverse architectures, this study identifies optimal design parameters that minimize overall storage and memory requirements while maintaining certification compliance. Results demonstrate that architectures with 3 to 5 hidden layers, each with approximately 50 to 100 nodes, combined with one-hot encoding, achieve the best balance. In these configurations, neural networks accurately represent at least 97 % of the data, while compact lookup tables handle the remaining errors. The resulting Safety Nets reduce the system size by almost three orders of magnitude, fitting within the memory budget of current avionics hardware while guaranteeing 100 % correct outputs across the entire discretized input space, as required by EASA guidelines. This work provides the first-ever open-source implementation of Safety Nets for HCAS and VCAS with replicable results, demonstrating a practical pathway toward certifiable AI-based systems in aviation and establishing Safety Nets as a viable Safety-by-Design solution for safety-critical applications.

AI.tldr: Safety Nets combine neural networks with lookup tables to enable certifiable AI in aviation by ensuring 100% correct outputs across discretized operational domains, achieving 1000x size reduction while meeting EASA certification requirements.
AI.motivation: AI integration in safety-critical aviation systems faces certification challenges, requiring Safety-by-Design approaches. While Safety Nets (neural networks + lookup tables) have been proposed, no comprehensive study exists on their performance characteristics and design trade-offs for practical implementation.
AI.method: Systematic analysis of trade-off between neural network and lookup table size in Safety Nets. Compared diverse neural network architectures to identify optimal design parameters that minimize storage/memory while maintaining certification compliance.
AI.result: Architectures with 3-5 hidden layers (50-100 nodes each) with one-hot encoding achieve best balance. Neural networks accurately represent ≥97% of data, while compact lookup tables handle remaining errors. Safety Nets reduce system size by almost three orders of magnitude, fitting avionics memory budgets while guaranteeing 100% correct outputs across discretized input space.
AI.conclusion: First-ever open-source implementation of Safety Nets for HCAS/VCAS demonstrates practical pathway to certifiable AI-based aviation systems, establishing Safety Nets as viable Safety-by-Design solution for safety-critical applications.

title: Systematic Evaluation of TabPFN-TS for Zero-Shot Probabilistic Heat Load Forecasting in District Heating Networks
comment: 33 pages, 10 figures; supplementary information included
summary: District heating energy hubs require reliable heat load forecasts for efficient operational scheduling. Conventional forecasting workflows train system-specific models on historical data, which can become burdensome when networks change through new consumers, retrofits, or changing operating regimes. Zero-shot time-series foundation models and in-context forecasting offer a promising alternative: they can adapt at inference time from recent observations rather than by repeated retraining. This study systematically evaluates TabPFN-TS against time-series foundation models and trained machine-learning baselines for probabilistic heat load forecasting in district heating networks. Unlike foundation models pretrained on large collections of real time series, TabPFN-TS relies on synthetic pretraining data, which avoids direct pretraining-test overlap but raises the question of whether the learned prior captures district heating dynamics. We analyze covariate choice, context length, temporal resolution, and prediction horizon on representative operating weeks, validate the selected configuration over a full year, and test transferability on a second network. The results identify hourly 24-hour forecasting with a 12-week rolling context and ambient temperature as a parsimonious high-performing configuration; longer context windows do not improve accuracy. TabPFN-TS remains close to Chronos-2 in deterministic accuracy, reaching CVRMSE values of 13.06% versus 12.48% on the main dataset, and lies within the critical-difference threshold in the daily-rank comparison. Although Chronos-2 achieves the lowest aggregate full-year error, TabPFN-TS shows better empirical calibration. Finally, the diagnostic findings motivate a Multi-Resolution Residual-Correction Forecaster that combines a low-frequency Base Forecaster with a short-horizon Residual Forecaster to improve longer-horizon planning accuracy.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates TabPFN-TS, a zero-shot time-series foundation model using synthetic pretraining, for probabilistic heat load forecasting in district heating networks, comparing it against time-series foundation models and trained ML baselines.
AI.motivation: District heating energy hubs need reliable heat load forecasts for efficient scheduling. Conventional models require burdensome retraining when networks change, so zero-shot foundation models that adapt at inference time offer a promising alternative.
AI.method: The study systematically evaluates TabPFN-TS against time-series foundation models and trained ML baselines. It analyzes covariate choice, context length, temporal resolution, and prediction horizon on representative operating weeks, validates configurations over a full year, and tests transferability on a second network.
AI.result: TabPFN-TS performs close to Chronos-2 in deterministic accuracy (13.06% vs 12.48% CVRMSE) and shows better empirical calibration. Optimal configuration is hourly 24-hour forecasting with 12-week rolling context and ambient temperature. Longer contexts don't improve accuracy. The findings motivate a Multi-Resolution Residual-Correction Forecaster combining low-frequency base forecasting with short-horizon residual correction.
AI.conclusion: TabPFN-TS with synthetic pretraining is a viable alternative for district heating forecasting, offering competitive accuracy with better calibration. The proposed multi-resolution approach could improve longer-horizon planning accuracy.

title: CLaST: Context-aware Contrastive VAE for Probabilistic Time Series Forecasting
summary: Probabilistic forecasting models are widely used for time series forecasting in domains such as energy systems, finance, medicine, and transportation. In recent years, deep generative models have shown strong results on probabilistic forecasting, yet many conventional approaches struggle to capture internal temporal dependencies, leading to latent representations with limited expressive power. To address this limitation, we propose \textit{CLaST}, a VAE framework for probabilistic multivariate time series forecasting. Unlike existing generative models, CLaST learns embeddings that preserve contextual similarity between observations through our contrastive loss function. Experiments across nine widely adopted benchmarks demonstrate that CLaST consistently surpasses strong baseline methods. In short-term forecasting tasks, our approach achieves improvements of up to $16.4\%$ in CRPS and $14.4\%$ in NMAE over the second-best method. Furthermore, in long-term prediction CLaST attains superior overall performance, exceeding the second-best method by up to $48.6\%$ and $25.1\%$ in CRPS and NMAE, respectively.

AI.tldr: CLaST is a VAE-based framework that uses contrastive learning for probabilistic multivariate time series forecasting, achieving state-of-the-art performance on both short-term and long-term forecasting tasks across multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current deep generative models for probabilistic forecasting struggle to capture internal temporal dependencies effectively, leading to limited expressive power in latent representations, which hampers their forecasting performance.
AI.method: Proposes CLaST, a VAE framework that learns embeddings preserving contextual similarity between observations through a novel contrastive loss function, specifically designed for probabilistic multivariate time series forecasting.
AI.result: CLaST consistently outperforms strong baselines across nine benchmarks. In short-term forecasting: up to 16.4% improvement in CRPS and 14.4% in NMAE. In long-term forecasting: up to 48.6% improvement in CRPS and 25.1% in NMAE over second-best methods.
AI.conclusion: CLaST's contrastive learning approach effectively captures temporal dependencies in time series data, leading to superior probabilistic forecasting performance compared to existing generative models, demonstrating the value of preserving contextual similarity in latent representations.

title: DECOWAM: Decoupled Whole-Body World-Action Model for Legged Mobile Manipulation
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures. Introduces DECOWAM, a decoupled whole-body world-action model for legged mobile manipulation, and the ARMDOG real-robot dataset
summary: Mobile manipulation requires a robot to predict how locomotion and arm motion jointly alter future observations and control. Existing world-action models, developed largely for fixed-base platforms, do not explicitly distinguish camera ego-motion from base and arm actions. Here we introduce DECOWAM, a whole-body world-action model that separates these factors through dedicated conditional interfaces. DECOWAM freezes an adapted FastWAM backbone and trains residual adapters, an action-equivalent future bottleneck distilled from privileged observations, adversarially separated base and arm latents, and base-velocity conditioning for video prediction. We further introduce ARMDOG, a real-robot dataset that synchronizes video, whole-body state and action, and language. On a fixed replay protocol, DECOWAM improved both future-video and action prediction over FastWAM, reducing action MSE by 21.7% with 25.95M trainable adaptation parameters. Across 79 closed-loop trials per method, it achieved the highest observed whole-body coordination and base-displacement robustness among the compared systems, while task completion remained comparable to the strongest baseline. These results show that embodiment-aware factorization can support parameter-efficient joint visual prediction and whole-body control under moving viewpoints.

AI.tldr: DECOWAM is a whole-body world-action model that factorizes camera ego-motion from base and arm actions, improving visual prediction and whole-body control for mobile manipulation.
AI.motivation: Existing world-action models don't distinguish camera ego-motion from base and arm actions, which is crucial for mobile manipulation where locomotion and arm motion jointly affect future observations and control.
AI.method: Freezes an adapted FastWAM backbone and trains residual adapters with an action-equivalent future bottleneck distilled from privileged observations, adversarially separated base and arm latents, and base-velocity conditioning for video prediction.
AI.result: Reduced action MSE by 21.7% compared to FastWAM on fixed replay protocol, achieved highest whole-body coordination and base-displacement robustness in 79 closed-loop trials per method, while maintaining comparable task completion to strongest baseline.
AI.conclusion: Embodiment-aware factorization supports parameter-efficient joint visual prediction and whole-body control under moving viewpoints for mobile manipulation.

title: An Inclusive and Lightweight Approach to Federated Continual Learning for Cultural Heritage
comment: 7 pages, 3 figures, Accepted at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Cyber Humanities (IEEE-CH 2026), Venice, Italy, September 7--9, 2026. Accepted author manuscript. Copyright 2026 IEEE
summary: Artificial intelligence can support cultural heritage and digital humanities through large-scale retrieval and analysis of digitized collections. However, cultural heritage data are often distributed across institutions, constrained by ownership and access restrictions, and continuously evolving over time. Federated Continual Learning (FCL) is well suited to this setting, as it enables models to learn from distributed and sequential data without sharing raw collections. In this paper, we propose FedCurv-DR, a lightweight, regularisation-based FCL strategy. The method accumulates parameter-importance estimates across clients and experiences to protect learned knowledge, while updating them only at fixed intervals to minimize communication and computation overhead. We evaluate FedCurv-DR in a continual learning scenario using the WikiArt image dataset for genre classification with evolving styles, reporting performance, energy, and fairness metrics. Our results show that FedCurv- DR reduces forgetting and balances performance, fairness, and energy efficiency for sustainable AI in cultural heritage.

AI.tldr: FedCurv-DR is a lightweight federated continual learning method for cultural heritage applications that accumulates parameter-importance estimates across clients to protect knowledge while minimizing communication overhead.
AI.motivation: Cultural heritage data faces challenges: distributed across institutions, constrained by ownership/access restrictions, and continuously evolving over time. Federated Continual Learning is needed to learn from distributed sequential data without sharing raw collections.
AI.method: FedCurv-DR is a regularization-based FCL strategy that accumulates parameter-importance estimates across clients and experiences to protect learned knowledge, while updating these estimates only at fixed intervals to minimize communication and computation overhead.
AI.result: Evaluation using WikiArt image dataset for genre classification with evolving styles shows FedCurv-DR reduces forgetting and balances performance, fairness, and energy efficiency metrics.
AI.conclusion: FedCurv-DR enables sustainable AI for cultural heritage by effectively addressing forgetting while maintaining balanced performance, fairness, and energy efficiency in federated continual learning scenarios.

title: DARS: Dual-Level Credit Assignment RL with Structured Reasoning for Instruction-Based Image Editing
summary: Instruction-based image editing uses a planner-renderer pipeline: a vision-language model (VLM) first converts the instruction into an edit plan, and a diffusion model then executes that plan. Training such systems with only final-image rewards is inefficient because a poor edit does not reveal whether additional optimization should place more emphasis on the planner or the renderer, and even planner-dominant cases remain difficult to localize within a free-form reasoning trace. We present DARS, a reinforcement learning framework for dual-level credit assignment in this two-stage setting. Across modules, multi-plan multi-render rollouts estimate between-plan and within-plan reward variability for soft module routing, while rollout mean rewards provide hardness estimates for an adaptive curriculum. Within the planner, a four-field structured reasoning output enables a prefix-gated reward and token-level advantage reweighting, turning outcome-level feedback into localized supervision. Experiments on five benchmarks show that DARS outperforms a Joint~RL baseline with the same backbone, data, reward model, and rollout budget, with the largest gains on reasoning-intensive edits.

AI.tldr: DARS is a reinforcement learning framework for dual-level credit assignment in instruction-based image editing systems that uses a planner-renderer pipeline, addressing credit assignment challenges through between-module routing and within-planner localization.
AI.motivation: Training instruction-based image editing systems with only final-image rewards is inefficient because poor edits don't reveal whether issues stem from the planner (vision-language model) or renderer (diffusion model), and planner-dominant failures are hard to localize within free-form reasoning traces.
AI.method: DARS uses a dual-level credit assignment approach: 1) Across modules: multi-plan multi-render rollouts estimate between-plan and within-plan reward variability for soft module routing, with rollout mean rewards providing hardness estimates for an adaptive curriculum. 2) Within planner: four-field structured reasoning output enables prefix-gated reward and token-level advantage reweighting to turn outcome-level feedback into localized supervision.
AI.result: Experiments on five benchmarks show DARS outperforms a Joint RL baseline with the same backbone, data, reward model, and rollout budget, with the largest gains on reasoning-intensive edits.
AI.conclusion: DARS effectively addresses credit assignment challenges in two-stage instruction-based image editing systems by providing both between-module routing and within-planner localization, leading to improved performance especially on complex reasoning tasks.

title: End-to-end Early Classification of Time Series in Non-Stationary Environments
summary: Early Classification of Time Series (ECTS) requires making accurate decisions as early as possible in inherently online and evolving environments. Yet, most existing methods assume stationarity and rely on separable designs, where classification and triggering are optimized independently, an assumption that fundamentally limits their adaptability under drift. In this work, we challenge this paradigm and study ECTS under non-stationary conditions. We provide the first systematic comparison between separable and end-to-end approaches across controlled drifting scenarios. Building on Reinforcement Learning, we introduce DQeND, a unified architecture that jointly learns representation, classification, and triggering decisions, while remaining directly comparable to state-of-the-art separable baselines. Across a wide range of drifts, DQeND demonstrates strong robustness across various non-stationary scenarios, consistently outperforming separable baselines. An ablation study further highlights that jointly updating representation and decision modules is critical to these gains. Overall, our results indicate that end-to-end learning can offer improved adaptation capabilities for ECTS in dynamic environments, and motivate further investigation of alternatives to separable designs.

AI.tldr: DQeND is a unified reinforcement learning architecture for early time series classification that jointly learns representation, classification, and triggering decisions, outperforming separable approaches in non-stationary environments.
AI.motivation: Existing early classification of time series (ECTS) methods assume stationarity and use separable designs where classification and triggering are optimized independently, limiting adaptability under drift. The paper challenges this paradigm by studying ECTS under non-stationary conditions.
AI.method: The authors introduce DQeND, a unified reinforcement learning architecture that jointly learns representation, classification, and triggering decisions while remaining comparable to separable baselines. They perform systematic comparison between separable and end-to-end approaches across controlled drifting scenarios.
AI.result: Across a wide range of drifts, DQeND demonstrates strong robustness across various non-stationary scenarios and consistently outperforms separable baselines. An ablation study shows that jointly updating representation and decision modules is critical to these gains.
AI.conclusion: End-to-end learning offers improved adaptation capabilities for ECTS in dynamic environments, motivating further investigation of alternatives to separable designs. The joint optimization of representation and decision-making is crucial for handling non-stationarity.

title: The Third Restructuring of Software Form: From the Three-Tier Architecture to Storage, Models, and Agents
summary: Software form has undergone two paradigm shifts since its inception: Software 1.0, in which instructions determine behavior, and Software 2.0, in which data determines behavior (machine learning). This paper argues that a third shift - Software 3.0, in which context and reasoning determine behavior - is now underway, and contends that its terminal form converges to three elements: a generalized database (the unified abstraction of all persistent state and memory), a large model (the intelligence core that performs reasoning and generation), and an agent (the execution loop connecting the first two). The core argument is as follows: in the traditional three-tier architecture, the user-interface layer will be absorbed by the model's ability to generate interfaces on demand, the business-logic layer will be re-partitioned along "expressibility x criticality" into model reasoning and storage constraints (with residual deterministic logic retained as tools), and only the data layer will be elevated into the sole persistent infrastructure. We formalize this convergence thesis, present a minimal reference architecture, report evidence from real prototypes and a live model, and systematically analyze both the conditions under which it holds and the boundaries where it fails - determinism, cost, security, and verifiability delimit the thesis's domain of applicability. We argue that the thesis holds in task domains that are expressible, verifiable, externally stateful, and tool-complete, and that it will reshape the roles of developers, the database industry, and the software-engineering discipline.

AI.tldr: A third paradigm shift in software is emerging: Software 3.0, where context and reasoning determine behavior, converging to three core elements: generalized database, large model, and agent.
AI.motivation: The paper argues that software evolution has gone through two major paradigm shifts (Software 1.0: instructions-based, Software 2.0: data/ML-based), and now a third shift is underway where context and reasoning determine behavior, necessitating a new architectural framework.
AI.method: The paper formalizes a convergence thesis, presents a minimal reference architecture, analyzes evidence from real prototypes and live models, and systematically examines the conditions under which the thesis holds and fails across dimensions like determinism, cost, security, and verifiability.
AI.result: The Software 3.0 paradigm converges to three core elements: generalized database (unified abstraction of persistent state), large model (intelligence core for reasoning/generation), and agent (execution loop connecting them). The thesis holds in task domains that are expressible, verifiable, externally stateful, and tool-complete.
AI.conclusion: Software 3.0 will reshape traditional three-tier architecture, absorbing the UI layer into model-generated interfaces, repartitioning business logic along expressibility and criticality axes, and elevating the data layer as sole persistent infrastructure, fundamentally transforming developer roles, database industry, and software engineering discipline.

title: DecoVAE: a Lightweight Interpretable Trend-Seasonal VAE Framework for Efficient Probabilistic Time Series Forecasting
summary: Probabilistic time series forecasting remains challenging, largely because modeling distinct trend and seasonal dynamics requires specialized approaches. Existing methods often fail to capture the unique inner properties of these components, lack interpretability, or suffer from heavy memory and runtime overhead. To address these limitations, we propose DecoVAE, a lightweight interpretable trend-seasonal VAE framework that explicitly decomposes time series into trend and seasonal components by applying domain-specific inductive biases. The trend stream enforces structural smoothness using a differential regularizer on the latent trajectory, analogous to the Hodrick-Prescott filter. Concurrently, the seasonal stream operates in the frequency domain via a complex Gaussian VAE, natively capturing the amplitude and phase of periodic patterns. Extensive evaluations across seven real-world benchmarks show that DecoVAE consistently outperforms strong baselines. It achieves reductions of up to 14.96\% in CRPS and 23.30\% in NMAE for short-term forecasting, and up to 52.68\% and 26.51\% for long-term horizons. Crucially, DecoVAE yields these accuracy gains while remaining highly efficient, reducing model weight by up to 93\% and accelerating speed by up to 74\% compared to the second-best method.

AI.tldr: DecoVAE is a lightweight interpretable VAE framework that explicitly decomposes time series into trend and seasonal components using domain-specific inductive biases, achieving superior probabilistic forecasting performance with significantly reduced computational overhead.
AI.motivation: Probabilistic time series forecasting is challenging due to difficulties in modeling distinct trend and seasonal dynamics. Existing methods often fail to capture unique component properties, lack interpretability, or suffer from heavy memory and runtime overhead.
AI.method: DecoVAE is a trend-seasonal VAE framework that explicitly decomposes time series: 1) Trend stream enforces structural smoothness using differential regularization on latent trajectories (analogous to Hodrick-Prescott filter), 2) Seasonal stream operates in frequency domain via complex Gaussian VAE to capture amplitude and phase of periodic patterns.
AI.result: Extensive evaluations across seven real-world benchmarks show DecoVAE consistently outperforms strong baselines: up to 14.96% reduction in CRPS and 23.30% in NMAE for short-term forecasting, and up to 52.68% and 26.51% for long-term horizons. Achieves these gains while reducing model weight by up to 93% and accelerating speed by up to 74% compared to second-best method.
AI.conclusion: DecoVAE provides an effective solution to probabilistic time series forecasting by combining explicit trend-seasonal decomposition with domain-specific inductive biases, offering superior accuracy, interpretability, and computational efficiency simultaneously.

title: MemTrapBench: Benchmarking Cognitive Traps in LLM Memory Use
comment: Work in progress
summary: Memory has become a key component of large language models, enabling them to retain information and learn from long-term interactions. However, existing memory benchmarks mainly evaluate whether information is correctly extracted, stored, and retrieved, while largely overlooking how retrieved memories reshape model reasoning and affect performance on the current task. We identify memory-induced cognitive traps: even faithfully recorded and semantically relevant memories can distort model reasoning or beliefs and degrade current task performance. To systematically evaluate these failure modes, we introduce MemTrapBench, which covers two forms of cognitive traps: Reasoning Fixation and Belief Distortion. Experiments across two model families and five representative memory frameworks show that MemTrapBench is challenging: all evaluated memory strategies underperform the no-memory setting, with even the strongest methods suffering drops of more than 10%. To mitigate these cognitive traps, we propose AdaptiveMem, a simple yet effective inference-time method that instructs LLMs to avoid memory traps. AdaptiveMem mitigates cognitive traps on MemTrapBench while preserving or improving performance on standard memory benchmarks across diverse memory frameworks.
